teile.einleitung: Archimedes’ principle explains why a huge steel ship floats and a small pebble sinks. It says that every body in a liquid receives an upward force, buoyancy, that is as great as the weight of the liquid it displaces. It was discovered by the Greek scholar Archimedes more than 2200 years ago.
wichtigste: Buoyancy is as great as the weight of the liquid displaced.
Archimedes came from Syracuse on Sicily.
A ship floats because it displaces as much water as it weighs itself.
A body floats if its density is lower than that of water.
One litre of water has a mass of about one kilogram.
You float more easily in the salty Dead Sea, because salt water is denser.
A hot-air balloon rises because the cold air it displaces is heavier than it is.

abschnitte.text: **Archimedes** lived in the 3rd century BC in **Syracuse** on the island of Sicily. He was a mathematician, physicist and inventor all at once. A famous story tells that the king wanted to check whether his crown was made of pure gold. Archimedes is said to have found the solution in the bath and shouted “Eureka”, which means “I have found it”.

When you dip an object into water, it pushes water aside; it **displaces** it. The water then pushes upwards with a force, **buoyancy**. This buoyancy is exactly as great as the weight of the displaced water. So if a stone displaces 3 litres of water, it is pushed upwards with the weight of 3 kilograms of water.

An object with a mass of 5 kilograms that displaces 2 litres under water seems to weigh only 3 kilograms there. That is why you can lift a friend much more easily in the swimming pool than on land. Whether something floats depends on its **density**, that is, on how much mass there is in a particular volume. Wood and ice have a lower density than water and float; stones and iron have a higher one and sink.

A steel ship is mostly hollow inside and filled with air. That is why its wide hull displaces as much water as the whole ship weighs, and it floats. A **submarine** fills tanks with water to dive and pushes the water out again with air to rise. Many fish control their buoyancy in a similar way with an air-filled **swim bladder**.

The principle applies not only in water but in all liquids and gases. A **hot-air balloon** is filled with warm, light air and displaces heavier cold air, so it rises. In Switzerland you can see many balloons every winter at the international balloon festival in **Château-d’Oex**. In the Dead Sea between Israel and Jordan the water is so salty and dense that people lie on top of it almost by themselves.

begriffe.erklaerung: Force with which a liquid or gas pushes a body upwards.
A body pushes liquid aside to make room for itself.
How much mass there is in a particular volume.
How much space something takes up, for example in litres.

gewusst: An iceberg also follows Archimedes’ principle, which is why only about a tenth of it sticks out of the water.
Nobody knows for sure whether the story of the bath and the cry of “Eureka” really happened, because it was only written down long after Archimedes.

teile.einleitung: Archaea are tiny single-celled living things that at first sight look like bacteria. But they form a quite separate large group of life. Many of them live in places that are far too hot, salty or acidic for almost all other living things.
wichtigste: Like bacteria, archaea have no cell nucleus.
Today all living things are divided into three large domains.
Carl Woese recognised the archaea as a separate group in the 1970s.
The name comes from the Greek word for “ancient”.
Many archaea live in hot springs and other extreme places.
Some archaea produce methane, for example in marshes and in the stomachs of cows.
As far as is known, archaea hardly cause any diseases in humans.

abschnitte.text: Archaea are **single-celled organisms**, that is, living things made of only one single cell. Like bacteria they have no **cell nucleus**; their genetic material lies freely in the cell. But in many important features, for example in the structure of their cell envelope, they are clearly different from bacteria. In some processes inside the cell they are even more like the cells of plants, animals and humans.

For a long time people thought there were only two kinds of cell, those with and those without a cell nucleus. In the 1970s the American researcher **Carl Woese** compared the genetic material of many microbes and found in 1977 that the archaea are a separate group. Today all living things are divided into three **domains**: bacteria, archaea and eukaryotes, which include animals and plants. The name archaea comes from the Greek word for “ancient”.

Many archaea are **extremophiles**, which means they love extreme conditions. Some live in boiling hot springs, for example in Yellowstone National Park, or at hot vents in the deep sea. Microbes that grow best at more than 80 degrees are called **hyperthermophiles**, and some can even stand more than 110 degrees. Other archaea live in very salty lakes and colour the water pink or red.

An important group are the **methanogens**, which produce the gas methane. They live where there is no oxygen, for example in the mud of marshes, in rice fields and in the stomachs of cows. Methane is a strong greenhouse gas that contributes to global warming. In biogas plants these archaea are used to obtain energy from manure and green waste.

Archaea do not only live in extreme places, but also in the sea, in the soil and in the human gut. In the ocean they are among the most common living things of all. As far as is known, they hardly cause any diseases in humans. Enzymes from heat-loving microbes are useful in research, for example for laboratory tests in which samples are heated strongly.

begriffe.erklaerung: A living thing that consists of only one single cell.
A separate area in many cells in which the genetic material lies.
The highest level into which all living things are divided.
Living things that live in extreme heat, cold or saltiness.
A flammable gas that is also a strong greenhouse gas.

gewusst: The pink colour of some salt lakes comes partly from salt-loving archaea.
Some researchers think that the cells of animals and plants once arose from a merger of archaea and bacteria.
Before they were discovered to be a separate group, archaea were thought to be bacteria for decades.

teile.einleitung: Al-Biruni was a great scholar who lived in Central Asia around the year 1000. He worked on astronomy, mathematics, geography, physics and the customs of foreign peoples. With a clever measurement from a mountain he even worked out the size of the Earth.
wichtigste: Al-Biruni lived around the year 1000 and was born in 973.
His birthplace is in present-day Uzbekistan.
He wrote most of his works in Arabic.
For many years he worked at the court of Mahmud of Ghazni.
He wrote a famous book about India, its religion, science and customs.
From a mountain he worked out the Earth’s radius using an angle to the horizon.
He measured the density of metals and gemstones very precisely.
He exchanged letters with the young scholar Ibn Sina.

abschnitte.text: Abu Rayhan Muhammad al-Biruni was born in 973 in the region of **Khwarazm**, whose territory now belongs to Uzbekistan. He is regarded as one of the most versatile scientists of the **Middle Ages**. His mother tongue was Khwarazmian; he also spoke Persian, but he wrote most of his works in **Arabic**, the language of science in his time. He died around 1050 in Ghazni in present-day Afghanistan. Altogether he is said to have written well over a hundred works.

In his youth Al-Biruni lived through troubled times and moved to various courts. From about 1017 he worked for many years for **Mahmud of Ghazni**, a powerful ruler. Mahmud led military campaigns into northern India, and Al-Biruni went with him. There he learnt **Sanskrit**, the ancient language of Indian scholars. This meant he could read Indian books himself.

Al-Biruni worked out the **Earth’s radius** with a clever method. First he measured the height of a mountain. Then he climbed up and measured how far the **horizon** lay below the horizontal. From this small angle and the height of the mountain he used geometry to calculate the radius of the Earth. His result was very close to today’s value of around 6370 kilometres.

Around 1030 Al-Biruni wrote a large work about **India**. In it he described the religion, philosophy, astronomy, numbers, festivals and customs of the people. He tried to present foreign views accurately and fairly and compared them with Greek knowledge. That is why some see him as an early **ethnologist**. The book is still an important source about India at that time.

Using a balance, Al-Biruni measured the **density** of many metals and gemstones astonishingly accurately. He also described how to tell minerals apart and wrote about the calendars and ways of counting time of different peoples. With the younger scholar **Ibn Sina** he exchanged letters about light, heat and the structure of the world. In them he asked critical questions about the teachings of the Greek philosopher Aristotle. He even discussed whether the Earth might turn on its own axis.

begriffe.erklaerung: A person who knows a great deal and does scientific research.
The distance from the centre of the Earth to its surface.
The line where the sky and the Earth seem to meet.
How heavy a substance is in relation to its size.
A very old language of India in which many religious and scientific texts are written.

gewusst: A crater on the Moon is named after Al-Biruni.
Al-Biruni wrote that he would only accept new findings if measurements and observations supported them.
His name probably means “the one from outside”, because he came from a suburb.

teile.einleitung: Augusta Raurica is a former Roman town near Augst and Kaiseraugst on the Rhine, east of Basel. It was founded more than 2000 years ago and was an important town in the Roman Empire. Today it is one of the best-preserved Roman towns north of the Alps and a large open-air museum.
wichtigste: Augusta Raurica was founded by the Romans; Lucius Munatius Plancus is regarded as its founder.
The site lies near Augst in the canton of Basel-Country and Kaiseraugst in the canton of Aargau.
You can visit a large Roman theatre, a forum, baths and temples there.
The people spoke Latin and lived in the Roman way.
In 1961 a famous late Roman silver treasure was discovered in Kaiseraugst.
Around AD 300 the Romans built the fortress of Castrum Rauracense on the Rhine.
Every year the Roman Festival takes place at Augusta Raurica.

abschnitte.text: Augusta Raurica lies about 10 km east of Basel on the south bank of the Rhine. The site is spread over the municipalities of **Augst** in the canton of Basel-Country and **Kaiseraugst** in the canton of Aargau. The name recalls the Emperor Augustus and the Rauraci, a Celtic tribe that lived in the area. The location was favourable because important roads and the Rhine as a waterway came together here. Today the site is one of the largest archaeological sites in Switzerland.

The Roman general **Lucius Munatius Plancus**, whose tomb stands in Gaeta in Italy, is regarded as the founder of the colony. The actual town grew up around the beginning of the Common Era, that is, more than 2000 years ago. In the 2nd century AD Augusta Raurica was a thriving town with craftspeople, traders and many thousands of inhabitants. It had water pipes, paved streets and public baths. In the 3rd century the upper town was largely abandoned after unrest.

The most impressive building is the large **Roman theatre**, which held thousands of people. At the centre lay the **forum**, the main square with a temple and a basilica, where people did business and held court. In the **baths** people bathed in cold, lukewarm and hot water. There are also remains of temples, workshops, an amphitheatre and an underground well-house. Around AD 300 the Romans built the fortress of **Castrum Rauracense** right on the Rhine.

In 1961 building workers in Kaiseraugst came across a large **silver treasure** from late Roman times. It includes splendid platters, bowls, spoons, coins and silver bars. It was probably buried around the middle of the 4th century, when Germanic peoples were threatening the area. The owner probably never came back to fetch it. Today the treasure is on display in the museum at Augusta Raurica and is one of the most valuable finds from Roman times.

In the reconstructed **Roman house** you can see how wealthy Romans lived, cooked and worked. An animal park shows old breeds of domestic animals as they were kept in Roman times. Every year at the end of August the site turns into a lively Roman town with gladiators, craftspeople and legionaries at the **Roman Festival**. School classes can bake bread, mint coins or write in Latin there. Excavations are still going on today and keep bringing new finds to light.

begriffe.erklaerung: Town founded by the Romans with Roman citizens.
Main square of a Roman town with a temple and a basilica.
Large public baths of the Romans.
Science that studies old traces and finds from the past.
Latin word for a fortified Roman fortress.

gewusst: In the restored theatre at Augusta Raurica, concerts and performances take place again in summer.
The Roman Festival at Augusta Raurica is regarded as the largest Roman festival in Switzerland.
In the Middle Ages many stones from Augusta Raurica were reused to build houses and churches in the area.

teile.einleitung: The Arctic is the region around the North Pole, with a large, often frozen sea in the middle and cold land areas all around. In winter it stays dark there for weeks, and in summer the sun sometimes does not set at all. Despite the cold, people and many amazing animals live in the Arctic.
wichtigste: The Arctic is the region around the North Pole.
At its centre lies the Arctic Ocean, which is partly covered by sea ice.
The peoples of the Arctic include the Inuit, for example in Canada.
In the past people built igloos out of blocks of snow for hunting trips.
Typical animals are the polar bear, walrus, narwhal, Arctic fox and reindeer.
The sea ice in the Arctic has been shrinking for many years.
The Arctic is warming faster than most other regions on Earth.

abschnitte.text: The Arctic includes the **Arctic Ocean** and the northernmost parts of Canada, Alaska, Greenland, Scandinavia and Russia. It is often bounded by the **Arctic Circle**. North of it there is at least one day in summer when the sun does not set, the midnight sun. In winter, on the other hand, there is the polar night, when the sun does not rise.

Unlike the Antarctic, the Arctic is not a continent but mainly a sea covered by **sea ice**. On land there is treeless **tundra** with mosses, lichens, grasses and dwarf shrubs. Beneath it the ground is often frozen all year round; this is called permafrost. Greenland, the largest island on Earth, is mostly covered by a thick ice sheet.

The **polar bear** hunts mainly seals on the sea ice. The walrus with its long tusks lies in large groups on ice floes and beaches. The **narwhal** has a long, twisted tooth that looks like a horn. The Arctic fox has white fur in winter, and reindeer roam the tundra in large herds.

Peoples have lived in the Arctic for thousands of years, for example the **Inuit** in Canada, Alaska and Greenland. In Scandinavia live the **Sami**, some of whom herd reindeer, which also pull sledges. In the past the Inuit built igloos out of blocks of snow for hunting trips; today most live in permanent houses. Many keep up their languages and traditions and combine them with modern life.

The Arctic is warming much faster than the Earth’s average. That is why the **sea ice** has been shrinking for many years, and polar bears are losing hunting grounds. Many countries research the Arctic, and experts from Switzerland also take part in expeditions. In 1912 the Swiss researcher Alfred de Quervain crossed the Greenland ice sheet with a team.

begriffe.erklaerung: Imaginary line north of which there is midnight sun and polar night.
Treeless landscape with mosses, lichens and low plants.
Ground that is frozen all year round.
People who have long lived in the Arctic of Canada, Alaska and Greenland.

gewusst: There is no land at the North Pole; you stand on drifting sea ice there.
The word Arctic comes from the Greek word for bear, because of the constellation of the Great Bear in the northern sky.

teile.einleitung: The anchoring effect is a thinking error in which a number mentioned beforehand influences our estimates, even when it has nothing to do with the question. We hold on to this number like a ship to its anchor. Advertising, negotiations and even court rulings can be influenced by it.
wichtigste: With the anchoring effect, a number mentioned beforehand influences our estimates.
In a famous experiment the psychologists Tversky and Kahneman created random anchors with a wheel of fortune.
They explained the effect with the rule of judgement “anchoring and adjustment”.
People who estimate 8 × 7 × 6 × 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 usually give higher values than with the reverse order; the correct answer is 40,320.
In experiments even numbers rolled on dice influenced the sentences proposed by experienced judges.
In negotiations the first offer often sets an anchor.
A crossed-out high price in a shop serves as an anchor.
It helps to look deliberately for reasons for other values.

abschnitte.text: The **anchoring effect** is a so-called **cognitive bias**, that is, a typical thinking error that almost everyone makes. When we have to estimate a number, we unconsciously go by a number we heard or saw shortly before. This number is the **anchor**. We do adjust our estimate, but usually not enough, and we stay close to the anchor. This even happens when we know that the anchor is random.

In 1974 the psychologists **Amos Tversky** and **Daniel Kahneman** published a famous experiment. In front of the participants they spun a **wheel of fortune** that was secretly set to stop only at 10 or 65. Afterwards people had to estimate what percentage of the countries in the United Nations were African. Those who had seen the 10 estimated much lower on average than those who had seen the 65. In 2002 Kahneman received the Nobel Prize in Economics, partly for research like this.

In another experiment people had a few seconds to estimate the result of 8 × 7 × 6 × 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 1. Another group got the same sum in reverse order. Those who started with 8 × 7 estimated much higher, because the first large numbers acted as an **anchor**. But both groups were far below the correct result of **40,320**. Tversky and Kahneman called the thinking rule behind it **anchoring and adjustment**.

Even experts are not immune to the anchoring effect. In experiments by German researchers, experienced **judges** read a made-up case and rolled a number on dice beforehand. Those who had rolled higher numbers proposed a longer sentence on average. This shows how strongly even random numbers influence our judgement. That is why it is important to know about such effects.

Shops often use the anchoring effect, for example with “Was 200 francs, now only 120 francs”. The high, crossed-out price acts as an **anchor**, and 120 francs suddenly seems cheap. In **negotiations** too it is often worth making the first offer, because it sets the direction. Menus sometimes include very expensive dishes so that the others seem good value.

The anchoring effect can hardly be switched off completely. But it helps to look deliberately for **reasons for other values**, for example: why might the price also be much lower? If you first find out for yourself how much something normally costs, you are less easily influenced. Sleeping on it or comparing prices in several shops can also help.

begriffe.erklaerung: A typical thinking error that occurs in a similar way in many people.
A number mentioned first, on which later estimates are based.
A simple rule of thumb with which we decide quickly, but which can lead to mistakes.
A conversation in which two sides agree on something, for example a price.

gewusst: The anchoring effect works even when people are told that the number is completely random.
In experiments even the last digits of people’s own phone or social security number influenced how much they were willing to pay for goods.
Daniel Kahneman wrote the famous book “Thinking, Fast and Slow” about such thinking errors.

teile.einleitung: An astrolabe is an old measuring instrument with which you could find the height of the Sun and stars and use it to work out the time. It was a kind of pocket computer for astronomers and was used for more than a thousand years. Many beautifully made brass astrolabes can be seen in museums today.
wichtigste: The astrolabe originally came from ancient Greece.
Many astrolabes were made of brass.
Muslim scholars used it, among other things, to work out the times of prayer.
Hermann the Lame of Reichenau Abbey wrote about it in the 11th century.
In 1391 the English poet Geoffrey Chaucer wrote a set of instructions for his son.
In seafaring it was replaced by the sextant in the 18th century.
With an astrolabe you could measure the heights of heavenly bodies and work out the time.

abschnitte.text: The name comes from Greek and means roughly “star taker”. An **astrolabe** is usually a round disc made of **brass** that is hung from a ring. On the back there is a pointer that can turn, with two small holes for sighting, called the **alidade**. On the front lies a cut-out star map that can be turned over a disc with lines.

First you sight a bright star or the Sun through the alidade and read its height above the horizon on the rim. Then you turn the star map on the front until it matches this reading. Now the astrolabe shows what the sky looks like at that moment, and you can read off the **time**. In this way sunrise, sunset and the position of the stars could also be worked out in advance.

The astrolabe came from **ancient Greece**; important foundations came from astronomers in Alexandria. Scholars in the Islamic world greatly improved it from the 8th century. They used it, among other things, to work out the **times of prayer** and the direction of Mecca. In the Middle Ages the knowledge reached Europe via Spain.

In the 11th century **Hermann the Lame**, a monk on the island of Reichenau in Lake Constance, wrote texts about the astrolabe. Despite being severely paralysed, he was one of the greatest scholars of his time. In 1391 the English poet **Geoffrey Chaucer** wrote a guide to the astrolabe for his young son. It is regarded as one of the oldest technical texts in the English language.

From the 15th century sailors, for example from Portugal, used a simplified **mariner’s astrolabe**. With it they measured the height of the Sun at midday and so worked out how far north or south they were. On a rolling ship, however, this was difficult. In the 18th century the more accurate **sextant** therefore took over.

begriffe.erklaerung: Pointer that can turn, with holes for sighting stars.
A shiny golden mixture of copper and zinc.
The line where the sky and the Earth seem to touch.
A seafaring instrument that measures the angle between the horizon and a heavenly body.

gewusst: Many astrolabes are real works of art with fine decorations and star names in Arabic script.
Some star names we use today, such as Aldebaran or Vega, come from Arabic.
A single astrolabe could solve dozens of different calculations.

teile.einleitung: Alessandro Volta was an Italian physicist who developed the first working electric battery around 1800. With his invention it was possible for the first time to produce a steady electric current. The unit for electrical voltage, the volt, is named after him.
wichtigste: Alessandro Volta lived from 1745 to 1827.
He was born in Como in northern Italy, near the Swiss border.
Around 1800 he built the voltaic pile, the first battery.
It consisted of discs of zinc and copper and cloth soaked in salt water.
For many years he was a professor at the University of Pavia.
He also discovered the gas methane.
The unit volt is named after him.

abschnitte.text: Alessandro Volta was born in **Como** on 18 February 1745, only a few kilometres from the Swiss border at Chiasso. Even as a young man he was interested in electricity. From 1779 he was professor of physics at the University of **Pavia**. He travelled around Europe and met many famous researchers of his time.

abschnitte.titel: The dispute over the frogs’ legs
abschnitte.text: The doctor Luigi Galvani had observed that frogs’ legs twitch when touched with two different metals. Galvani believed that the electricity came from the animal itself. Volta, on the other hand, suspected that the current was produced by the **two metals**. To prove this, he built his own source of current without any frog.

In 1800 Volta presented the **voltaic pile**. He stacked discs of zinc and copper alternately and put cardboard or cloth soaked in salt water between them. The higher the stack, the stronger the electrical **voltage**. With this he had invented the first battery that supplied current continuously.

As early as 1775 Volta developed the electrophorus, a device that can produce electric charge again and again. A year later, in the marshes by Lake Maggiore, he discovered a flammable gas, **methane**. He also built a kind of pistol in which an electric spark set off a mixture of gases. Napoleon was impressed by his work and made him a count.

With the battery, researchers could experiment with electric current for longer periods for the first time. Soon afterwards, for example, they managed to split water into hydrogen and oxygen using electricity. Since 1881 the unit of electrical voltage has been called the **volt**. Every battery in a remote control or a mobile phone ultimately goes back to Volta’s idea.

begriffe.erklaerung: A device that turns stored chemical energy into electric current.
It says how strongly the electric current is driven, measured in volts.
The unit of electrical voltage.
A flammable gas that forms, for example, in marshes.

gewusst: A normal household socket in Switzerland has a voltage of 230 volts.
Volta was pictured on the Italian 10,000-lire banknote.

teile.einleitung: Altmetrics are measures of how much attention a piece of research gets on the internet. They count, for example, mentions in news, blogs or social media. In this way they add to the classic measure of how often a paper is cited by other researchers.
wichtigste: Altmetrics record online attention for research papers.
The part “alt” stands for “alternative”.
Typical sources are mentions in news articles, blogs and social media.
One advantage is that they show the response very quickly.
They are criticised for measuring attention, not quality.
Classic measures are the h-index and Eugene Garfield’s Journal Impact Factor.
The coloured “donut” from the company Altmetric shows which sources the attention comes from.

abschnitte.text: The word **altmetrics** is short for “alternative metrics”, that is, other ways of measuring. It means numbers that show how often a scientific paper gets noticed online. The term became known in 2010 through a manifesto by young researchers around Jason Priem. What is counted includes mentions in **news articles**, blogs, social media, Wikipedia or political reports. How often a paper is saved in reference management programs can also be part of it.

Traditionally the influence of research is measured by **citations**, that is, how often other scientific articles mention a paper. The information scientist **Eugene Garfield** developed the **Journal Impact Factor**, which shows how often articles in a journal are cited on average. The **h-index** was proposed in 2005 by the physicist Jorge Hirsch. A researcher has an h-index of 10 if she has 10 papers that have each been cited at least 10 times.

It usually takes several years before a paper is cited often, because new scientific articles take time. Altmetrics, on the other hand, show the response very **quickly**, often just a few days after publication. They also show whether research reaches people outside science, for example journalists, politicians or the public. In this way papers that are important for society but rarely cited can also stand out.

The company **Altmetric**, founded in 2011, calculates a score for many scientific articles. It shows this in a coloured ring, the so-called **donut**. Each colour stands for a source, for example news, blogs or social networks. The more colourful the ring, the more varied the sources of attention. Many publishers show the donut right next to their articles.

The main criticism is that altmetrics measure **attention**, not **quality**. A paper with a funny title or a controversial result can get a lot of attention even though it is weak. In addition, clicks and mentions can be manipulated, for example by automated accounts. That is why many experts call for research not to be judged only by numbers. The San Francisco Declaration on Research Assessment, **DORA** for short, has been campaigning for this since 2012.

begriffe.erklaerung: When a scientific text refers to another because it uses its results.
A number used to measure and compare something.
A number that says how many of a person’s papers have been cited at least that many times.
A measure of how often articles in a journal are cited on average.

gewusst: Some research papers are shared so often on social media that in a few days they get more attention than others do in decades.
Every year the company Altmetric publishes a list of the research articles that received the most attention online.
Eugene Garfield had the idea for a citation index as early as the 1950s.

teile.einleitung: Arctic sea ice is frozen seawater that floats on the Arctic Ocean. Its area grows in winter and shrinks in summer, but for decades there has been less and less of it overall. That is why it is regarded as one of the clearest warning signs of climate change.
wichtigste: Arctic sea ice normally reaches its smallest extent in September.
The smallest summer area so far was measured in 2012.
Since 1979 the extent has been measured continuously by satellites.
Seawater with the usual salt content freezes at about -1.8 °C.
Melting sea ice hardly raises sea level, because it is already floating.
The Arctic is warming much faster than the global average.
The share of multi-year ice has fallen sharply.

abschnitte.text: Sea ice forms when the surface of the sea freezes. Because salt water has a lower **freezing point** than fresh water, it only freezes at about -1.8 °C. As it freezes, much of the salt is squeezed out of the ice. That is why old sea ice is almost salt-free and was even melted by sailors in the past as drinking water.

The sea ice usually reaches its largest area in March and its smallest in **September**. Ice that survives a summer is called **multi-year ice**; it is thicker and tougher. In the past such ice covered large parts of the Arctic; today its share has shrunk sharply. Much of the ice is now only one year old and melts away again the next summer.

Since **1979** satellites have measured the extent of the sea ice without a break. They show that the summer area has become clearly smaller over the decades. The lowest value so far was in September **2012**. From 2019 to 2020 the German research ship Polarstern also let itself be frozen into the ice for a year and drifted with it through the Arctic.

Bright ice reflects a large part of the sunlight, while dark water absorbs a lot of heat. When ice melts, more dark water is exposed, which warms up further and melts even more ice. This cycle is called the **ice-albedo feedback**. It is one reason for **Arctic amplification**, that is, for the fact that the Arctic is warming much faster than the rest of the Earth.

For polar bears, seals and walruses the sea ice is a hunting ground and resting place, so they are losing habitat. The peoples of the Arctic, who hunt and travel on the ice, are affected too. Melting sea ice hardly raises **sea level**, because it is already floating, like an ice cube in a glass. But less ice opens up new shipping routes through the Arctic Ocean, which raises new questions about environmental protection and safety.

begriffe.erklaerung: Measure of how much light a surface reflects.
Temperature at which a liquid turns into ice.
Sea ice that has survived at least one summer.
When a change strengthens itself even more.

gewusst: In winter Arctic sea ice can cover an area several hundred times the size of Switzerland.
Young sea ice often first forms as a thin, slushy layer, which because of its shape is sometimes called pancake ice.

teile.einleitung: Barbara McClintock was an American researcher who worked with maize all her life. She discovered that some genes can change their position in the genetic material, the so-called jumping genes. For a long time people did not believe her, but in 1983 she received the Nobel Prize for it.
wichtigste: Barbara McClintock came from the USA and lived from 1902 to 1992.
She did research with maize all her life.
In 1931, with Harriet Creighton, she showed under the microscope that chromosomes exchange pieces during inheritance.
She discovered genes that can change their position in the genetic material.
These movable sections are commonly called jumping genes.
With them she explained the colourful spots on some maize kernels.
In 1983 she became the first woman to receive the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine on her own.

abschnitte.text: **Barbara McClintock** was born in Hartford in the US state of Connecticut in 1902 and grew up in New York. She studied botany and genetics at **Cornell University**, which was still unusual for women at the time. From 1942 she worked at the **Cold Spring Harbor** research laboratory on Long Island. She lived modestly, worked very carefully and spent countless hours at the microscope and in the maize field.

McClintock chose **maize** as her research plant because inheritance can be seen clearly in the kernels. Each kernel on a cob is a separate little offspring with its own colour. In addition, the **chromosomes** of maize are easy to see under the microscope. McClintock was able to tell individual chromosomes apart and link them with visible features.

In 1931 she made an important discovery together with her student **Harriet Creighton**. The two showed visibly under the microscope for the first time that chromosomes exchange pieces with each other during inheritance. At the same time the features of the plants changed in exactly the matching way. This proved that the genes really are located on the chromosomes.

In the 1940s McClintock studied **maize kernels** with colourful spots and stripes. She found out that certain sections of the genetic material can change their position. If such a piece jumps into a colour gene, it switches the gene off; if it jumps out again, the gene becomes active again. This is how the speckled kernels come about. Today these sections are called **transposons** or, in everyday language, jumping genes.

When McClintock presented her results around 1950, many experts did not understand her or did not believe her. At that time it was assumed that genes sit firmly in their place. Only decades later were jumping genes also found in bacteria, animals and humans. In 1983 she received the **Nobel Prize** in Physiology or Medicine, as the first woman who did not have to share this prize. She died in 1992 at the age of 90.

Today we know that a large part of the human genetic material consists of transposons or their remains. Jumping genes have helped shape the development of living things over millions of years. They also play a role in how bacteria pass on resistance to antibiotics. That is why McClintock is regarded as one of the most important geneticists of the 20th century.

begriffe.erklaerung: A section of the genetic material that controls a particular characteristic.
A carrier of genetic material in the cell nucleus, visible as a little rod under the microscope.
A section of the genetic material that can change its position, a jumping gene.
The science of inheritance.

gewusst: Barbara McClintock was already 81 years old when she was awarded her Nobel Prize.
A large part of the human genetic material consists of remains of jumping genes.
The speckled kernels of colourful ornamental maize show exactly the spots that McClintock studied.

teile.einleitung: Avicenna, whose real name was Ibn Sina, was a Persian doctor and philosopher who lived around a thousand years ago. His textbook “The Canon of Medicine” was so good that students in Europe were still learning from it centuries later. He is regarded as one of the most important scholars of the Islamic world in the Middle Ages.
wichtigste: Ibn Sina is known in Europe by the name Avicenna.
He was born around 980 near the city of Bukhara and died in 1037.
His most famous medical work is called “The Canon of Medicine”.
The Canon was used as a textbook at European universities until the 17th century.
His great work on philosophy and natural science is called “The Book of Healing”.
As a young doctor he cured the ruler of Bukhara and was allowed to use his library in return.
His tomb stands in the city of Hamadan in present-day Iran.

abschnitte.text: **Ibn Sina**’s full name was Abu Ali al-Husayn ibn Abdallah ibn Sina. In Europe this was turned into the Latin name **Avicenna**. He was born around 980 in a village near **Bukhara**, which is now in Uzbekistan. He was Persian and wrote most of his works in Arabic, the language of science in the Islamic world.

Even as a child Ibn Sina learnt very quickly; at about ten years old he knew the Koran by heart. Then he studied mathematics, logic, philosophy and medicine, teaching himself much of it. As a young man of about 17 he cured the sick ruler of Bukhara. As a reward he was allowed to use the ruler’s large **library**, where he read many rare books.

His main work is **The Canon of Medicine**, a huge textbook in five parts. In it he collected the knowledge of Greek doctors such as Galen and added his own experience. He described diseases and medicines and recognised, for example, that some diseases are contagious. The book was translated into Latin in the 12th century. At European universities it served as an important textbook until the 17th century.

Ibn Sina shaped not only medicine but also **philosophy**. His great work on it is called “The Book of Healing”; it deals with logic, natural science, mathematics and questions about the soul. He tried to combine the teachings of the Greek philosopher Aristotle with belief in God. His thought experiment of the “floating man”, with which he reflected on consciousness, is well known.

Ibn Sina lived at a time of many wars and changing rulers. He had to flee several times and worked at various courts as a doctor and even as a minister. He wrote many of his books on the move or at night. He died in 1037 in **Hamadan** in present-day Iran, where a large tomb commemorates him.

Avicenna is regarded as one of the most influential scholars of the Middle Ages. In Iran, Uzbekistan and Tajikistan he is still honoured as a national hero. A **lunar crater** and a plant genus bear his name. His work shows how much science in Europe benefited from the knowledge of the Islamic world.

begriffe.erklaerung: Here, a large, authoritative textbook that people follow.
Thinking about big questions such as knowledge, truth and life.
A person who knows a great deal and does research.
The period in Europe roughly between AD 500 and 1500.

gewusst: The Canon of Medicine was already printed in Europe in the 15th century, shortly after printing was invented.
Ibn Sina is said to have told how he read a book by Aristotle forty times before he understood it.
There is a crater on the Moon named after Avicenna.

teile.einleitung: Antoine Laurent de Lavoisier was a French scientist who fundamentally changed chemistry in the 18th century. With precise measurements he showed what really happens when things burn, and he gave important elements their names. That is why he is often called the father of modern chemistry.
wichtigste: Lavoisier lived in France from 1743 to 1794.
He disproved the old phlogiston theory of burning.
He gave oxygen its name, which means acid former.
He called hydrogen hydrogène, that is, water former.
He proved that water is a chemical compound.
The precision balance was his most important measuring instrument.
His wife Marie-Anne helped him with experiments, drawings and translations.

abschnitte.text: Antoine Laurent de Lavoisier was born **in Paris in 1743** and came from a wealthy family. He first studied law but soon became much more interested in science. He earned his money as a member of the **Ferme générale**, a company that collected taxes for the king. With this money he set up one of the best laboratories in Europe.

In his experiments Lavoisier weighed all the substances very precisely before and afterwards with a **precision balance**. In this way he realised that in a chemical reaction no mass is lost or newly created overall. This principle is now called the **law of conservation of mass**. An example: when metal burns to ash, it becomes heavier because it takes up part of the air.

In the past researchers believed that burnable substances contained a fire substance called **phlogiston**, which escapes when they burn. Lavoisier showed that, on the contrary, a gas from the air is taken up during burning. He called this gas, which Joseph Priestley and Carl Wilhelm Scheele had discovered before him, **oxygen**. He also realised that breathing is a kind of slow burning in the body.

Lavoisier proved that **water** is not a basic substance but consists of hydrogen and oxygen. He split water and also built it up again from the two gases. In 1789 he published a chemistry textbook with a list of the **elements** known at the time. Together with other chemists he developed a uniform system for naming chemical substances, parts of which are still used today.

His wife **Marie-Anne Paulze** worked closely with him. She recorded experiments, drew the copper engravings for his books and translated English scientific texts. During the **French Revolution** the former tax collectors were put on trial. Lavoisier was executed by guillotine in Paris in 1794, and soon many scholars regretted the loss of this great researcher.

begriffe.erklaerung: Basic substance that cannot be broken down any further chemically, for example oxygen.
Substance that is firmly made up of several elements, such as water.
Made-up fire substance of an old theory that has been disproved.
Very accurate scales that measure the tiniest differences in weight.

gewusst: Lavoisier also worked on a commission that prepared the metric system with the metre and the kilogram.
The name oxygen is based on a mistake, because Lavoisier believed that every acid contains oxygen.

teile.einleitung: An atom is a tiny building block of matter made of a nucleus and an electron shell. Everything you can see and touch, whether air, water, stones or your own body, is made of atoms. They are so small that a drop of water has room for thousands of billions of billions of them.
wichtigste: Atoms are the tiny building blocks that all substances are made of.
An atom consists of an atomic nucleus and an electron shell.
Protons and neutrons sit in the nucleus, and electrons move in the shell.
The number of protons decides which chemical element it is.
Today 118 chemical elements are known.
An atom is about a ten-millionth of a millimetre across.
With a scanning tunnelling microscope, which was invented in Zurich, individual atoms can be made visible.

abschnitte.text: An **atom** is the smallest particle of a chemical element that still has its properties. The word comes from Greek and means “indivisible”. As early as about 400 BC the Greek thinker **Democritus** suspected that everything is made of tiny particles. Today we know that atoms themselves are made of even smaller particles.

In the middle of the atom is the **atomic nucleus** with positively charged protons and uncharged neutrons. Around the nucleus the negatively charged **electrons** move in the electron shell. Almost all the mass is in the nucleus, even though it is much smaller than the whole atom. If an atom were as big as a football stadium, the nucleus would only be about the size of a pea in the middle.

The number of protons in the nucleus is called the **atomic number** and decides the element. Hydrogen has one proton, carbon six, oxygen eight and gold 79. All 118 known elements are arranged in the periodic table. When atoms join together, molecules form, for example water from two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom.

Around 1800 the Englishman John Dalton showed that chemical substances are made of atoms in fixed proportions. In 1911 **Ernest Rutherford** discovered the tiny atomic nucleus with an experiment on a thin gold foil. Shortly afterwards Niels Bohr presented a model of the atom in which electrons orbit the nucleus on particular paths. In 1981 Gerd Binnig and Heinrich Rohrer at IBM in Rüschlikon near Zurich invented the **scanning tunnelling microscope**, with which individual atoms can be pictured.

If you understand atoms, you can explain why substances burn, rust or conduct electricity. In **nuclear power stations** such as Gösgen or Leibstadt, heavy atomic nuclei are split to produce electricity. In the Sun, on the other hand, light atomic nuclei fuse and release huge amounts of energy. Computer chips, medicines and new materials are also developed using knowledge about atoms.

begriffe.erklaerung: The tiny centre of an atom, made of protons and neutrons.
A very light, negatively charged particle in the shell of the atom.
A substance made only of atoms with the same number of protons, for example gold.
A table in which all the chemical elements are arranged.

gewusst: An atom consists almost entirely of empty space.
Binnig and Rohrer received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1986 for the scanning tunnelling microscope.
Most of the atoms in your body are hydrogen atoms.

teile.einleitung: The arithmetic mean is what we usually just call the average in everyday life. You add up all the values and divide the total by the number of values. In this way you can work out, for example, the average mark in a school report or the mean temperature of a week.
wichtigste: The arithmetic mean is the sum of all values divided by how many there are.
The arithmetic mean of 4, 8, 6, 10 and 7 is 7.
The marks 5, 4.5, 6 and 4.5 give an average of 5.
If you know the average and the number of values, you get the sum by multiplying.
Negative numbers can also be part of a mean.
A single very large or very small value can shift the average a lot.
As well as the arithmetic mean there are other averages such as the median.

abschnitte.text: To calculate the **arithmetic mean**, you first add up all the values. Then you divide this **sum** by the number of values. For the numbers 4, 8, 6, 10 and 7 the sum is 35, and 35 divided by 5 gives 7. In mathematics the mean is often written as x with a bar over it.

In Switzerland school marks usually go from 1 to 6, with 4 being a pass. If Lea has the marks 5, 4.5, 6 and 4.5, the sum is 20, and 20 divided by 4 is an **average mark** of 5. You can also work backwards: if Tim has an average of 5 after four tests, his total is 20. For an average of 5.2 after five tests he needs a total of 26, so a 6 in the fifth test.

If 12, 15, 9, 14 and 10 degrees are measured at midday during a week, the **average temperature** is 12 degrees. If three children get 10, 15 and 20 francs of pocket money, that is 15 francs per child on average. Sports results, fuel consumption or the average height of a class are worked out in the same way. It even works with negative numbers: for -3, 5 and 4 the sum is 6, and the mean is 2.

A single extreme value, called an **outlier**, can change the average a lot. If nine people each earn 5000 francs and one earns 1 million, the average is suddenly around 104,500 francs. But that does not describe anyone in the group well. That is why people sometimes use the **median**, the value that is exactly in the middle when you put all the values in order of size.

Sometimes not all values count equally. If an exam counts twice as much as a small test, you calculate a **weighted mean**. The more important mark is put into the sum twice and also counted twice. Statistics offices and researchers use averages every day to sum up large amounts of data in an understandable way.

begriffe.erklaerung: The result when you add numbers together.
Everyday word for the arithmetic mean.
The middle value of a list of numbers put in order of size.
A value that is much larger or smaller than the others.

gewusst: An average does not have to appear in the list of numbers; the mean of 1 and 2, for example, is 1.5.
The name arithmetic comes from the Greek word arithmos, which means number.

teile.einleitung: A non-stick coating is a smooth layer, for example in a frying pan, to which fried eggs or rösti hardly stick. The best known is made of the plastic PTFE, which many people know by the brand name Teflon. Behind this handy kitchen helper there is a chance discovery from 1938.
wichtigste: Many non-stick coatings are made of the plastic PTFE.
PTFE was discovered by chance in 1938 by the chemist Roy Plunkett.
PTFE consists only of carbon and fluorine.
Hardly anything sticks to PTFE, because other substances are hardly attracted to it.
Metal forks can scratch the coating.
If heated empty on the highest setting, the coating can break down.
There are also ceramic coatings without PTFE.

abschnitte.text: A non-stick coating is a thin layer on pans, baking tins or waffle irons. It makes sure that food does not burn and stick. That is why you need less fat when frying, and the pan is easy to clean. The most common coating is made of **polytetrafluoroethylene**, PTFE for short.

PTFE is a plastic made of long chains that consist only of **carbon** and **fluorine**. The fluorine atoms form a kind of smooth protective coat around the chain. As a result other substances are hardly attracted to the surface, neither water nor fat. PTFE is also one of the most slippery solid materials known.

In 1938 the American chemist **Roy Plunkett** was working on new refrigerants for the company DuPont. In a gas cylinder he suddenly found a white, waxy powder instead of gas. It was PTFE, which had formed by itself in the cylinder. In the 1950s a French engineer had the idea of coating pans with it and founded the company Tefal.

Metal forks or knives can **scratch** the coating; wooden or silicone spatulas are better. You should not heat an empty pan on the highest setting, because PTFE can break down when overheated. This produces fumes that are especially dangerous for birds such as budgies. With medium heat and a little oil, a pan lasts much longer.

As an alternative there are **ceramic coatings**, which do without PTFE but often lose their effect more quickly. PTFE belongs to a large group of fluorine compounds, the **PFAS**, which are very hard to break down and are therefore viewed critically today. Plumbers use PTFE as white sealing tape for threads on water pipes. The plastic is also found in cables, waterproof jackets and medical devices.

begriffe.erklaerung: Artificially made material consisting of long chains of molecules.
Short for polytetrafluoroethylene, a very smooth plastic.
Thin layer that is applied to an object.
Spiral groove on screws and pipes for screwing them together.

gewusst: PTFE is so smooth that even geckos, which can run up glass, slip off it.
PTFE was originally used not for the kitchen but for technology and industry.

teile.einleitung: An antigen is a feature by which our immune system recognises something, a bit like a face on a wanted poster. More precisely, it is a structure that is recognised very specifically by antibodies or by the receptors of T cells. Antigens sit, for example, on viruses, bacteria, pollen or even on our own blood cells.
wichtigste: An antigen is specifically recognised by antibodies or T-cell receptors.
The small area to which an antibody binds is called an epitope.
The matching binding site on the antibody is called a paratope.
A hapten only triggers an immune response when it is bound to a carrier protein.
A rapid antigen test detects virus proteins in a sample.
The blood groups in the ABO system are determined by sugar structures on red blood cells.
Vaccines train the immune system with harmless antigens.

abschnitte.text: An **antigen** is usually a protein or a sugar molecule on the surface of a pathogen or a cell. The immune system constantly checks whether a structure belongs to the body itself or is foreign. If it recognises a foreign antigen, it starts a defence. The name comes from the fact that such substances can trigger the formation of antibodies.

An antibody does not bind to the whole antigen, but only to a small piece of it, the **epitope**. The matching site on the antibody is called the **paratope**. The two fit together like a key in a lock, which is why each antibody only recognises very particular antigens. A large antigen can have several different epitopes.

B cells form **antibodies**, which float freely in the blood and grab antigens directly. T cells, on the other hand, only recognise antigens when other cells display small fragments of them on their surface. Very small molecules, the **haptens**, are too small on their own for an immune response. Only when they attach themselves to one of the body’s own proteins can an allergy develop, for example.

Depending on the person, different sugar structures sit on the red blood cells. These antigens determine the **blood groups** A, B, AB and 0, which the Austrian Karl Landsteiner discovered in 1901. If someone receives blood with foreign blood-group antigens, the immune system attacks the foreign cells. In organ transplants too, certain tissue antigens must match as well as possible.

A **rapid antigen test** looks for a virus’s proteins in a sample from the nose or throat, as many people got to know during the coronavirus period. Vaccinations contain weakened pathogens, parts of them or a blueprint for an antigen so that the body can practise its defence. Superantigens are dangerous: they activate a great many T cells non-specifically and can cause toxic shock. In cancer research, scientists are interested in neoantigens, which arise newly through mutations in tumour cells and can help the immune system recognise cancer cells.

begriffe.erklaerung: Y-shaped protein of the immune system that binds to foreign substances.
Small part of an antigen that an antibody fits exactly.
Small molecule that is only recognised together with a protein.
The body’s own defence against pathogens.

gewusst: Even harmless things such as pollen carry antigens, and in hay fever the immune system overreacts to them.
An antibody can tell an antigen apart so precisely that even a small change in the epitope stops it fitting.

teile.einleitung: An excavation is the careful investigation of a place in the ground where people lived in the past. Archaeologists uncover it layer by layer and look for traces of the past. Because an excavation destroys the site, everything is documented very precisely.
wichtigste: In an excavation, traces of earlier people in the ground are uncovered.
The deeper layers in the ground are usually older than the upper ones.
The excavation area is often divided into squares of equal size.
Every find is photographed, measured in and put into a labelled bag.
The earth is sieved so that even tiny finds are not lost.
Before many building projects there are excavations so that finds are not destroyed.
With ground-penetrating radar, remains of walls can be tracked down without digging.

abschnitte.text: An excavation is the most important working method of **archaeology**, the science of the human past. People look for **finds** such as pottery fragments, tools or coins. Just as important are **features**, that is, traces in the ground that cannot be moved, such as post holes, pits or remains of walls. Together they show how people lived in the past.

Before digging starts, the place is often investigated without a spade. Aerial photographs sometimes show hidden walls as lines in the corn. With **ground-penetrating radar** or magnetic measurements, remains of walls can be tracked down without opening the ground. The top layer of soil is then often carefully removed with a **digger**.

Over centuries many layers build up on top of each other in the ground, like the pages of a pile of newspapers. The **deeper layers** are usually older; this is what **stratigraphy** studies. A **plan** is a horizontally exposed surface, and a **section** is a vertical cut that shows the layers. Archaeologists dig very slowly with trowels, brushes and small tools so that nothing breaks.

Because the layers are **destroyed for ever** during digging, everything has to be documented. The area is divided into squares of equal size so that the find spot of every object can be recorded exactly. Every find is photographed, drawn and measured in. Small finds go into labelled bags, and the earth is sieved to find tiny things such as beads or seeds.

In Switzerland the **cantonal archaeology services** are responsible for excavations. Many digs are **rescue excavations** before houses, roads or tunnels are built, because otherwise the finds would be destroyed. Famous sites are the Roman town of **Augusta Raurica** near Basel and the pile-dwelling settlements on lake shores. Since 2011 the prehistoric pile dwellings around the Alps have been a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

In the laboratory the finds are cleaned, examined and restored. With the **radiocarbon method** or from the tree rings in wood, it is possible to work out how old something is. The results are published in reports. Later you can see the finest pieces in the museum.

begriffe.erklaerung: Science that studies the human past from finds in the ground.
Movable object from the past, for example a pottery fragment or a coin.
Immovable trace in the ground, for example a post hole or a wall.
The study of the order of the layers in the ground.
Excavation before a building project so that finds are not lost.

gewusst: From dark stains in the ground, archaeologists can recognise the ground plan of wooden houses even though the wood rotted away long ago.
In the mud on lake shores wood is sometimes preserved for thousands of years, because hardly any oxygen gets there.
Many archaeologists say that an excavation is like a book that you tear up page by page as you read it.

teile.einleitung: A bacterial colony is a visible heap of identical bacteria that are all descended from a single cell. Single bacteria are tiny, but a colony of millions of cells can be seen as a dot with the naked eye. Researchers grow colonies on culture media in order to study and identify bacteria.
wichtigste: A bacterial colony is a visible heap of identical bacteria.
It forms when a single bacterium divides again and again.
Colonies are grown in a flat dish with a lid, the Petri dish.
The culture medium is usually made firm with agar, a substance from algae.
In the 19th century Robert Koch introduced solid culture media to obtain pure cultures.
The shape, colour and edge of a colony give clues to the kind of bacterium.
Petri dishes are incubated upside down so that no condensation drips onto the medium.

abschnitte.text: A single bacterium is only about a thousandth of a millimetre in size and invisible without a **microscope**. If it lands on a good culture medium, it divides into two cells again and again. One cell becomes two, four, eight and after a day often many millions. This heap is a **bacterial colony**, and because all the cells come from the same mother cell, they are almost identical.

Colonies are grown in a **Petri dish**, a flat round dish with a lid made of glass or plastic. It is named after the German researcher Julius Richard Petri, a colleague of Robert Koch. Inside is a **culture medium** with sugar, protein building blocks and salts. It is made firm by **agar**, a substance from red algae that does not melt even at body temperature.

After inoculation the dish goes into an **incubator**, which keeps it warm, for many bacteria at about 37 degrees, as in the human body. The dishes are placed upside down, that is, with the lid at the bottom. This way condensation from the lid does not drip onto the medium and smear the colonies. After one or two days the colonies can usually be seen clearly.

Each kind of bacterium forms typical colonies. They can be round or irregular, smooth or wrinkled, shiny or matt. Some are white, others yellow, red or even purple. The edge, whether smooth, wavy or frayed, is also a feature. For a reliable identification, however, laboratory tests are also needed.

abschnitte.titel: Robert Koch and the pure culture
abschnitte.text: The German doctor **Robert Koch** introduced solid culture media around 1881. This allowed him to separate individual colonies from each other and obtain a **pure culture**, that is, a culture of only one kind of bacterium. The idea of using agar instead of gelatine came from Fanny Hesse, the wife of a colleague, who knew agar from the kitchen. With these methods Koch discovered the pathogen that causes tuberculosis in 1882.

If you press an unwashed finger onto a culture medium and incubate the dish, many bacterial colonies grow. With a freshly washed finger there are far fewer. This experiment shows clearly why **handwashing** is so important. However, such experiments should only be done under supervision, and the dishes must be disposed of sealed afterwards, because harmful bacteria can also grow.

begriffe.erklaerung: A visible heap of identical bacteria descended from one cell.
A flat round dish with a lid for growing bacteria.
A substance from algae that makes the culture medium as firm as jelly.
A culture in which only one single kind of bacterium grows.
A base with nutrients on which bacteria can grow.

gewusst: Some bacteria such as Escherichia coli can divide about every 20 minutes under ideal conditions.
Agar is also used in desserts and gummy bears without gelatine.
Alexander Fleming discovered penicillin in 1928 because a mould on one of his dishes of bacteria made the colonies around it disappear.

teile.einleitung: The adaptive immune system is the part of our body’s defences that can learn. It recognises pathogens very precisely and remembers them, so that it can react much faster the next time. Vaccinations also work because of this.
wichtigste: The adaptive immune system is specific and has an immunological memory.
Its most important cells are B cells and T cells, both lymphocytes.
With a first infection it takes about a week for the defence to work fully.
The secondary response on renewed contact is faster and stronger.
Lymphocytes that have recognised a pathogen multiply strongly; this is called clonal expansion.
Only vertebrates with jaws have an adaptive immune system with antibodies.
If it attacks the body’s own tissue, an autoimmune disease develops.

abschnitte.text: Our body has two defence systems that work together. The **innate immune system** reacts at once but rather generally, for example with scavenger cells and fever. The **adaptive immune system** takes longer but recognises pathogens very precisely. This precision is called specificity, and in addition there is the immunological memory.

The most important cells are the **lymphocytes**, a group of white blood cells. B cells produce **antibodies**, proteins that fit exactly onto a particular feature of a pathogen, the antigen. Killer T cells destroy infected body cells. Helper T cells control the other immune cells with messenger substances, the cytokines.

With a first infection it takes about a week for the **primary response** to become effective. When a cell recognises the pathogen, it multiplies strongly; this is called **clonal expansion**. After that, memory cells often stay in the body for years. If the same pathogen comes again, the secondary response is faster and stronger, and you often do not get ill at all.

A **vaccination** uses the memory of the adaptive immune system. The vaccine shows the body harmless parts or weakened forms of a pathogen, and the body forms memory cells. In a real infection the defence is then already prepared. If ready-made antibodies are given instead, this is called passive immunisation, which works quickly but lasts only a few weeks.

Only **jawed vertebrates**, that is, vertebrates with jaws such as fish, birds and mammals, have an adaptive immune system with antibodies. Lymphocytes form in the bone marrow; T cells also mature in the thymus gland behind the breastbone. Sometimes the system mistakenly attacks the body’s own tissue; this is an autoimmune disease such as type 1 diabetes. In allergies it reacts far too strongly to harmless substances such as pollen.

begriffe.erklaerung: Feature of a pathogen that is recognised by the immune system.
Protein that binds exactly to a particular antigen.
White blood cell, for example a B cell or T cell.
Immune cell that remembers a pathogen for a long time.

gewusst: The body can form antibodies against millions of different features, even against pathogens it has never met.
Thanks to the immune memory, anyone who has had chickenpox usually does not get it a second time.
The name lymphocyte comes from lymph, a fluid in which these cells travel around the body.

teile.einleitung: Observing means looking and listening very carefully and recording what you notice. Observation is one of the most important methods of science. Many great discoveries began with someone patiently observing and noticing something new.
wichtigste: Anyone who observes looks closely and notices things with all their senses.
With a magnifying glass you can see small animals such as ants bigger.
Birds in the distance are watched with binoculars.
With a microscope you can see tiny things that are invisible to the naked eye.
Animals in the forest are best watched quietly and calmly.
Jane Goodall became famous because she watched wild chimpanzees for many years.
In 1610 Galileo Galilei discovered moons of Jupiter with his telescope.

abschnitte.text: In an **observation** you notice something attentively and on purpose. You use not only your eyes but all your senses: you hear whether a bird is singing, and you smell whether a flower has a scent. It is important to describe exactly what you really see and not to interpret it straight away. Researchers write down their observations in a **record** with the date, place and time.

Many things are too small or too far away for our eyes. With a **magnifying glass** you can see ants, leaves or stones bigger. **Binoculars** bring faraway birds or chamois close. With a **microscope** you can see tiny cells and bacteria, and a telescope shows moons and planets. Today camera traps, cameras and measuring instruments also help with observing.

If you want to watch animals in the forest, it is best to be **quiet and calm**. Wear clothes that do not stand out, move slowly and wait patiently. Good times are early in the morning and at dusk, when many animals are active. Keep your distance and do not disturb the animals, especially not when they have young. In Switzerland nature conservation organisations often offer guided wildlife watching.

In 1960 the Briton **Jane Goodall** began watching wild chimpanzees in Gombe in Tanzania. She spent decades with the animals and got to know each one. In doing so she was the first to see that chimpanzees use tools, for example twigs with which they fish termites out of their mound. Until then people had believed that only humans could make tools. Goodall worked all her life to protect the animals and died in 2025.

abschnitte.titel: Galileo and the moons of Jupiter
abschnitte.text: In 1610 the Italian researcher **Galileo Galilei** pointed his home-made telescope at the planet Jupiter. He noticed small points of light that changed their position from night to night. Galileo realised that they are **moons** orbiting Jupiter. This observation showed that not everything goes round the Earth, and it changed people’s view of the world.

In science, observation is often at the start of a question. This leads to a guess, which is tested with an **experiment** in which something is changed on purpose. To make observations reliable, they are repeated and compared with others. In **citizen science** projects children and adults also report their observations, for example of birds or butterflies, and so help research.

begriffe.erklaerung: Careful, purposeful noticing with the senses.
A written note of what you have observed.
A device that shows tiny things greatly enlarged.
A test in which something is changed on purpose to check a guess.
Research in which non-experts also help, for example with observations.

gewusst: The four large moons of Jupiter that Galileo discovered are still called the Galilean moons today.
Jane Goodall gave the chimpanzees names instead of numbers, which was unusual at the time.
When watching birds, you can often recognise many of them more quickly by their song than by how they look.

teile.einleitung: Albert Einstein was one of the most famous physicists of all time and developed the theory of relativity. He changed our understanding of space, time, light and gravity. He spent an important part of his life in Switzerland, where he studied and had his most important ideas.
wichtigste: Albert Einstein lived from 1879 to 1955.
He was born in Ulm in Germany and became a Swiss citizen in 1901.
He studied at ETH Zurich and later worked at the patent office in Bern.
In 1905 he published the special theory of relativity and the formula E = mc².
In 1915 the general theory of relativity about gravity followed.
In 1921 he received the Nobel Prize in Physics.
From 1933 he lived in the USA.

abschnitte.text: Albert Einstein was born in Ulm on 14 March 1879 and grew up in Munich. Even as a child he was fascinated by a compass, because an invisible force moved the needle. He took his school-leaving exam, the Matura, in 1896 at the cantonal school in **Aarau**. After that he studied at the Polytechnic in Zurich, today’s **ETH Zurich**, to become a teacher of mathematics and physics.

After his studies Einstein at first found no post at a university. From 1902 he worked at the **patent office** in Bern, checking inventions. In his spare time he did research, and in 1905 he published several groundbreaking papers at once. That is why 1905 is called his **miracle year**. His flat on the Kramgasse in Bern is now a museum, the Einstein House.

The **special theory of relativity** of 1905 says that time and space are not the same for everyone. For someone moving very fast, time passes more slowly. The famous formula E = mc² also follows from it, according to which mass and energy are connected. In the **general theory of relativity** of 1915 he explained gravity as a curving of space and time.

When a solar eclipse in 1919 confirmed that light is bent by the Sun, Einstein became world-famous. In 1921 he received the **Nobel Prize** in Physics, but for explaining the photoelectric effect. He taught at the universities of Zurich, Prague and Berlin, among others. When the National Socialists came to power, the Jewish scientist emigrated to the USA in 1933 and worked in Princeton.

Without Einstein’s theories the GPS navigation system would not work accurately, because the clocks in the satellites run differently. He also predicted **gravitational waves**, which were measured for the first time in 2015. Einstein campaigned for peace and warned against nuclear weapons. He died in Princeton on 18 April 1955.

begriffe.erklaerung: Einstein’s theory about space, time, motion and gravity.
An office that checks whether an invention is new and protects it.
Light can knock tiny particles, electrons, out of metal.
Tiny waves in space that form when very heavy bodies in space move.

gewusst: Einstein was a Swiss citizen for almost his whole life, even when he lived in America.
Einstein liked playing the violin and played it well.
The chemical element einsteinium is named after him.

teile.einleitung: Alan Turing was a British mathematician and is regarded as one of the fathers of computer science. During the Second World War he helped at Bletchley Park to decipher the secret radio messages of the German Enigma. His ideas about computing machines and artificial intelligence still have an effect today.
wichtigste: Alan Turing was born in Great Britain in 1912.
He studied mathematics at the University of Cambridge.
In 1936 he described the imaginary computing model of the Turing machine.
During the Second World War he worked at Bletchley Park as a codebreaker.
He helped develop the Bombe, a machine for deciphering the Enigma.
With the Turing test he asked the question whether machines can think.
The Turing Award is the most important prize in computer science.

abschnitte.text: Alan Turing was born in London on 23 June 1912. Even as a child he was fascinated by numbers and science. He studied **mathematics** at the University of Cambridge and later also did research at Princeton in the USA. He died in 1954, aged only 41.

In 1936 Turing described an imaginary computing model, the **Turing machine**. It consists of an endless tape divided into squares, a read and write head and simple rules. Turing showed that such a simple machine can in principle compute anything that can be computed at all. In this way he laid the foundation for every modern computer, long before such machines existed.

During the Second World War the German army encrypted its radio messages with the **Enigma**, a machine with turning rotors. Poland was the first to crack the Enigma and passed its knowledge on to the British and French in 1939. One weakness helped the codebreakers: no letter was ever encrypted as itself. This allowed them to rule out many possible settings from the start.

At **Bletchley Park**, a country estate north of London, thousands of people worked in secret on deciphering messages. Turing helped develop the **Bombe** there, an electromechanical machine that searched for the daily Enigma keys. Another computing machine, called Colossus, was used not for the Enigma but for the Lorenz cipher machine. Many experts believe that the work at Bletchley Park shortened the war.

After the war Turing designed one of the first computers with a stored program. In 1950 he proposed the **Turing test**: a person has a written conversation with a partner and has to find out whether it is a human or a machine. With modern chat programs this question is more topical than ever. Turing also studied how patterns such as spots and stripes on animals form in nature.

The **Turing Award** has been given since 1966; it is regarded as a kind of Nobel Prize for computer science. Since 2021 Turing has been pictured on the British 50-pound note. Bletchley Park is now a museum where you can see real Enigma machines and a replica of the Bombe. Turing’s life has also been told in films and books.

begriffe.erklaerung: The science of processing information with computers.
Changing a message so that only people in the know can read it.
An imaginary, very simple model of a computer.
Exact step-by-step instructions for solving a task.

gewusst: Turing was an excellent long-distance runner and ran a marathon in under three hours.
The work at Bletchley Park remained top secret for decades, and many of those involved were never allowed to talk about it.

teile.einleitung: The bearded vulture is one of the largest birds of the Alps and has a special preference: it eats almost nothing but bones. In the past it was wrongly persecuted and wiped out in the Alps. Since 1991 bearded vultures have been released again in Switzerland, and today they are circling over our mountains once more.
wichtigste: The bearded vulture eats mainly bones.
It gets its name from the black feathers under its beak, which look like a beard.
It drops large bones onto rocks until they break.
Its breast is often orange because it bathes in iron-rich mud.
Its wingspan is almost three metres.
It was wiped out in the Alps in the past.
In 1991 the first bearded vultures were released in the Swiss National Park.
It is not dangerous to people, because it only eats dead animals.

abschnitte.text: With a wingspan of almost three metres, the **bearded vulture** is one of the largest birds in Europe. It weighs about five to seven kilograms. The head, neck and breast are pale, often coloured orange, and the back and wings are dark. Under its beak it has black feathers that look like a **beard** and gave it its name. Its red eye rings and long wedge-shaped tail are also striking.

The bearded vulture feeds mostly on the **bones** of dead animals such as chamois, ibex or sheep. Its stomach acid is so strong that it can dissolve bones. It swallows small bones whole. It carries large bones into the air and drops them onto rocks until they break. In Spain it is therefore called the bone breaker.

The bearded vulture’s breast is actually white. But it bathes in **iron-rich mud** or water and rubs itself in it. The iron oxide colours its plumage rusty red to orange. Why it does this is not fully understood; perhaps a strong colour shows others of its kind how strong a bird is.

The bearded vulture lives in high mountains with steep rock faces, for example in the Alps, the Pyrenees, the Himalayas and Africa. It glides for hours along the slopes looking for carcasses. It builds its nest in rock niches. It breeds in the middle of winter so that in spring the chick gets enough food from the animals that died during the winter.

In the past people wrongly believed that the bearded vulture stole lambs or even children and called it the lamb vulture. That is why it was hunted and poisoned until it had been **wiped out** in the whole of the Alps at the beginning of the 20th century. From 1986 an international **reintroduction project** began with birds from zoos and breeding stations. In 1991 the first bearded vultures in Switzerland were released in the **Swiss National Park** in the Engadine.

Later more release sites were added, for example in the Calfeisen Valley in the canton of St Gallen and in Central Switzerland. In 2007 a wild pair of bearded vultures bred successfully in Switzerland for the first time in more than a hundred years. Today there is a growing population in the Alps again. The Pro Bartgeier foundation follows the birds with transmitters and counts them regularly.

begriffe.erklaerung: An animal that feeds on dead animals.
The body of a dead animal.
An animal species that had died out is released again in its old habitat.
The distance from one wing tip to the other with the wings spread out.

gewusst: The bearded vulture’s stomach acid is extremely acidic and can even dissolve bones.
The old name lamb vulture is based on a mistake, because the bird does not hunt living lambs.
Young bearded vultures are still quite dark and only get their pale plumage after a few years.
