teile.einleitung: Alfred Nobel was a Swedish chemist and inventor who invented dynamite. He became very rich from his explosives. In his will he decided that his fortune should be used for prizes, and that is how the famous Nobel Prizes came about.
wichtigste: Alfred Nobel lived from 1833 to 1896.
He was born in Stockholm in Sweden.
In 1867 he received the patent for dynamite.
Dynamite made the dangerous explosive nitroglycerine safer.
Nobel held more than 350 patents and owned many factories.
Since 1901 the Nobel Prizes have been awarded with his fortune.
The prizes are presented every year on 10 December, the anniversary of Nobel’s death.

abschnitte.text: Alfred Nobel was born in **Stockholm** on 21 October 1833. As a child he moved with his family to St Petersburg in Russia, where his father made mines and weapons. Alfred learnt several languages and studied chemistry in Paris and elsewhere. He travelled a lot and lived in Sweden, France and Italy.

The liquid explosive **nitroglycerine** was very powerful but exploded even with small shocks. In 1864 there was a serious explosion at the Nobel family’s factory near Stockholm. Alfred’s younger brother Emil was killed. After that, Nobel looked for a way to make the explosive safer.

Nobel discovered that a porous rock called **kieselguhr** can soak up nitroglycerine. This produced a solid mass that could be shaped and transported safely. In 1867 he patented this invention as **dynamite**. It was set off with a detonator, which Nobel had also developed.

Dynamite was soon used all over the world in mining, road building and the construction of tunnels. It was also used to build the **Gotthard railway tunnel** in Switzerland between 1872 and 1882. Sadly, explosives were also used in wars. Nobel founded more than 90 factories and companies in many countries.

In his will of 1895 Nobel decided that his money should reward people who had brought the greatest benefit to humanity. Since 1901 the **Nobel Prizes** have been awarded for physics, chemistry, medicine, literature and peace. Later a prize for economics was added. The first Nobel Peace Prize in 1901 went, among others, to **Henry Dunant** from Geneva, the founder of the Red Cross.

The prizes are presented every year on 10 December in Stockholm, and the Nobel Peace Prize in Oslo. Many researchers from Switzerland have received a Nobel Prize, for example the Geneva astronomers Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz in 2019. Alfred Nobel died in Sanremo in Italy on 10 December 1896. The chemical element **nobelium** is named after him.

begriffe.erklaerung: A substance that burns very fast and causes a powerful explosion.
A document in which someone sets out what should happen to their property after their death.
A soft, porous rock made from the shells of tiny algae.
A legal protection for an invention.

gewusst: Nobel also wrote poems and a play.
Nobel never married and had no children.

teile.einleitung: The ARPANET was a computer network in the USA and is regarded as the forerunner of today’s internet. In 1969 the first message was sent over it between two computers, but it broke off after two letters. We still use many ideas from the ARPANET today, such as data packets and email.
wichtigste: The ARPANET was funded by the US Department of Defense.
The first message was sent over the ARPANET in 1969.
Only the letters LO arrived before the system crashed.
The University of Utah was one of the first four nodes.
The ARPANET used packet switching.
The switching computers were called Interface Message Processors.
On 1 January 1983 the ARPANET switched over completely to TCP/IP.

abschnitte.text: After the Soviet Union had sent the first satellite, Sputnik, into space in 1957, the USA founded the research agency **ARPA**. It belonged to the Department of Defense and promoted new technology. One aim was to connect expensive mainframe computers at different universities with each other. This led to the idea of a computer network, the **ARPANET**.

On 29 October 1969 a student at the University of California in Los Angeles wanted to send the word LOGIN to a computer at Stanford. After the letters **LO** the system crashed. About an hour later the transmission worked completely. By the end of 1969 four **nodes** were connected, including the University of Utah.

The ARPANET used **packet switching**: a message is split into small packets that travel through the network separately. At the destination they are put back together, a bit like a jigsaw puzzle sent in several letters. If a line fails, the packets simply take a different route. The switching was done by separate small computers, the **Interface Message Processors**.

In 1971 the programmer **Ray Tomlinson** sent the first email between two computers and introduced the @ sign. Email soon became one of the most popular uses of the ARPANET. In the 1970s Vint Cerf and Bob Kahn developed the rules called **TCP/IP**, which allow different networks to work together. On 1 January 1983 the whole ARPANET switched over to them, which is regarded as the birth of the internet.

abschnitte.titel: From the ARPANET to the internet
abschnitte.text: The ARPANET grew to hundreds of computers and was switched off in 1990, because newer networks had taken over its tasks. The internet that grew out of it now connects billions of devices. The **World Wide Web** was invented in Switzerland: Tim Berners-Lee developed it from 1989 at the research centre **CERN** near Geneva. The web with its websites runs over the internet, but it is not the same thing as the internet.

begriffe.erklaerung: Several computers that are connected and exchange data.
A connected computer or distributor in a network.
Fixed rules for how computers exchange data with each other.
Data are divided into small packets and sent separately.

gewusst: So the very first message on the forerunner of the internet was just LO, which in English also sounds like an exclamation of surprise.
The first switching computers of the ARPANET were as big as a fridge.

teile.einleitung: The Antarctic is the region around the South Pole with the ice-covered continent of Antarctica in the middle. It is the coldest, windiest and driest place on Earth. Nobody lives there for ever, but researchers from many countries study the climate, ice and animals here.
wichtigste: Under the thick ice of the Antarctic lies solid land.
The Antarctic is bigger than Europe.
At its thickest points the ice is more than 4 kilometres thick.
It has already been almost minus 90 degrees cold there.
The Antarctic counts as a desert because very little snow and rain fall there.
Nobody lives in the Antarctic for their whole life.
A treaty between many countries allows only peaceful research.
It is summer there when it is winter here.

abschnitte.text: The Antarctic lies around the **South Pole**. Its core is the continent of **Antarctica**, which at around 14 million square kilometres is bigger than Europe. That is about 340 times the size of Switzerland. Almost the whole land is covered by a huge **ice sheet**, which at its thickest points is more than 4 kilometres thick. The highest mountain is the Vinson Massif at around 4900 metres.

The Antarctic is the coldest place on Earth. At the Russian station Vostok, minus 89.2 degrees was measured in 1983. Because very little **precipitation** falls, the Antarctic counts as the largest **cold desert** in the world. Icy downslope winds often blow from the high plateau down to the coast. Because it lies in the southern hemisphere, it is **summer** there when it is winter here, and the sun then shines for months at the South Pole.

Only a few animals live on the ice itself, but the coasts and the sea are full of life. **Emperor penguins** breed on the sea ice in the middle of the Antarctic winter. Adélie penguins, seals such as the leopard seal and many seabirds also live here. The sea teems with **krill**, small crustaceans that whales, seals and penguins feed on. There are no polar bears in the Antarctic; they only live in the Arctic.

For a long time nobody knew for sure whether there was a continent in the south at all. Only in 1820 did sailors first sight the Antarctic mainland. There was a famous race to the **South Pole**: the Norwegian **Roald Amundsen** reached it on 14 December 1911. The Briton Robert Falcon Scott arrived just over a month later and died with his companions on the way back.

In 1959 twelve countries signed the **Antarctic Treaty**; later many more joined, including Switzerland. It lays down that the Antarctic may only be used **peacefully**, above all for research. Military bases and mining are banned. There are many research stations; in summer a few thousand people work there, in winter far fewer. Nobody lives there for their whole life.

The ice of the Antarctic stores most of the Earth’s fresh water. If it melts, **sea level** rises worldwide. In cores drilled from the ice, researchers find air bubbles that are hundreds of thousands of years old. From these they can read how the climate changed in the past. Researchers from the University of Bern also take part in such studies.

begriffe.erklaerung: A very large connected part of the Earth, such as Europe or Africa.
The southernmost point of the Earth, around which the Earth turns.
A very cold area where hardly any precipitation falls.
Small, shrimp-like crustaceans that live in large swarms in the sea.
An agreement between many countries that protects the Antarctic for peace and research.

gewusst: In the Dry Valleys of the Antarctic it has not rained or snowed for a very long time.
At the South Pole the sun rises only once a year and sets only once.
Because all lines of longitude meet at the South Pole, you can walk round the whole world there in a few steps.

teile.einleitung: Speciation is the formation of new species of living things. It usually happens very slowly over many generations, when groups of a species become separated and develop differently. In this way the huge variety of animals and plants has arisen over the course of the Earth’s history.
wichtigste: The formation of new species is called speciation.
Often a population is first divided into separate groups.
In allopatric speciation, mountains, seas or rivers separate the groups.
In sympatric speciation, new species arise in the same area.
Many whitefish species formed in Swiss lakes after the last Ice Age.
In Lake Victoria in Africa, cichlid fish formed hundreds of species.
Species that occur only in one particular area are called endemic.

abschnitte.text: A **species** is made up of living things that can breed with each other and have offspring together. A dog and a wolf, for example, are regarded as closely related, but a dog and a cat are not. Speciation explains how one species becomes two or more species over time. Charles Darwin described this idea in 1859 in his famous book on the origin of species.

Speciation often begins when a **population** is divided into separate groups. This can happen because of a mountain range, a sea, a river or a desert. The groups then adapt differently to their surroundings over many generations. This form is called **allopatric speciation** and is regarded as the most common.

abschnitte.titel: New species in the same place
abschnitte.text: Sometimes new species also arise in the same area without any outside barrier; this is called **sympatric speciation**. One example is the **whitefish** in Swiss lakes such as Lake Constance, Lake Lucerne or Lake Thun. After the last Ice Age, different groups used different depths and food and developed into separate species. In a similar way, hundreds of species of cichlid fish arose in Lake Victoria in Africa.

On remote islands, animals and plants are separated from the mainland for a long time. That is why species often develop there that exist nowhere else; they are **endemic**. Famous examples are **Darwin’s finches** on the Galápagos Islands, whose beaks are shaped very differently depending on their food. Many endemic animals also live on Madagascar, for example the lemurs.

Speciation is the reason for the great **biodiversity** on Earth. It shows that nature is constantly changing, even if we hardly notice it in our own lives. But research on whitefish also shows that species can disappear again if their habitats change a lot. When Swiss lakes were over-fertilised by sewage in the 20th century, some whitefish species were lost.

begriffe.erklaerung: Group of living things that can have offspring together.
Group of living things of one species that live in the same area.
Occurring only in one particular area in the world.
Change that helps a living thing in its surroundings.

gewusst: Many whitefish species in Swiss lakes each occur in only a single lake.
The cichlids in Lake Victoria split into a great many species in what is a very short time in the history of the Earth.

teile.einleitung: Aerogel is one of the lightest solid materials there is. Because it consists almost entirely of air and looks bluish and see-through, it is also called “frozen smoke”. Even so, it is solid and protects extremely well against heat and cold.
wichtigste: Aerogel is a solid material whose volume is more than 90 per cent air.
Because of its smoky, see-through look it is called “frozen smoke”.
The American Samuel Kistler made the first aerogel in 1931.
The most common aerogel is made of silicon dioxide, the substance that sand and glass are also made of.
It is made from a gel that loses its liquid through supercritical drying without collapsing.
Aerogel is an excellent heat insulator.
The NASA probe Stardust used aerogel to catch dust from a comet.
Empa, together with an industrial partner, developed an aerogel insulating render for building façades.

abschnitte.text: An aerogel is a solid foam with tiny pores that are much smaller than the thickness of a hair. More than 90 per cent of its volume, often even more than 99 per cent, is filled with **air**. The solid framework is usually made of **silicon dioxide**. That is why a piece of aerogel is extremely light and feels almost like solid smoke. But it is brittle and can crumble under pressure.

First a **gel** is made, that is, a fine framework filled with liquid, a bit like a jelly. If you simply let it dry, the liquid would pull the delicate framework together as it evaporated. That is why **supercritical drying** is used: under high pressure and the right temperature, the liquid enters a state between gas and liquid. In this way it can escape without the framework collapsing.

The American chemist **Samuel Kistler** was the first to make an aerogel, in 1931. He supposedly wanted to prove that the liquid in a gel could be replaced by gas. For a long time aerogel stayed expensive and was hardly used. Only from the 1980s did production become easier, and research increased greatly. Today there are also aerogels made of carbon, metal oxides or cellulose.

Because the tiny pores hardly conduct heat, aerogel is an excellent **insulating material**. Even a thin layer holds back as much heat as a much thicker layer of conventional material. The Swiss research institute **Empa** in Dübendorf developed an **insulating render** with aerogel for façades together with an industrial partner. It is especially suitable for old houses whose appearance should be preserved. Mats for pipes and clothing for extreme cold also contain aerogel.

The NASA probe **Stardust** was launched in 1999 and flew to the comet Wild 2. There it used panels of aerogel to catch tiny **dust grains** from the comet. The grains bored into the soft material and were gently slowed down instead of burning up or shattering. In 2006 the capsule with the samples landed back on Earth. Aerogel was also used as heat protection for the electronics on Mars rovers.

begriffe.erklaerung: A solid, extremely light material that consists almost entirely of air in tiny pores.
A fine framework of particles in which liquid is trapped, as in jelly.
A drying method under high pressure in which the framework of the gel does not collapse.
Protection against heat escaping through a wall or a material.
A substance made of silicon and oxygen, which quartz sand and glass are also made of.

gewusst: A piece of aerogel can carry many times its own weight, even though it consists almost entirely of air.
If you hold a flame under a thin aerogel panel, you can lay a flower on top without it burning.
Aerogel holds several entries in the Guinness Book of Records, including as one of the lightest solids.

teile.einleitung: Behaviourism is a school of psychology that studies only what can be observed from outside: behaviour. Thoughts and feelings were deliberately left out. With experiments on dogs, cats, rats and pigeons, behaviourists found out how living things learn.
wichtigste: Behaviourism studies mainly behaviour that can be observed.
It was founded in 1913 by the US psychologist John B. Watson.
Ivan Pavlov discovered classical conditioning with dogs.
Burrhus F. Skinner developed operant conditioning and the Skinner box.
Edward Thorndike set out the law of effect using cats in puzzle boxes.
Reward and reinforcement make a behaviour more frequent, punishment makes it rarer.
From about 1960 behaviourism lost influence, because people also wanted to study thinking.

abschnitte.text: The word comes from **behaviour**. Behaviourists thought that you cannot look inside a person’s head. That is why psychology should measure what a living thing does and which **stimulus** it reacts to. In 1913 John B. Watson demanded that psychology should work as strictly as the natural sciences.

The Russian physiologist **Ivan Pavlov** was actually researching digestion and received the Nobel Prize for it in 1904. While doing so he noticed that his dogs started producing saliva before the food arrived. If a signal always sounded before feeding, the dogs soon drooled at the signal alone. This learning by connection is called **classical conditioning**.

Edward Thorndike shut cats in puzzle boxes from which they could free themselves with a lever. He set out the **law of effect**: behaviour with pleasant consequences is repeated. **Burrhus F. Skinner** built operant conditioning on this and invented the Skinner box, in which rats or pigeons got food for pressing a key. In negative reinforcement an unpleasant stimulus is removed, and this too makes a behaviour more frequent.

With **shaping**, a new behaviour is formed step by step by rewarding closer and closer attempts. This is how animal trainers teach dogs or dolphins complicated tricks. If the reinforcement stops, a learnt response gradually disappears again. This process is called **extinction**.

Watson’s **Little Albert experiment** of 1920 showed that fear can be conditioned in a small child. Today this experiment is considered ethically unacceptable. In 1959 the linguist **Noam Chomsky** criticised Skinner’s explanation of how children learn to speak. He argued that language cannot be explained by imitation and reward alone.

After that, **cognitive psychology** put thinking, remembering and planning at the centre. Even so, the learning rules of behaviourism are still used today. Examples are reward systems in schools, dog training or behaviour therapy for fears. Apps and games also use rewards on purpose so that people keep coming back.

begriffe.erklaerung: Something a living thing perceives, for example a sound or a light.
Learning in which a connection forms between a stimulus, a behaviour and a consequence.
A consequence that makes a behaviour more frequent, for example a reward.
The slow disappearance of a learnt behaviour when the reinforcement stops.

gewusst: During the Second World War Skinner worked on a plan to train pigeons to guide missiles.
Pavlov received his Nobel Prize not for conditioning but for researching digestion.
If your mouth waters at the smell of pizza, that is a form of conditioning.

teile.einleitung: Baker’s yeast is a tiny single-celled fungus that makes bread and Zopf, the Swiss plaited loaf, light and airy. In the dough it eats sugar and produces gas bubbles that make the dough rise. Without yeast there would be no Sunday Zopf and no airy bread.
wichtigste: Baker’s yeast is a fungus and consists of single, microscopically small cells.
Its scientific name is Saccharomyces cerevisiae.
Yeast feeds on sugar and produces the gas carbon dioxide.
The gas bubbles make the dough rise and create the holes in bread.
Yeast works best at a lukewarm temperature.
In the hot oven the yeast dies.
You can buy yeast fresh as a block or dried as dried yeast.

abschnitte.text: **Baker’s yeast** is one of the **fungi**, but it is not a mushroom with a cap and stalk like those in the forest. It consists of single round cells that are only a few thousandths of a millimetre in size. One gram of fresh yeast contains many billions of such cells. Its scientific name **Saccharomyces cerevisiae** means roughly sugar fungus of beer. That is because the same kind of yeast is also used for brewing beer and making wine.

Yeast loves to eat **sugar**, including the sugar that comes from the starch in flour. In **fermentation** it produces the gas **carbon dioxide** and a little alcohol. The gas stays trapped in the stretchy dough and forms countless small bubbles. This makes the dough bigger and airy. The holes in the finished bread are the traces of these gas bubbles; the alcohol evaporates during baking.

Yeast is a living thing and needs the right temperature. That is why **lukewarm** milk or lukewarm water is used for a yeast dough, because too hot harms the yeast and too cold makes it sluggish. Then the dough is left to rest, covered, so that the yeast has time to work. In the hot **oven** the yeast dies, and the shape of the bread becomes firm. A dough can also rise slowly overnight in the fridge, which often gives more flavour.

In the shop there is **fresh yeast** as a light brown, soft block in the chiller cabinet. It only keeps for about two weeks and must be stored cool. **Dried yeast** is yeast dried into a powder in a sachet and keeps for many months. Baker’s yeast is made in factories, where it is grown in large tanks of sugar solution, usually made from molasses.

In Switzerland the **Zopf** is the best-known yeast bake; many families eat it on Sunday morning. Gipfeli (Swiss croissants), Grittibänzen (bread men) and pizza are also made with yeast. People have been baking light bread for thousands of years, but for a long time they did not know why it rose. Only the French researcher **Louis Pasteur** showed in the 19th century that living yeast cells cause fermentation.

begriffe.erklaerung: A process in which yeast turns sugar into gas and alcohol without oxygen.
An invisible gas that puffs up the dough, chemically CO₂.
A living thing that consists of only one single cell.
Yeast dried into a powder that keeps for a long time.
The way yeast cells multiply: a small daughter cell grows out of a cell.

gewusst: Yeast cells multiply by growing a small bud on a cell, which then breaks off.
As well as wild yeasts, sourdough contains lactic acid bacteria, which is why sourdough bread tastes slightly sour.
A yeast dough can roughly double its volume as it rises.

teile.einleitung: Tardigrades are tiny animals with eight little legs that plod through moss like little bears. They are among the toughest living things in the world. When dried out, they survive cold, heat, radiation and even a trip into space.
wichtigste: Tardigrades have eight legs with small claws.
Most are smaller than half a millimetre.
They do not consist of one cell but are animals made of many cells.
They are easy to find in moss.
If their moss dries out, they draw themselves together into a little barrel.
They got their German name, “little bears”, because they plod slowly like a bear.
Dried-out tardigrades have already survived in space.

abschnitte.text: **Tardigrades** are usually only 0.1 to 0.5 millimetres in size; the largest reach just over a millimetre. Their body is plump and has four pairs of legs, that is, eight legs. On their feet there are small **claws** with which they hold on. Because they walk slowly and clumsily like a bear, the German pastor Johann August Ephraim Goeze called them “little water bears” in 1773. Even though they are so tiny, they have a brain, muscles and a gut.

Tardigrades live almost everywhere on Earth: in the sea, in lakes, in the soil and above all in **moss** and lichens. They have been found in high mountains, in the deep sea and in Antarctica. Well over a thousand species are now known. They are easy to find in Switzerland too, for example in a cushion of moss from a wall or a roof.

Many tardigrades suck out plant cells from mosses and algae. For this they have two pointed mouth stylets with which they pierce the cells. Other species eat tiny animals such as roundworms or rotifers. To be active, they always need a thin film of water around them.

If the moss dries out, tardigrades pull in their legs and head and become a dry **tun**, a little barrel. In this state, called **cryptobiosis**, their metabolism almost stops. In this way they survive temperatures close to absolute zero, great heat and radiation that would be deadly for humans. When they get water again, they often come back to life after minutes to hours.

In 2007 researchers sent dried-out tardigrades into **space** on a satellite. There they were exposed to the vacuum and the cold surroundings for ten days. After their return many woke up again and went on living. This made them the first animals to have survived unprotected in space.

Put a piece of dry moss in a bowl of water overnight. The next day squeeze out the moss and look at the water with a magnifying glass or a simple microscope. With some patience you can see the little animals slowly crawling about. Researchers study tardigrades to understand how sensitive substances such as vaccines could be made to keep better.

begriffe.erklaerung: A state in which a living thing has almost no metabolism left and so survives.
The dried-up, barrel-shaped form of a tardigrade when it has no water.
A device with which you can see tiny things greatly enlarged.
All the processes in the body by which food is turned into energy and building materials.

gewusst: Dried-out tardigrades can last for many years and then come back to life.
Tardigrades can stand radiation hundreds of times stronger than what would kill a human.
Almost every cushion of moss on a Swiss wall can contain tardigrades.

teile.einleitung: Al-Khwarizmi was a Persian scholar who lived in Baghdad more than 1100 years ago and is regarded as one of the most important mathematicians of the Middle Ages. The word “algorithm” comes from his name, and the word “algebra” from the title of one of his books. Without him we might still be calculating with Roman numerals today.
wichtigste: Al-Khwarizmi lived from about 780 to 850.
He worked in Baghdad at the famous “House of Wisdom”.
His patron was the caliph al-Ma’mun.
In one book he solved quadratic equations systematically.
The word algebra comes from the word “al-jabr” in the book’s title, which means “completing”.
He made the Indian numerals with zero known in the Arab world.
The word algorithm goes back to his name.

abschnitte.text: His full name was **Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi**. The surname means “the one from Khwarazm”, a region on the River Amu Darya in present-day Uzbekistan. He lived from about 780 to 850 and was a mathematician, astronomer and geographer. Little is known about his personal life, but his books became world-famous.

Al-Khwarizmi worked in **Baghdad**, at that time one of the largest and richest cities in the world. There the caliph **al-Ma’mun** supported the “House of Wisdom”, a kind of library and research centre. Scholars there translated books from Greek, Persian and Indian languages into Arabic. In this way a lot of ancient knowledge came together and was developed further.

Around the year 820 Al-Khwarizmi wrote a book about calculating by **completing and balancing**. In it he solved quadratic equations step by step and explained the methods with words and geometric drawings, because letters and equals signs were not yet used then. The Arabic word “al-jabr” roughly means completing. In Europe this became the word **algebra**.

In another book he explained how to calculate with the **Indian numerals** from 1 to 9 and zero. With this place-value system it is much easier to calculate than with Roman numerals such as MCMXC. The book was translated into Latin in the 12th century and began with the words “Dixit Algorizmi”, that is, “Algorizmi has said”. From this name came the word **algorithm** for exact instructions for a calculation.

Al-Khwarizmi also calculated **astronomical tables** that could be used to work out the positions of the Sun, Moon and planets. He revised the description of the Earth by the Greek scholar Ptolemy and listed the positions of cities, mountains and rivers. Such tables helped with keeping time and with working out the direction of prayer towards Mecca. His works were still used centuries later.

Through Latin translations his knowledge reached Europe and changed the way people calculated there. The numerals we now call “Arabic numerals” slowly caught on in this way. Every computer program is based on **algorithms**, whose name reminds us of him. In Uzbekistan he is honoured with monuments, and a university bears his name.

begriffe.erklaerung: Branch of mathematics in which you calculate with equations and unknown numbers.
Exact step-by-step instructions for solving a task.
A ruler in the Islamic world.
An equation in which an unknown number appears multiplied by itself.
Way of writing numbers in which the value of a digit depends on the position it is in.

gewusst: The numerals we call “Arabic” actually come from India.
Al-Khwarizmi wrote his equations entirely without symbols such as x or =, using only words.
On a Soviet stamp from 1983, Al-Khwarizmi was honoured for his 1200th birthday, which was celebrated at that time.

teile.einleitung: Amber is fossilised resin from trees that grew millions of years ago. It looks like a golden yellow gemstone but is light and feels warm in the hand. Sometimes tiny insects are trapped inside, enclosed since prehistoric times as if in a time capsule.
wichtigste: Amber is fossil tree resin, that is, ancient resin that has hardened.
The best-known amber comes from the Baltic Sea and is around 40 million years old.
In amber you sometimes find trapped insects or bits of plants.
If you rub amber on wool, it attracts small scraps of paper.
The word electricity comes from the Greek name for amber, “elektron”.
Amber is very light and can burn.
Amber has been made into jewellery since the Stone Age.

abschnitte.text: Many trees, above all conifers, give off a sticky **resin** when they are injured. It seals wounds and protects the tree from pests. If resin is covered by earth or sand, it can harden over millions of years. Volatile substances evaporate, and the resin becomes **fossil** resin, amber. So amber is not a real mineral but a substance from plants.

When the resin was still liquid, midges, ants, spiders or leaves sometimes got stuck to it. The resin flowed around them and so enclosed them perfectly. Such **inclusions** are very valuable for researchers, because they show what animals and plants looked like millions of years ago. Even fine hairs and wing veins can often still be seen.

If you rub amber on a woollen cloth, it becomes **electrostatically** charged and attracts light things such as scraps of paper or hair. The ancient Greeks already observed this. They called amber “**elektron**”, and later the word electricity came from it. So a piece of tree resin gave its name to a whole field of physics.

Amber is much lighter than stones and feels warm in the hand. It even floats in very salty water, which is why it is washed up on the beach on the Baltic coast after storms. It is soft and easy to polish. Amber can burn; it burns with a sooty flame and smells of resin, which is also where its German name comes from, Bernstein, meaning roughly “burning stone”.

abschnitte.titel: Where it is found and how it is used
abschnitte.text: The largest deposits are on the **Baltic Sea**, especially near Kaliningrad in Russia. A lot of amber is also found in the Dominican Republic and in Myanmar. People already wore amber as jewellery in the Stone Age, and it was carried along old trade routes as far as the Mediterranean. The **Amber Room** is famous: a splendid room with walls made of amber, which disappeared during the Second World War and was later rebuilt.

begriffe.erklaerung: Sticky sap that trees give off when they are injured.
Preserved from prehistoric times and turned to stone or hardened.
An animal or bit of plant that is trapped in amber.
Electric charge that builds up through rubbing and can attract things.

gewusst: Amber floats in very salty water, but it sinks in fresh water.
Most pieces of amber are golden yellow, but there are also white, red, green and even bluish ones.
Because real amber with inclusions is very valuable, fakes are sometimes made from plastic.

teile.einleitung: An anemometer is an instrument for measuring wind speed. You often see one on weather stations, ships, airports or mountain tops, where small cups spin in the wind. Its readings help with weather forecasts, storm warnings and running wind turbines.
wichtigste: An anemometer measures wind speed.
The name comes from the Greek word “anemos” for wind.
The cup anemometer has three or four spinning half-cups.
An ultrasonic anemometer measures the wind using the travel time of sound signals.
10 metres per second equals 36 kilometres per hour.
A short, violent burst of wind is called a gust.
In aviation and shipping, wind is often given in knots.
On the Beaufort scale, force 12 means a hurricane.

abschnitte.text: An **anemometer** is a device that measures how fast the wind is blowing. The name is made up of the Greek “anemos” for wind and “metron” for measure. It is often combined with a **wind vane**, which shows the wind direction. Anemometers are found on weather stations, airports, ships, bridges, cable cars and wind turbines. MeteoSwiss runs automatic measuring stations all over the country that record the wind constantly.

The best known is the **cup anemometer**, with three or four half-cups on a cross that can turn. The wind pushes harder into the open side of a cup than onto its rounded back, so the cross turns. The faster the wind, the faster it spins. The **ultrasonic anemometer** has no moving parts. It sends sound signals back and forth between small transmitters and measures how much the wind speeds them up or slows them down.

Wind speed is given in metres per second, kilometres per hour or **knots**. To convert metres per second into kilometres per hour, you multiply by 3.6. So 10 metres per second equals exactly 36 km/h. A knot is one nautical mile per hour, that is, about 1.85 km/h. In aviation and shipping the knot is the usual unit.

At the beginning of the 19th century the British admiral **Francis Beaufort** developed a scale for estimating wind strength without an instrument. It ranges from 0 for calm to 12 for a **hurricane** with more than 117 km/h. At force 6, for example, the wind whistles audibly in wires; at force 9 roof tiles can fall off. Short, violent blasts of wind are called **gusts**. For storm warnings, the peak gusts are often more important than the average wind.

As early as around 1450 the Italian scholar **Leon Battista Alberti** described a device with a plate that the wind pushes aside. The cup anemometer was invented by the Irish astronomer **Thomas Romney Robinson** in 1846. Later came hot-wire anemometers and ultrasonic devices. Today satellites and radar also measure the wind over large areas.

Without wind measurements good **weather forecasts** would hardly be possible. Airports need them so that aeroplanes can take off and land safely. Cable cars and cranes have to stop in strong winds, and anemometers make sure of this. Wind turbines turn to face the wind and switch off in a storm. The measured wind also plays an important role in ski jumping or sailing.

begriffe.erklaerung: How fast the air is moving.
A short, violent burst of wind.
A unit of speed in aviation and shipping, one nautical mile per hour.
A scale from 0 to 12 that divides wind strength according to its effects.
Sound that is so high that people cannot hear it.

gewusst: The highest wind gust ever measured outside tornadoes reached more than 400 km/h in Australia in 1996.
On many Swiss mountain tops there are weather stations that have to measure the wind even in ice and storms.
In ski jumping the wind is measured at several points along the jump and included in the scoring.

teile.einleitung: Archaeopteryx is a famous prehistoric animal that lived around 150 million years ago. It had feathers and wings like a bird, but also teeth, claws and a long tail like a reptile. That is why it is often called the “first bird”.
wichtigste: Archaeopteryx is called the “first bird” because it had features of birds and reptiles.
It lived in the Jurassic, around 150 million years ago.
Its fossils were found near Solnhofen in Bavaria.
On its wings it had claws on its fingers.
How well Archaeopteryx could fly is still disputed among experts today.
One of the most famous specimens is in the Natural History Museum in London.
In Greek the name means roughly “ancient feather”.

abschnitte.text: Archaeopteryx was about the size of a magpie or a raven. It had feathers and **wings** like a bird. At the same time it had small pointed **teeth**, three fingers with **claws** on each wing and a long bony tail. Today’s birds, on the other hand, have a toothless beak and only a short stump of bone as a tail.

Archaeopteryx lived in the **Jurassic** period, when many dinosaurs also roamed the Earth. Today’s Bavaria was then a warm landscape of islands on a shallow sea with lagoons. The fine lime mud at the bottom of these lagoons covered dead animals and preserved them in great detail. It turned into the **Solnhofen limestone**, in which you can even see the imprints of individual feathers.

In 1861 first a single feather and shortly afterwards a skeleton were discovered near Solnhofen. This specimen was bought by the **Natural History Museum** in London. Later the Berlin specimen was found, which is considered the finest because the head and wings are well preserved. To this day only about a dozen skeletons are known.

The find came at exactly the right time: in 1859 Charles Darwin had published his **theory of evolution**. Archaeopteryx showed that there were animals that stood between reptiles and birds. Today researchers know that birds are descended from small meat-eating dinosaurs. Archaeopteryx is therefore one of the best-known fossils in the world.

Whether and how well Archaeopteryx could fly is still **disputed** today. Its feathers were shaped like those of today’s flying birds. But it lacked a large breastbone and strong flight muscles. Many experts think that it could at least flutter or glide short distances.

begriffe.erklaerung: Petrified remains or imprint of a living thing from prehistoric times.
A period of Earth’s history about 200 to 145 million years ago, named after the Jura Mountains.
The slow change of living things over many generations.
Fine limestone that can be split into thin slabs.

gewusst: The Jurassic period is named after the Jura Mountains, which also lie in Switzerland.
One specimen of Archaeopteryx was thought for a long time to be a small dinosaur, until the feather imprints were noticed.
Fish, dragonflies and pterosaurs are also found in the Solnhofen limestone.

teile.einleitung: Fear is a strong feeling that everyone knows. It warns us of danger and gets the body ready in a flash to run away or defend itself. Sometimes, though, fear is bigger than it needs to be, and then it helps to talk about it.
wichtigste: Fear is useful because it warns of danger.
When you are afraid, your heart often beats faster.
When you get a big fright, your body often jumps.
Many children are afraid of the dark at night; a small night light often helps.
Slow, deep breathing calms you down when you are worked up.
If a fear bothers you for a long time, it is good to talk to someone you trust.
Animals feel fear too; the opossum often plays dead when in danger.

abschnitte.text: Fear is a **feeling**, just like joy, anger or sadness. It arises when we see something as dangerous or threatening. Even our ancestors in the Stone Age needed fear to be on their guard against wild animals or thunderstorms. Without fear we would act much more recklessly, for example simply running across a busy road.

In the brain there is a small area, the **amygdala**, that recognises dangers very quickly. It raises the alarm, and the body releases the hormone **adrenaline**. The heart beats faster, you breathe more quickly, the muscles tense up and you may sweat. Sometimes you also get goose bumps or a funny feeling in your tummy.

Experts speak of the **fight-or-flight response**. The body gets ready to run away or defend itself. Some animals freeze instead, so that enemies do not notice them. The opossum from America even plays dead when in danger and then lies completely still.

Many younger children are afraid of the **dark**, of thunderstorms, dogs or monsters under the bed. Older children are more likely to be afraid of tests, of being laughed at or of having no friends. Such fears are normal and often get smaller as you grow older. A night light, a cuddly toy or an open door can help at night.

**Breathing** slowly and deeply calms the body, for example breathing in for four seconds and out for six. It also helps to put the fear into words and talk about it with parents, teachers or friends. If you face a fear in small steps, you often notice that it gets weaker. Exercise, enough sleep and doing things you enjoy also make you stronger.

Sometimes fear becomes so strong that it gets in the way of everyday life; this is called an **anxiety disorder**. A very strong fear of something particular, for example spiders or small spaces, is called a **phobia**. Such fears can be treated well with the help of professionals. In Switzerland children and young people can also call the Pro Juventute number 147 free of charge at any time.

begriffe.erklaerung: A hormone that quickly gets the body ready for action when there is danger.
A small part of the brain that recognises danger and triggers fear.
A very strong fear of something particular that is much bigger than the real danger.
Someone you trust and can talk to about your worries.

gewusst: Goose bumps are left over from the time when our ancestors had much more body hair.
Some people like being scared, for example on a roller coaster, because afterwards the body releases happy feelings.
Many adults are afraid of giving a speech in front of other people.

teile.einleitung: An antibiotic is a medicine that kills bacteria or stops them from multiplying. Since the discovery of penicillin in 1928, antibiotics have saved millions of lives. But because bacteria can become resistant, they must be used carefully.
wichtigste: Antibiotics work against bacteria, not against viruses.
Penicillin was discovered by Alexander Fleming in 1928.
The first penicillin came from a mould.
In Switzerland a doctor prescribes an antibiotic, and you collect it from the chemist’s with a prescription.
You take it for as long as the doctor says.
Using it too often or wrongly makes bacteria resistant.
Bacteria against which almost no antibiotic works any more are called multi-resistant germs.

abschnitte.text: An **antibiotic** is a medicine against **bacteria**, tiny living things that can cause pneumonia or middle ear infections, for example. It kills the bacteria or stops them from multiplying. An antibiotic does not help against **viruses**, which cause colds and flu, for example. Children often take it as a tablet or syrup; in hospital it is sometimes given through a drip.

In 1928 the Scottish researcher **Alexander Fleming** in London noticed that a mould on one of his dishes of bacteria had killed the bacteria all around it. He called the active substance **penicillin**. Only more than ten years later did other researchers manage to produce penicillin in larger amounts. In 1945 Fleming received the Nobel Prize in Medicine together with Howard Florey and Ernst Chain.

Penicillin disturbs the building of the bacteria’s **cell wall**, so that they burst. Other antibiotics block, for example, the making of proteins in the bacterial cell. Human cells are built differently and are therefore hardly attacked. However, antibiotics can also harm useful bacteria in the gut, which sometimes leads to tummy ache or diarrhoea.

In Switzerland a doctor prescribes an antibiotic, and you collect it with the prescription from the **chemist’s**. You take it exactly as long and as often as the doctor says. Leftover tablets are returned to the chemist’s instead of being thrown away or used yourself later. You should never share antibiotics with other people.

If antibiotics are used too often or wrongly, bacteria can become **resistant**, and the drug no longer works against them. The surviving bacteria pass on this resistance. Bacteria against which almost no antibiotic works any more are called **multi-resistant germs**; they are feared in hospitals. That is why in 2015 Switzerland adopted a national strategy against antibiotic resistance that covers people, animals and farming.

Before antibiotics were discovered, many people died of infections that are easy to cure today, for example an infected wound. Many operations have also only become safe thanks to antibiotics. Antibiotics are also used for sick animals. Researchers are constantly looking for new active substances, because bacteria keep adapting.

begriffe.erklaerung: Tiny single-celled living things, some of which cause illness.
An even smaller pathogen against which antibiotics do not work.
When a medicine no longer works against a pathogen.
A written order from the doctor with which you get a medicine.

gewusst: Fleming’s discovery was an accident: before his holiday he had left a dish of bacteria standing open.
Many antibiotics come from fungi or bacteria in the soil, which use them to defend themselves against competitors.

teile.einleitung: The demarcation problem is a big question in the philosophy of science: how can you tell whether something is science or not? It is about distinguishing science from pseudoscience, belief or mere opinion. The answer by the philosopher Karl Popper became especially famous.
wichtigste: The demarcation problem asks how to distinguish science from non-science.
Karl Popper proposed falsifiability as the criterion.
A scientific theory must be able to be disproved by observations.
Popper named astrology as an example of a theory that protects itself against being disproved.
Imre Lakatos distinguished progressive from degenerating research programmes.
Larry Laudan declared the demarcation problem a failure in 1983.
The question also matters in court and in schools.

abschnitte.text: Many statements claim to be scientific. The **demarcation problem** asks which features distinguish real science from **pseudoscience**. This is important because we rely on trustworthy knowledge in medicine, technology and environmental protection. Philosophers have been arguing about the right answer for almost a hundred years.

The Austrian-British philosopher **Karl Popper** published his book “Logik der Forschung” (The Logic of Scientific Discovery) in 1934. He argued that a theory is only scientific if it could be disproved by an observation; this is called **falsifiability**. The statement “All swans are white” is scientific, because a single black swan would disprove it. “Tomorrow it will rain or it will not rain”, on the other hand, is always true and therefore not empirical.

Popper named **astrology** as an example of a teaching that is worded so vaguely that it can never fail. Anyone who rescues a theory after every wrong prediction with excuses made up afterwards is using an **immunisation strategy**. This makes a theory impossible to attack, but also empty. Real science, by contrast, dares to make clear predictions that can go wrong.

Before Popper, the Vienna Circle had proposed that only statements that can be checked should count as meaningful. The Hungarian philosopher **Imre Lakatos** argued that whole research programmes should be judged. Progressive programmes predict new facts, while degenerating ones only lag behind the observations. Thomas Kuhn stressed that science is also shaped by communities and their shared ways of thinking.

In a well-known essay in 1983, the American philosopher **Larry Laudan** declared the demarcation problem a failure, because no single criterion fits all cases. Even so, answers are needed in everyday life. In 1982 a US judge in the case McLean v. Arkansas had to decide whether creationism could be taught as science in biology lessons, and ruled that it could not. Today several features are usually checked together, such as testability, openness to criticism and progress.

begriffe.erklaerung: Branch of philosophy that studies how science works.
A statement can be disproved by an observation.
A teaching that seems scientific but is not.
Shielding a theory from all criticism with excuses.

gewusst: According to Popper, a general theory can never be finally proved, only not yet disproved.
Black swans, the famous example of a disproof, really do live in Australia.
Popper was originally impressed by Einstein’s theory of relativity too, because it made bold predictions that could be tested.

teile.einleitung: Archaeology is the science that studies how people lived in the past. For this, archaeologists search the ground for traces such as pottery fragments, tools, walls or bones. Like detectives, they put together a picture of the past from many small clues.
wichtigste: Archaeology studies how people lived in the past.
The Greek word “archaios” means old.
The things discovered in the ground are called finds.
Dinosaur bones are not studied by archaeologists but by palaeontologists.
The age of old wood can be worked out from its tree rings.
Archaeologists explore sites under water by diving.
In Switzerland the cantonal archaeology service in each canton looks after old finds.

abschnitte.text: The word is made up of the Greek words **archaios** for old and logos for study. Archaeology examines traces left by people from past times, from the Stone Age to the Middle Ages and beyond. It is especially important for times from which there are no written records. After they have been studied, important finds often go to a **museum**, where everyone can look at them.

In an **excavation** the ground is carefully removed layer by layer, often with small trowels, brushes and sieves. Every find spot is measured exactly, photographed and drawn. Because an excavation destroys the site, this **documentation** is very important. Often digging is done before a house or road is built; this is called a rescue excavation.

From old **bones** you can tell how old a person became, whether they were ill and sometimes even what they ate. Fragments of pots show how people cooked and which patterns they liked. The age of wood is worked out from the tree rings; this method is called **dendrochronology**. The radiocarbon method can also be used to estimate the age of bones, seeds or remains of cloth.

In many Swiss lakes lie the remains of **pile dwellings**, that is, villages from the Stone Age and Bronze Age on the lake shore. To study them, archaeologists dive in the cold, murky water. Because there is hardly any oxygen in the mud under water, wood, seeds and even remains of bread are astonishingly well preserved. Since 2011 the prehistoric pile dwellings around the Alps have been a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

In Switzerland every canton has a **cantonal archaeology service**, which protects sites and carries out excavations. Well-known places are the Roman town of **Augusta Raurica** near Basel and the legionary camp of Vindonissa in Windisch. A whole stage of the Iron Age is even named after the site of La Tène on Lake Neuchâtel. On the Schnidejoch in the Bernese Alps, melting ice has released objects that are several thousand years old.

Today aeroplanes, **drones** and laser scans from the air also help to discover hidden walls under meadows and forests. With ground-penetrating radar you can look into the earth without digging. In the laboratory experts study the genetic material from old bones and find out where people came from. Anyone who makes a find themselves must report it to the canton in Switzerland, because archaeological finds belong to the public.

begriffe.erklaerung: An object that is discovered in the ground during an excavation.
Carefully uncovering old traces in the ground.
A method of working out the age of wood from its tree rings.
Houses on posts that stood on lake shores in the Stone Age and Bronze Age.
The science of fossils such as dinosaurs, not of people.

gewusst: Even an old rubbish pit is a treasure for archaeologists, because it reveals a lot about people’s everyday lives.
In Swiss pile-dwelling settlements remains of bread more than 5000 years old have been found.
The glacier mummy Ötzi was found in 1991 in the Ötztal Alps on the border between Austria and Italy.

teile.einleitung: Antarctic krill is a small, reddish, see-through crustacean that lives in huge swarms in the Southern Ocean around Antarctica. Although a single animal is only about as long as a little finger, krill is one of the most important animals on Earth. Almost all life in the icy sea depends on it directly or indirectly.
wichtigste: Krill is a small crustacean and grows to around 6 centimetres long.
It feeds mainly on tiny algae, the plant plankton.
Krill lives in swarms that can be many kilometres across.
The blue whale, the largest animal on Earth, eats mainly krill.
Despite its name, the crabeater seal feeds almost only on krill.
Thanks to light organs, krill can give off light.
Krill is caught mainly for fish feed and krill oil.

abschnitte.text: The scientific name of Antarctic krill is **Euphausia superba**. It has a see-through shell with red spots, large black eyes and many small legs. A fully grown animal is around 6 centimetres long and weighs only about 1 to 2 grams. On its body there are **light organs** with which krill can give off greenish-blue light.

Krill lives in the cold **Southern Ocean**, which surrounds Antarctica. There it forms huge swarms in which thousands of animals can swim in one cubic metre of water. Such swarms are sometimes so big that they can even be seen as reddish patches on satellite images. According to estimates, all the Antarctic krill together weighs several hundred million tonnes.

Krill eats mainly tiny algae, the so-called **phytoplankton**. With its fine, hairy front legs it forms a catching basket and filters the algae out of the water. In winter, when few algae drift in the open water, it scrapes algae off the underside of the sea ice. If it finds no food for a long time, it can even become a little smaller when it moults and so save energy.

Krill is right at the bottom of the **food chain** and is therefore vital for almost all larger animals in the Antarctic. Blue whales, fin whales and humpback whales filter it out of the sea by the tonne. Penguins such as the Adélie penguin, many fish, squid and seabirds also eat krill. The crabeater seal even has special teeth that work like a sieve.

Since the 1970s ships have been catching krill in large quantities. It is used mainly to make **fish feed** for fish farms and krill oil as a food supplement. So that not too much is caught, an international commission for the conservation of Antarctic marine life sets catch limits. Climate change is a danger, because when the sea ice shrinks, young krill find less food and shelter in winter.

begriffe.erklaerung: Animal with a hard shell and many legs, such as a crab, lobster or krill.
Tiny living things that float in the water and are carried by the current.
A very large group of animals that move together.
A sequence showing who eats whom, for example alga, krill, whale.

gewusst: A blue whale can eat several tonnes of krill in a single day.
The word krill comes from Norwegian and means roughly young fry of fish.
Krill can live for several years, which is astonishingly long for such a small crustacean.

teile.einleitung: Sorting rubbish means separating waste by type so that as much of it as possible can be recycled. In this way old bottles, cans and newspapers become new products, and fewer raw materials and less energy are needed. In Switzerland sorting rubbish is part of everyday life for almost every family.
wichtigste: Sorted rubbish can be recycled, that is, made into new products.
In Switzerland the household waste from the rubbish bag is burned.
Many municipalities charge a fee per rubbish bag.
Paper, glass, PET, aluminium and green waste are collected separately.
Broken electrical appliances are taken back to a specialist shop or a collection point.
Anyone who simply throws rubbish on the ground is littering.
Avoiding rubbish is even better than sorting it.

abschnitte.text: Many materials in rubbish are valuable **raw materials**. Old glass becomes new glass, waste paper becomes cardboard or newsprint, and melted-down aluminium can be reused almost endlessly. This reuse is called **recycling**. It saves energy, protects nature and reduces the amount of rubbish.

abschnitte.titel: What happens to household waste in Switzerland
abschnitte.text: Whatever is not recycled goes into the rubbish bag as **household waste** (in Swiss German Kehricht). In Switzerland, burnable waste has not been allowed to go to landfill since 2000. It is burned in a **waste incineration plant**. The heat is used to produce electricity and heat homes. In many municipalities you pay a bag fee for every rubbish bag, so sorting also pays off for your purse.

In many municipalities **waste paper** and cardboard are tied into bundles with string and put out by the roadside. Glass is taken to the bottle bank sorted by colour, that is, clear, brown and green. PET bottles and empty aluminium cans go into the right collection containers, which are often right where you do your shopping. Vegetable peelings and garden waste go into the **green waste** or onto the compost heap.

Some waste is dangerous for the environment and never belongs in the household waste. Batteries contain harmful substances and must go back to a shop that sells them. A specialist shop takes back broken electrical appliances, including electric toys, free of charge. Paints, medicines and chemicals are handed in at special collection points or at the chemist’s.

When someone carelessly throws rubbish on the ground, this is called **littering**. In many Swiss towns and cantons this can mean a fine. Dropped rubbish harms animals, pollutes lakes and meadows and costs a lot of money to clean up. The best thing is not to create rubbish in the first place, for example by using a water bottle or a snack box instead of throwaway packaging.

begriffe.erklaerung: Turning waste back into new raw materials or products.
Swiss word for the mixed waste in the rubbish bag.
Fee you pay when you buy official rubbish bags.
Carelessly throwing away or leaving rubbish in public places.
Plant waste from the kitchen and garden, from which compost or biogas is made.

gewusst: Aluminium can be melted down again and again without losing quality.
In digestion plants green waste can be turned into biogas, which can even power vehicles.
Switzerland is one of the countries that produce especially much rubbish per person, but it also collects and recycles a great deal of it.

teile.einleitung: Antarctica is the continent around the South Pole. It is almost completely covered by a huge sheet of ice and is the coldest, windiest and driest place on Earth. No people live here permanently, but penguins, seals and researchers on temporary stays do.
wichtigste: Antarctica is the continent around the South Pole and is surrounded by the Southern Ocean.
Around 98 per cent of its area is covered by ice.
In 1983 a temperature of around -89 °C was measured at a research station.
Despite all the ice, Antarctica counts as a desert, because very little precipitation falls.
The highest mountain is Mount Vinson.
The Transantarctic Mountains divide the continent into East and West Antarctica.
Summer there is from December to February.

abschnitte.text: Antarctica lies around the **South Pole** and is surrounded by the Southern Ocean. The continent covers about 14 million square kilometres, that is, more than 300 times the size of Switzerland. The **Transantarctic Mountains** divide it into the larger East Antarctica and the smaller West Antarctica. The highest mountain is Mount Vinson at almost 4900 metres.

Around 98 per cent of the area is covered by an enormous **ice sheet**. In some places the ice is more than 4000 metres thick. It holds most of the Earth’s fresh water. If all the ice melted, sea level worldwide would rise by many dozens of metres.

On 21 July 1983 a temperature of around -89 °C was measured at the Russian station **Vostok**, the lowest air temperature ever measured at a station. Because hardly any precipitation falls, Antarctica counts as a **cold desert**. Ice-cold downslope winds rush down from the mountains and reach enormous speeds. Because Antarctica lies in the southern hemisphere, summer there is from December to February, and in winter it stays dark for weeks.

abschnitte.titel: Animals at the edge of the ice
abschnitte.text: On the coasts live **emperor penguins**, Adélie penguins, seals such as the Weddell seal and many seabirds. In the sea there are huge swarms of **krill**, small crustaceans that are food for whales, penguins and seals. In the interior there is almost no life, at most lichens, mosses and tiny animals. There are no land mammals such as polar bears in Antarctica; they live in the Arctic.

Only in the 19th century did sailors first sight the continent. On 14 December 1911 the Norwegian **Roald Amundsen** was the first to reach the South Pole. The Briton Robert Scott arrived about a month later and died with his companions on the way back. Today there is an American research station at the South Pole.

Since the **Antarctic Treaty** of 1959, Antarctica has not belonged to any one country and may only be used peacefully. Mining for mineral resources is banned, and nature is specially protected. Switzerland has also joined the treaty, and Swiss researchers work there, for example on ice drilling. With **ice cores** the climate can be traced back hundreds of thousands of years, because tiny air bubbles from the past are trapped in the ice.

begriffe.erklaerung: A very large, connected piece of land, for example Europe or Africa.
A huge, very thick layer of ice that covers a whole country.
Small crustaceans that live in huge swarms in the sea.
A long column of ice drilled out of the ice that tells us about the climate of the past.

gewusst: In Antarctica there are valleys where hardly any rain or snow has fallen for millions of years.
The emperor penguin breeds in the middle of the Antarctic winter in freezing temperatures.
Antarctica has no time zone of its own; the stations usually use the time of their home country or the country that supplies them.

teile.einleitung: In biology, analogy means that body parts of different living things look similar or do the same job even though they do not come from the same ancestor. A good example is the wings of birds and insects. Analogies show that nature often finds similar solutions to the same problems.
wichtigste: Analogy means similarity because of the same function without common descent.
Analogous structures arise through convergent evolution.
The wings of a bird and an insect are analogous.
The mole cricket has digging legs that resemble the front legs of the mole.
Bats and toothed whales developed echolocation independently of each other.
The eyes of octopuses and vertebrates are analogous; octopuses have no blind spot.
In systematics such similarities are called homoplasy.

abschnitte.text: The word **analogy** comes from Greek and means “correspondence”. In biology it refers to features that are similar because they have the same **function**, not because they were inherited from the same ancestor. A bird’s wing consists of bones, muscles and feathers. An insect’s wing, on the other hand, is a thin skin made of chitin. Both are used for flying, but they arose completely independently.

Analogous features arise through **convergent evolution**, that is, a development that runs together. When different living things live in similar environments, similar solutions are often selected. Sharks, dolphins and the extinct ichthyosaurs, for example, all have a streamlined body shape, even though a fish, a mammal and a reptile have little to do with each other. Water simply requires a shape that glides through it well.

The **mole cricket** is an insect with broad digging shovels on its front legs that strongly resemble the hands of a mole. Both dig tunnels in the earth, but they are not closely related. **Bats** and **toothed whales** such as dolphins find their way around with sound that bounces back from objects. They invented this echolocation independently of each other. Octopuses and vertebrates have also each developed a **lens eye**, but in the octopus the nerves lie behind the retina, so it has no blind spot.

In the dry regions of Africa, column-shaped **spurges** grow that look confusingly like American **cacti**. Both store water in their thick stems and have thorns instead of large leaves. Even so, they belong to completely different plant families. You can tell the difference, for example, by the white milky sap of the spurge, which can be poisonous.

The counterpart of analogy is **homology**. Homologous organs come from the same ancestor, even if they look different today. The human arm, the bat’s wing and the whale’s flipper, for example, have the same basic bone plan. In systematics, a similarity without common descent is called **homoplasy**. Researchers must tell the two apart carefully, otherwise they put living things in the wrong place in the family tree.

begriffe.erklaerung: Similarity of features because of the same job, not because of common origin.
Similarity of features because they come from the same ancestor.
When unrelated living things independently develop similar features.
Finding your way by sending out sounds and listening to the echo.
Technical term for a similarity that is not based on common descent.

gewusst: In the history of the Earth, flight was invented independently at least four times: by insects, pterosaurs, birds and bats.
The word “analogy” is also used in language, for example when new words are formed on the pattern of known words.
The Australian marsupial mole looks astonishingly like the mole, even though it is a marsupial.

teile.einleitung: The Antarctic Circumnavigation Expedition, ACE for short, was a large research voyage all the way round Antarctica. It took place from December 2016 to March 2017 and was organised by the Swiss Polar Institute. Researchers from all over the world studied how climate change and pollution are changing the Southern Ocean.
wichtigste: The expedition took place in the southern summer from December 2016 to March 2017.
It was the first large expedition of the Swiss Polar Institute.
The research ship was called the Akademik Treshnikov.
It started and ended in Cape Town in South Africa.
The voyage was divided into three legs.
The focus was on the Southern Ocean with the Antarctic Circumpolar Current.
Remote sub-Antarctic islands were visited on purpose.
One main aim was to research the effects of climate change and pollution.

abschnitte.text: The **Antarctic Circumnavigation Expedition** was a scientific voyage round Antarctica. It was organised by the **Swiss Polar Institute**, which was founded in 2016 by EPFL, ETH Zurich, the University of Bern and the research institute WSL, among others. It was this institute’s first large expedition. Around 150 researchers and helpers from 21 countries took part. In this way Switzerland, even though it has no sea, became a host of polar research.

The voyage took place on board the Russian research ship **Akademik Treshnikov**. It began and ended in **Cape Town** in South Africa. The first leg went to Hobart in Tasmania, the second to Punta Arenas in Chile and the third back to Cape Town. Altogether the ship travelled more than 33,000 kilometres. The expedition took place in the **southern summer**, when the sea ice draws back and the weather is a little calmer.

The focus was on the **Southern Ocean**, the sea around Antarctica. There the **Antarctic Circumpolar Current** flows all the way round the continent; it is the most powerful ocean current on Earth. The ship followed this current from west to east. The Southern Ocean takes up a lot of heat and carbon dioxide from the air and is therefore very important for the climate of the whole Earth.

As well as taking measurements on the open sea, the expedition visited **sub-Antarctic islands** on purpose. These islands lie far from inhabited land and are only rarely studied. Many seabirds, penguins and seals live there. The researchers studied plants, animals, soils and glaciers on the islands. They also wanted to find out whether species brought in from elsewhere threaten the native wildlife.

One main aim was to study the effects of **climate change** and **pollution** in the Southern Ocean. The teams worked on more than 20 projects, for example on plankton, sea ice, air quality, whales and **microplastics**. They took water, air and ice samples that were still being analysed years later. The data were made freely available to all researchers. In this way they help to predict the climate of the future better.

begriffe.erklaerung: A research journey to a little-known area.
An ocean current that flows all the way round Antarctica.
Areas that lie north of Antarctica in the cold Southern Ocean.
Tiny living things that float in the water and are food for many animals.
Very small plastic particles that get into water, soil and air.

gewusst: The Swiss Polar Institute is based in Switzerland, a country with no sea and no polar regions.
Before the actual expedition, the ship sailed with students on board from Bremerhaven in Germany to Cape Town.
The Antarctic Circumpolar Current carries many times more water than all the rivers on Earth put together.

teile.einleitung: Baking powder is a fine white powder that makes cake mixture light and airy. In the oven it forms small gas bubbles that make the mixture rise. Without baking powder a cake would be as flat and hard as a brick.
wichtigste: Baking powder makes dough light by producing carbon dioxide during baking.
The most important ingredient is bicarbonate of soda, a white powder.
In addition there is an acid and usually some starch.
Baking powder works best when the mixture gets wet and hot.
A mixture with baking powder does not need to rest but goes into the oven soon.
Baking powder is first mixed with the flour.
It is used mainly for sponge-type cakes such as a loaf cake.

abschnitte.text: **Baking powder** is a **raising agent**, that is, a substance that makes dough rise. It looks like a fine white powder and is usually sold in small sachets. It consists of three parts: bicarbonate of soda, an acid and a separating agent such as cornflour. The starch makes sure that the bicarbonate and the acid stay dry in the sachet and do not react too early.

The chemical name of **bicarbonate of soda** is sodium hydrogen carbonate. When it comes into contact with water and an acid, the gas **carbon dioxide** is produced. Part of it forms while stirring, but the larger part only forms with the heat of the oven. The many small gas bubbles expand in the heat and puff up the mixture. When the mixture sets, the holes remain as a light crumb.

Baking powder is used mainly for **cake mixtures** such as loaf cakes, muffins or marble cake. It is first mixed with the flour so that it spreads evenly and does not form lumps. Unlike a yeast dough, a mixture with baking powder does not need to rest for hours. It goes into the preheated oven soon after mixing, otherwise too much gas escapes.

abschnitte.titel: Do not open the oven too early
abschnitte.text: While it is baking, the cake is still soft, and the gas bubbles hold it up. If you open the oven too early, cold air streams in and the gas contracts. Then the **cake sinks** and becomes soggy in the middle. At the end you check whether a cake is done with a wooden skewer: if no mixture sticks to it, it is cooked through.

In the past dough was made to rise with **yeast** or sourdough, which took a long time. In the 19th century chemists in Europe and America developed the first baking powders. In Germany the pharmacist August Oetker sold baking powder in small sachets for one cake from the 1890s. This made baking cakes at home much easier and more popular.

begriffe.erklaerung: A substance that makes dough light with gas bubbles.
A white powder, chemically sodium hydrogen carbonate, that forms gas with acid.
An invisible gas that is also found in sparkling mineral water.
A soft mixture that is stirred, for example for a loaf cake.

gewusst: Bicarbonate of soda, the main ingredient of baking powder, is also used for cleaning and against heartburn.
If you add some baking powder to vinegar, it foams up strongly at once, because a lot of gas is produced.
Baking powder loses its strength over time if it is stored somewhere damp.

teile.einleitung: A barometer is an instrument for measuring air pressure. Air pressure exists because the air above us has weight and presses on everything. You can read on a barometer whether the weather is more likely to get better or worse.
wichtigste: Evangelista Torricelli invented the mercury barometer in 1643.
At normal air pressure at sea level the column of mercury is 760 millimetres high.
An aneroid barometer works with an airless metal capsule that changes shape depending on the air pressure.
A barograph records the air pressure continuously as a curve.
Rapidly falling air pressure usually points to the weather getting worse.
Climbers’ altimeters work on the principle of the barometer.
The Greek word “baros” means weight.

abschnitte.text: The Earth’s atmosphere is many kilometres thick and has weight. This weight presses on everything beneath it; this is called **air pressure**. At sea level normal air pressure is about **1013 hectopascals**. We do not feel it because our body pushes back from inside just as strongly.

In 1643 the Italian researcher **Evangelista Torricelli** filled a glass tube with mercury and stood it upside down in a dish. The mercury only sank down to a height of about 76 centimetres, that is, 760 millimetres. Above it an almost empty space formed, a **vacuum**. Torricelli realised that the pressure of the air on the dish holds up the column.

In 1648 the Frenchman Blaise Pascal had his brother-in-law carry a barometer up the mountain **Puy de Dôme** in France. At the top the column of mercury was clearly shorter than down in the valley. This proved that air pressure decreases with height. Today the unit of pressure is named after Pascal.

Mercury is poisonous and heavy, so today an **aneroid barometer** is usually used. Inside there is a flat, airless metal capsule that is squeezed a little when the pressure is high and expands again when the pressure is low. A pointer makes these small movements visible. A **barograph** records the pressure continuously as a curve on paper, and many mobile phones today have tiny electronic pressure sensors.

High air pressure usually brings fine, dry weather; this is called a **high**. If the air pressure falls quickly, a low with clouds, rain or wind is often approaching. That is why many old barometers are marked “Fair”, “Change” and “Rain”. What matters more than the exact value is whether the pressure is rising or falling.

Because air pressure decreases as you go up, a barometer can also be used to work out **height**. Climbers’ altimeters, hiking watches and aircraft altimeters are based on this. On the Jungfraujoch, at around 3450 metres, the air pressure is only about two thirds of the value at sea level. By the way, a barometer with water instead of mercury would have to be about 10 metres high, because water is much lighter.

begriffe.erklaerung: The force with which the air presses on everything because of its weight.
The unit in which air pressure is usually given in weather reports.
A space with almost no air left in it.
A barometer that records the air pressure as a curve.
Areas of high or low air pressure that determine the weather.

gewusst: The air presses on every square centimetre of our skin about as hard as a weight of one kilogram.
Anyone who changes height quickly in a lift or aeroplane often feels the changed air pressure in their ears.
The name barometer literally means something like weight measurer.

teile.einleitung: The Bee-Bot is a small robot in the shape of a yellow and black bee. Children program it with buttons on its back so that it follows a particular route. In this way you learn through play how computers carry out commands one after the other.
wichtigste: The Bee-Bot looks like a bee and is yellow and black.
You program it with buttons on its back.
One step forward is 15 centimetres long.
A turn command turns the Bee-Bot a quarter turn.
With the GO button it sets off and carries out all the commands.
If it is to go 3 squares straight ahead, you press the forward button 3 times.
The Bee-Bot is often used in kindergarten and primary school.

abschnitte.text: The **Bee-Bot** is a small learning robot from England that looks like a bee. It has yellow and black stripes and big eyes. It was made for children from about four years old. You need no computer and no tablet to use it.

On its back the Bee-Bot has several **buttons**: arrows for forward, backward, left and right. With the **GO** button it starts, and with a pause button it waits for a moment. The clear button deletes all stored commands. This is important, because otherwise the Bee-Bot adds new commands to the old ones.

A step forward or backward is always exactly **15 centimetres** long. That is why there are matching play mats with squares of 15 by 15 centimetres. With left or right, the Bee-Bot turns on the spot by a **quarter turn**, that is, by 90 degrees. After each step it flashes and beeps briefly, so you can count along.

Anyone who controls the Bee-Bot is actually writing a small **program**, that is, a series of commands. You have to think ahead: how many squares must it go, and where must it turn? If it goes the wrong way, you look for the mistake and correct it; this is called **debugging**. Programmers work in exactly the same way.

In Switzerland computing is part of the subject Media and Computer Science in the **Lehrplan 21** curriculum. The Bee-Bot is used in many kindergartens and primary schools.
