Children build routes on a map, for example, and let the bee travel from flower to flower. For older children there are similar robots that are controlled with a tablet.

begriffe.erklaerung: A machine that carries out tasks according to a program.
A series of commands that a computer carries out one after the other.
A single instruction, for example “one step forward”.
Looking for and fixing mistakes in a program.

gewusst: The Bee-Bot has a rechargeable battery that can be charged with a cable.
The Bee-Bot has a brother called Blue-Bot, which is see-through and can also be controlled by tablet.
Two quarter turns one after the other make the Bee-Bot face exactly the opposite way.

teile.einleitung: Drug development is the long road from a first idea to a new medicine at the chemist’s. It usually takes 10 to 15 years and costs a great deal of money. Switzerland, with its large pharmaceutical companies in Basel, plays an important role in it worldwide.
wichtigste: Developing a new medicine typically takes about 10 to 15 years.
First a target is looked for, usually a protein on which the medicine is to act.
In high-throughput screening hundreds of thousands of substances are tested automatically.
A promising molecule is called a lead compound and is optimised further.
Only about one in ten candidates in clinical trials is finally approved.
A patent generally protects a new active substance for 20 years from the application.
In Switzerland Swissmedic decides on the approval of medicines.

abschnitte.text: At the start is the question of what goes wrong in the body in a disease. Researchers look for a **target**, that is, a target molecule, usually a protein, that can be influenced with a medicine. Then in **high-throughput screening** robots test hundreds of thousands of substances to see whether they act on the target. Today computers and artificial intelligence also help with this.

A molecule that shows a desired effect is called a **lead compound**. Chemists change it step by step so that it works better and has fewer side effects. Then, in the **preclinical** phase, it is tested in the laboratory on cells and, where required, on animals. This shows whether it is poisonous and how it is distributed and broken down in the body.

Only then is the active substance tested on people, in several **phases**. In phase I its tolerability is checked on a few healthy volunteers. In phases II and III more and more patients receive the medicine, often hundreds to thousands, to prove that it works and is safe. Only about one in ten candidates that reach clinical trials is approved in the end.

Before a medicine may be sold, an authority checks all the data; in Switzerland this is **Swissmedic** in Bern. Even after approval, doctors keep watching for rare side effects. A **patent** generally protects the new active substance for 20 years from the application, so that the high costs pay off. After that other companies may make cheaper copies, which are called generics.

Sometimes chance helps, as in 1928, when Alexander Fleming discovered **penicillin**. In **drug repurposing** a known active substance is used for a new disease, which saves time and money. Medicines for rare diseases are called **orphan drugs** and are given special support at approval. Without this support many such developments would hardly be worthwhile for companies.

The large pharmaceutical companies **Roche** and Novartis have their headquarters in Basel. There are also many smaller companies and research groups at universities such as ETH Zurich or the University of Basel. Pharmaceutical products are among Switzerland’s most important exports. Developing a single new medicine can cost more than a billion francs altogether.

begriffe.erklaerung: The substance in a medicine that has the actual effect.
The target molecule in the body on which a medicine is meant to act.
A carefully planned test of a new medicine on people.
A cheaper copy made after the patent has run out.
A medicine for a very rare disease.

gewusst: Of many thousands of substances tested at the beginning, often only a single one becomes a finished medicine.
The word orphan is used because for a long time hardly anyone looked after rare diseases.
In clinical trials often neither the participants nor the doctors know who is getting the real medicine, so that the result is not distorted.

teile.einleitung: The basic reproduction number, R0 for short and pronounced “R nought”, tells you how many other people an infected person infects on average when nobody is immune yet. It shows how quickly a disease can spread. It can also be used to calculate how many people need to be vaccinated to stop an epidemic.
wichtigste: R0 says how many people an infected person infects on average when everyone else can still catch the disease.
If the reproduction number stays below 1, an epidemic dies down.
With R0 equal to 4, at least 75 per cent must be immune to reach herd immunity.
Measles has a very high basic reproduction number, so a very high share of people must be vaccinated.
The effective reproduction number takes into account the current situation with immunity and measures.
R0 is not a fixed constant of nature but also depends on how people behave.
With R equal to 2 there are already 32 new cases in the fifth generation of infection.

abschnitte.text: The **basic reproduction number** R0 describes how infectious a disease is at the start of an outbreak. If R0 is 3, a sick person infects three other people on average. If R0 is greater than 1, the disease spreads; if it is less than 1, it disappears again. The value is an **average**; individual people can infect many more or nobody at all.

R0 depends on three things: how many **contacts** a sick person has, how likely an infection is per contact and how long the person is infectious. If someone has 10 contacts a day, infects with a 5 per cent chance at each contact and is infectious for 6 days, the result is 10 times 0.05 times 6, that is, about 3. Because people’s behaviour determines the contacts, R0 is not a fixed constant of nature. In a densely populated city the same pathogen can have a higher value than in a remote village.

If R is greater than 1, the number of cases grows **exponentially**, that is, faster and faster. With R equal to 2, one case infects two, these infect four, then eight, sixteen and already 32 in the fifth generation of infection. After ten generations there would already be more than a thousand new cases. That is why it is important to react very early in an outbreak.

When enough people are immune, the pathogen hardly finds any new victims; this is called **herd immunity**. The share needed is calculated with the formula 1 minus 1 divided by R0. With R0 equal to 4 that is 1 minus a quarter, that is, 75 per cent. **Measles**, with an R0 of about 12 to 18, is one of the most infectious diseases, so around 95 per cent of the population should be vaccinated. Herd immunity also protects people who cannot be vaccinated, for example babies.

During an epidemic people become immune, and there are protective measures. The **effective reproduction number** Re or Rt describes the current situation. You get it roughly by multiplying R0 by the share of people who can still catch the disease. If R0 is 3 and 40 per cent are immune, a sick person infects on average only 3 times 0.6, that is, 1.8 people. During the Covid-19 pandemic this number was estimated every day in Switzerland too and mentioned in the news.

The idea of the reproduction number comes from research on **malaria** at the beginning of the 20th century. The British doctor Ronald Ross and later George Macdonald developed mathematical models for it. Today R0 is an important tool of **epidemiology**, the science of how diseases spread. It helps authorities decide which vaccinations and measures are needed.

begriffe.erklaerung: A disease that spreads to many people in a short time.
So many people are immune that a pathogen can no longer spread.
Protected against a disease, for example after a vaccination or after having the illness.
A number doubles or multiplies again and again and so grows very fast.
The science that studies how diseases spread in the population.

gewusst: In an unprotected group, a single case of measles can infect more than a dozen other people on average.
Even a small drop in R below 1 decides whether an epidemic grows or shrinks.
In an outbreak some people infect especially many others; they are called superspreaders.

teile.einleitung: Albert Hofmann was a Swiss chemist who discovered the effect of LSD in Basel in 1943. LSD is a very powerful substance that greatly changes the brain’s perception and is illegal today. But Hofmann also researched medicines from fungi and plants that still help people today.
wichtigste: Albert Hofmann lived from 1906 to 2008 and reached the age of 102.
He was born in Baden in the canton of Aargau.
He worked as a chemist for the company Sandoz in Basel.
In 1938 he made LSD for the first time.
In 1943 he discovered the strong effect of LSD by chance.
He researched active substances from ergot, a fungus on cereals.
LSD is illegal in Switzerland and most countries.

abschnitte.text: Albert Hofmann was born in **Baden** in Aargau on 11 January 1906. He studied chemistry at the University of Zurich. In 1929 he began working for the Basel pharmaceutical company **Sandoz**, which is now part of Novartis. There he looked for new medicines from natural substances.

Hofmann studied substances from **ergot**, a fungus that grows on rye and other cereals. In the Middle Ages ergot in bread poisoned many people. But in small, exact amounts these substances can be used to make medicines. Hofmann developed, for example, a medicine that stops heavy bleeding after a birth.

In 1938, during his research, Hofmann made the substance **LSD**, but at first found nothing special about it. Five years later, in April 1943, he studied it again and probably absorbed a tiny amount through his skin by accident. He felt strange and saw unusual images. On 19 April 1943 he deliberately took a small amount and experienced a very strong effect while cycling home.

Even in amounts of millionths of a gram, LSD changes how the brain perceives colours, sounds, time and feelings. Such substances are called **hallucinogens**. The effect is unpredictable and can cause fear, panic and dangerous behaviour. In Switzerland LSD is banned by the Narcotics Act. Today it is only in strictly controlled studies that researchers investigate whether similar substances can help with certain illnesses.

In 1958 Hofmann succeeded in isolating the active substance **psilocybin** from Mexican mushrooms. He wrote books about his research and about the connection between people and nature. Hofmann himself warned against taking LSD carelessly. He died on 29 April 2008 in Burg im Leimental in the canton of Basel-Country.

begriffe.erklaerung: A person who researches substances and how they change.
A poisonous fungus that grows on ears of cereal.
A substance that changes perception so much that you see or hear things that are not there.
The part of a medicine that has the actual effect.

gewusst: Because of Hofmann’s bike ride, 19 April is called “Bicycle Day” in some countries.
Hofmann lived to be 102 and so saw almost the whole of the 20th century.

teile.einleitung: Ants are small insects that live in large, well-organised communities called ant colonies. They are found almost everywhere on Earth, from deserts to forests. In Switzerland the large mounds of the red wood ant are especially well known.
wichtigste: Ants live in colonies with one or more queens and many workers.
Only the queen lays eggs; the workers do all the other jobs.
Ants communicate mainly through scents, and they smell and feel with their antennae.
An ant can carry many times its own weight.
The red wood ant builds large mounds of needles and small twigs.
The mounds of the red wood ant are protected in Switzerland.
More than 13,000 species of ant are known worldwide.

abschnitte.text: Ants are **insects** and, like all insects, have six legs. Their body consists of a head, a thorax and an abdomen, which are joined by a narrow “waist”. They smell and feel with their bent **antennae**. With strong jaws, the mandibles, they grab prey, carry loads and build. Many ants can drag many times their own body weight.

An ant colony works like a large family. The **queen** lays all the eggs and in some species can live for many years. Most of the animals are **workers**: they look after the larvae, look for food, build and defend the nest. Hundreds of thousands of ants can live in a large wood ant mound. They pass food from mouth to mouth to other ants, so the whole colony is fed.

When an ant has found food, it lays a **scent trail** on its way home. Other ants follow this trail and strengthen it if they find food too. In this way real ant roads are formed. Ants also use scents to warn each other of danger. Such messenger substances are called pheromones.

In the forest the **red wood ant** builds large mounds of needles, small twigs and resin that can be more than a metre high. Underground the nest often goes just as deep. It defends itself against enemies by spraying **formic acid**. It eats many caterpillars and other insects and so keeps the forest healthy. It collects sweet honeydew from aphids and protects the aphids in return.

In South and Central America **leafcutter ants** cut pieces of leaf and carry them into the nest. There they grow a fungus on them, which they use as food. Army ants roam about in huge groups and build no fixed nests. Weaver ants sew leaves together with silk threads from their larvae. Ants have existed for more than 100 million years; they have been found in ancient amber.

More than a hundred species of ant live in Switzerland, from the small black garden ant to the large carpenter ant in wood. The mounds of wood ants are protected and must not be destroyed. Many animals like to eat ants, especially the **green woodpecker**, which pokes into the tunnels with its long, sticky tongue. Spiders, lizards and many other birds also hunt ants. If you want to watch a mound, it is best to stay on the path and not disturb the animals.

begriffe.erklaerung: Large community of ants with a queen and workers.
Ant that lays the eggs in the colony.
Ant that looks for food, builds, cares for the young and defends.
Stinging substance with which ants defend themselves against enemies.
Sweet liquid given off by aphids.

gewusst: All the ants in the world together probably weigh about as much as all wild birds and mammals together, or even more.
Some ant queens live for more than 20 years.
Wood ants help to spread the seeds of plants such as violets in the forest.

teile.einleitung: Alexander von Humboldt was a German naturalist and one of the most famous explorers in history. On his great journey through the Americas from 1799 he collected thousands of plants, measured mountains and rivers and described nature as one connected whole. A penguin, an ocean current and many places are named after him.
wichtigste: Alexander von Humboldt came from Germany; he was born in Berlin in 1769.
From 1799 he explored South and Central America with Aimé Bonpland.
In 1802 he tried to climb the volcano Chimborazo in Ecuador.
The Humboldt penguin and the Humboldt Current are named after him.
He helped to found plant geography.
In 1817 he introduced isotherms on maps.
His great work “Kosmos” consists of five volumes.

abschnitte.text: Alexander von Humboldt was born in **Berlin** on 14 September 1769 and died there in 1859. His older brother Wilhelm von Humboldt was a well-known scholar and helped found the university in Berlin. Alexander was interested in plants, rocks, stars and peoples all at once. He paid for his great research journeys himself with what he inherited from his mother.

In 1799 Humboldt set off for the Americas with the French botanist **Aimé Bonpland**. The two travelled for five years through Venezuela, Cuba, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru and Mexico. They travelled on the Orinoco through the rainforest, collected huge numbers of plants and measured mountains, temperatures and stars. At the end they visited the USA, where Humboldt met President Thomas Jefferson.

In 1802 Humboldt tried to climb the volcano **Chimborazo** in Ecuador, which is more than 6200 metres high. He did not reach the summit, but he got higher than any European before him. On the mountain he realised that the plant life changes with height in a similar way to the journey from the equator to the poles. From this came **plant geography**, which he helped to found.

Humboldt saw nature as a web in which climate, soil, plants, animals and people are connected. In 1817 he introduced **isotherms**, lines on maps that join places with the same average temperature. Even then he warned that cutting down forests changes the climate and the water balance. That is why today he is regarded as a pioneer of ecology.

In Berlin in 1827 and 1828 Humboldt gave his famous Kosmos lectures, which thousands of listeners attended. From them came his great work “**Kosmos**”, which was meant to describe the whole world. It consists of five volumes; the last appeared only after his death. The Greek word kosmos means order and refers to the ordered world.

In 1829 Humboldt travelled through Russia as far as the border of China. The **Humboldt penguin**, the cold Humboldt Current off South America, a squid and many places, schools and universities are named after him. The Humboldt University in Berlin bears the name of the two brothers. In Latin America he is still honoured as the second discoverer of the continent.

begriffe.erklaerung: Someone who observes and studies nature closely.
The study of where particular plants grow and why.
A line on a map that joins places with the same average temperature.
The science of the relationships between living things and their environment.

gewusst: More plants, animals and places are named after Humboldt than after almost anyone else.
During his life Humboldt wrote tens of thousands of letters to researchers all over the world.

teile.einleitung: Archaeological prospection means tracking down sites in the ground without digging straight away. For this, researchers use aerial photographs, measuring instruments and careful observation in the field. In this way, as if with X-ray vision, they can spot hidden walls, ditches or fireplaces.
wichtigste: Prospection means finding sites without digging.
Geomagnetics measures small deviations in the Earth’s magnetic field.
Ground-penetrating radar sends out waves that are reflected by layers in the ground.
Geoelectrics measures the electrical resistance of the ground.
In fieldwalking, finds are collected on ploughed fields.
A higher phosphate content points to former settlement or livestock.
Thermal images can show walls, because they store heat differently from soil.

abschnitte.text: The word **prospection** means exploring or searching. An excavation always destroys part of the site, because what has been dug up never lies in the ground as it did before. That is why people first try to find out where digging is worthwhile at all. Sometimes prospection is even enough to map a site and then protect it in the ground.

In **aerial archaeology**, fields are photographed from aeroplanes or with drones. Corn grows less well over a buried wall, but higher and greener over an old ditch. On freshly ploughed fields, ploughed-over walls appear as **light stripes** of mortar and stones. With laser scanners from the air, banks and paths can even be made visible under dense forest.

**Geomagnetics** measures tiny deviations in the Earth’s magnetic field that come, for example, from fireplaces, ovens or filled-in pits. **Ground-penetrating radar** sends radar waves into the earth, which are reflected back by walls and layers. In geoelectrics, a weak current is passed into the ground and the electrical resistance is measured. Damp earth conducts better than dry stone walls, so the walls show up clearly.

In **fieldwalking**, experts walk in rows across ploughed fields and pick up pottery fragments, tiles or tools. Every find is recorded with its exact position, so you can see where people used to live. Soil samples also reveal a lot, because a high **phosphate content** points to rubbish, manure or former livestock. Thermal cameras also show where walls in the ground store heat differently from the surrounding soil.

In Switzerland the **cantonal archaeology services** look after the protection of sites. By law, archaeological finds belong to the canton in which they are found. Anyone who wants to search for treasure with a metal detector needs a permit in many cantons. In the Roman town of **Augusta Raurica** near Basel, geophysical measurements help to identify buildings that are still in the ground.

begriffe.erklaerung: Place where traces of people from earlier times lie in the ground.
Science that uses measuring instruments to study what lies underground.
The Earth’s invisible magnetic field, which a compass lines up with.
Substance found, for example, in manure, bones and rubbish.

gewusst: In very dry summers, many old ground plans suddenly show up on meadows and fields that you cannot see otherwise.
Laser scans from the air have discovered whole Maya cities in the rainforest of Central America that were hidden under trees.

teile.einleitung: In biology, adaptive radiation is the splitting of an ancestral species into many new species that are adapted to different ways of life. This often happens when animals or plants reach a new habitat with many empty niches. Famous examples are Darwin’s finches on the Galápagos Islands and the whitefish in Swiss lakes.
wichtigste: In adaptive radiation an ancestral species splits into many adapted species.
The trigger is often new habitats or empty ecological niches.
Darwin’s finches on the Galápagos Islands are regarded as the textbook example.
In Swiss lakes on the edge of the Alps many whitefish species formed after the last Ice Age.
After the dinosaurs died out around 66 million years ago, the great radiation of mammals took place.
On Hawaii the honeycreepers developed very different beak shapes.
A key innovation can open up many new niches for a group.

abschnitte.text: The word radiation means spreading out, and **adaptive** means adapted. Many new species arise from a single **ancestral species** in a relatively short time. Each one adapts to a different **ecological niche**, that is, to a particular way of living and feeding. As a result the species often look very different, even though they are closely related.

On the **Galápagos Islands** live around a dozen species of finch, all descended from one common ancestor species. Some have thick beaks for cracking hard seeds, others pointed beaks for insects. Charles Darwin collected these birds in 1835 on his voyage on the Beagle. On Hawaii the **honeycreepers** show an even more impressive variety, with short, thick, long and curved beaks.

After the last Ice Age, numerous species of **whitefish** of their own formed in Swiss lakes on the edge of the Alps, such as Lake Lucerne, Lake Thun and Lake Brienz. Some live in open water and eat plankton, others hunt on the bottom. Some spawn in winter, others at other times of year or at other depths. Sadly, because the lakes were over-fertilised in the 20th century, some of these species have disappeared again.

On the large Caribbean islands, the **anole** lizards independently formed similar types for trunk, twigs and ground on each island. In Lake Victoria in Africa hundreds of species of cichlid fish arose. In Australia the **marsupials** filled many niches that are filled by other mammals elsewhere, for example as kangaroos, wombats or marsupial mice. After the dinosaurs died out around 66 million years ago, mammals spread worldwide into many new forms.

Radiation often happens when living things reach new islands or new lakes where there is little competition. A **key innovation** can also set it off, for example wings in insects or feathers in birds. Adaptive radiation shows especially clearly how evolution produces new species. That is why it is an important subject of study for research.

begriffe.erklaerung: The common original species from which many new species arise.
The particular way of life of a species, for example what it eats and where it lives.
The formation of new species from an existing species.
A new feature that makes many new ways of life possible.

gewusst: Darwin’s finches are not actually true finches but belong to the tanager family.
Some whitefish species in Swiss lakes are only a few thousand years old.
With Darwin’s finches, researchers were able to watch beak size change within just a few generations after a drought.

teile.einleitung: Agroscope is the federal government’s centre of excellence for agricultural research. Here experts study how farms can produce healthy food while protecting the environment. Its work ranges from new wheat varieties to cheese bacteria.
wichtigste: Agroscope belongs to the Federal Office for Agriculture.
Its research is spread across several sites all over Switzerland.
At Changins near Nyon there has long been research into vines and wine.
The red grape variety Gamaret was bred at Changins.
At Wädenswil on Lake Zurich the focus is on fruit growing and food.
Agroscope supplies many Swiss cheese dairies with bacterial cultures.
The Swiss Bee Research Centre looks after the health of honeybees.

abschnitte.text: Agroscope is a federal research institute and belongs to the **Federal Office for Agriculture**. It grew out of several older agricultural research stations, some of which were more than a hundred years old. Agroscope researches plants, animals, soils and food. The results help farming families, authorities and the food industry.

Agroscope has sites in different parts of the country. At **Changins** near Nyon the work is on vines, wine and arable crops. At **Wädenswil** on Lake Zurich fruit growing, vegetables and food are studied. At Posieux in the canton of Fribourg the research is mainly on farm animals and animal feed, and other sites are, for example, at Zurich-Reckenholz and Bern-Liebefeld.

Changins has a long tradition in wine research. New grape varieties were bred there, including the red variety **Gamaret**, which now grows in many Swiss vineyards. The researchers are also looking for vines that are less prone to fungal diseases. That way less plant protection product has to be sprayed.

Together with partners, Agroscope breeds new **wheat varieties** for Swiss fields. They should give good yields, be good for making bread and resist diseases. Apple and pear varieties are also tested and developed further. In addition, researchers study how soils stay fertile and how weeds can be controlled with as few chemicals as possible.

Many Swiss cheese dairies get **bacterial cultures** from Agroscope, which are important for making cheeses such as Emmental or Gruyère. These tiny helpers give the typical flavour and, in some cheeses, also the holes. Agroscope also studies how food stays safe and healthy. This includes milk, meat, fruit and vegetables.

At the **Swiss Bee Research Centre**, experts study why bee colonies become ill and how they can be helped. A big problem is the varroa mite, a small pest that weakens bees. At Posieux researchers study how cows, pigs and other farm animals can be fed and kept healthily. This is important for animal welfare and for the quality of milk and meat.

begriffe.erklaerung: A place where experts find out and try out new things.
A particular kind of grapevine with its own grapes and its own taste.
A quantity of useful bacteria grown on purpose, for example for cheese.
Crossing plants or animals on purpose to get better characteristics.

gewusst: Without Agroscope’s bacterial cultures, many Swiss cheeses would taste different.
The grape variety Gamaret came from a cross between Gamay and another variety.
Agroscope researches not only plants and animals but also tiny living things in the soil.

teile.einleitung: Albedo tells you how much of the incoming sunlight a surface reflects. Bright surfaces such as snow reflect a lot of light, dark surfaces such as tarmac absorb it. This is crucial for how fast glaciers melt and how warm the Earth is.
wichtigste: Albedo is a number between 0 and 1.
An albedo of 0 means that all the radiation is absorbed.
Fresh snow has the highest albedo of all natural surfaces.
Bare, clean glacier ice has an albedo of around 0.2 to 0.5.
As snow gets older, its albedo falls.
Saharan dust darkens the snow and so speeds up glacier melting.
The Earth as a whole has an albedo of about 0.3.

abschnitte.text: The word comes from the Latin **albus**, which means white. Albedo says what share of the solar radiation is reflected. With an albedo of 0.9, 90 per cent is reflected and only 10 per cent absorbed. What is taken in is said to be absorbed, and it warms the surface.

You can easily work out how much energy a surface takes in. If 800 watts per square metre fall on a glacier surface with an albedo of 0.6, 60 per cent is reflected. So 40 per cent is absorbed, which is **320 W/m²**. The smaller the albedo, the more heat stays in the surface.

Fresh **snow** often reflects 80 to 90 per cent of the light. Over time the snow grains become bigger and the snow picks up dirt, so its albedo falls. Bare glacier ice is only around 0.2 to 0.5. That is why a fall of fresh snow in summer slows down glacier melting a lot for a few days.

Sometimes **Saharan dust**, carried by the wind from Africa, lands on Swiss glaciers. It colours the snow yellowish or reddish and lowers the albedo. Dark deposits of dust, soot and microorganisms are called **cryoconite**. They warm up in the sun and melt small holes into the ice.

Oceans are dark and have a very low albedo, often below 0.1. When ice and snow melt, dark ground or dark water appears, which absorbs more heat. As a result even more ice melts; this is called the **ice-albedo feedback**. This effect strengthens global warming especially in the Arctic and in the Alps.

A black T-shirt gets much hotter in the sun than a white one. This is because of the different albedo of the colours. That is why houses in hot countries are often painted white. Some cities are testing light-coloured roofs and road surfaces so that they heat up less in summer, because dark **tarmac** stores a lot of heat.

begriffe.erklaerung: Light is thrown back by a surface.
A surface takes in radiation and warms up as it does so.
Dark dust with tiny living things that forms melt holes on glaciers.
An effect strengthens its own cause, so that everything speeds up.

gewusst: The Moon looks bright but has an albedo of only about 0.12, similar to dark tarmac.
To protect glaciers, some ice surfaces in the Alps are covered with light-coloured sheets in summer.
Clouds have a high albedo and cool the Earth by reflecting sunlight back into space.

teile.einleitung: Antibodies are Y-shaped proteins with which our immune system recognises and fights pathogens. Each antibody fits exactly to a particular feature of an invader, like a key to a lock. They are also the reason why vaccinations protect us.
wichtigste: Antibodies are made and released in large quantities by plasma cells.
A typical IgG antibody consists of two heavy and two light chains.
IgG is the most common class of antibody in the blood.
IgM is formed first in a first infection.
IgE plays the main role in immediate allergic reactions.
IgA mainly protects the mucous membranes.
In 1975 Köhler and Milstein developed the hybridoma technique for monoclonal antibodies.

abschnitte.text: Antibodies, also called **immunoglobulins**, are proteins in the blood and body fluids. They recognise foreign substances called **antigens**, for example parts of viruses or bacteria. They are formed by white blood cells, the B cells. When these are activated, they develop into **plasma cells**, which can produce thousands of antibodies per second.

A typical antibody has the shape of a **Y** and consists of four chains, two heavy and two light. At the tips of the two arms are the binding sites, which fit exactly to an antigen. The stem of the Y is called the **Fc fragment**. It binds to scavenger cells and to complement proteins and so calls up further defence helpers.

There are five classes of antibody: IgG, IgM, IgA, IgE and IgD. **IgG** is the most common in the blood and provides long-lasting protection. IgM is formed first in a first infection and usually consists of five Ys joined together, a pentamer. IgA protects the mucous membranes in the nose, mouth and gut, and **IgE** is involved in allergies such as hay fever.

In **neutralisation**, antibodies block pathogens or poisons so that they can no longer dock onto body cells. They also mark invaders so that scavenger cells can recognise and swallow them more easily. They can also clump pathogens together. Together with the complement system they can even make bacteria burst.

After an infection, **memory cells** remain that remember the pathogen. If it comes back, matching antibodies are formed much faster, and you often do not get ill at all. A **vaccination** uses exactly this by showing the body harmless parts of a pathogen. A blood test can detect antibodies and so find out whether someone is protected.

In 1975 **Georges Köhler** and César Milstein developed the hybridoma technique, with which large amounts of identical, so-called **monoclonal antibodies** can be produced. For this they received the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 1984, together with Niels Jerne, who was then head of the Basel Institute for Immunology. Today antibodies are among the most important medicines, for example against cancer, rheumatism or asthma. Swiss pharmaceutical companies such as Roche also make such medicines.

begriffe.erklaerung: A feature of a foreign substance that an antibody recognises.
The body’s own defence against pathogens.
A white blood cell that produces antibodies in large amounts.
Many exactly identical antibodies that are made in the laboratory.
Antibodies block a pathogen so that it can no longer do harm.

gewusst: The body can form billions of different antibodies, so that one fits almost every invader.
Many rapid tests, for example for flu or coronavirus, contain antibodies that make the pathogen visible on a test strip.
Medicines made from antibodies can often be recognised by the ending “-mab” in their name.

teile.einleitung: The eradication of smallpox is regarded as one of the greatest successes of medicine. Smallpox was a dangerous viral disease from which countless people died over the centuries. Thanks to a worldwide vaccination campaign, the World Health Organization declared the disease eradicated in 1980.
wichtigste: Smallpox was caused by the variola virus and was very contagious and often deadly.
The World Health Organization WHO led the worldwide eradication programme.
From 1967 the WHO greatly stepped up its programme.
The last natural case of smallpox occurred in Somalia in 1977.
In 1980 the WHO officially declared smallpox eradicated.
Eradication succeeded because the virus only infects humans and there was a good vaccine.
Today smallpox viruses are officially stored only in two laboratories, in the USA and in Russia.
In 2011 rinderpest became only the second disease ever to be eradicated.

abschnitte.text: **Smallpox** was a viral disease with high fever and many pus-filled blisters on the skin. About one in three people with the severe form died. Those who survived often had scars on their faces, and some became blind. In the 20th century alone, hundreds of millions of people are estimated to have died of smallpox. In Switzerland too there were large smallpox epidemics again and again until the 19th century.

As early as 1796 the English country doctor **Edward Jenner** carried out a famous experiment. He transferred material from harmless cowpox to a boy and showed that the boy was afterwards protected against real smallpox. This was the origin of **vaccination**, whose name comes from the Latin word for cow, “vacca”. In the 19th and 20th centuries vaccinations were introduced in many countries, and smallpox disappeared from Europe and North America.

The **World Health Organization** WHO decided to wipe out smallpox all over the world. From 1967 it greatly stepped up its programme; at that time there was still smallpox in more than 30 countries. Thousands of helpers travelled to remote villages in Africa, Asia and South America. A simple forked needle made vaccinating quick and cheap. The freeze-dried vaccine also helped, because it kept for a long time without a fridge.

Instead of vaccinating everyone, they relied on **ring vaccination**. They looked for every new case of the disease and immediately vaccinated all the contacts in the surrounding area. In this way they formed a protective ring that the virus could not get past. This strategy worked because smallpox is easy to recognise and the virus only infects humans. With no animals to hide in, the virus had nowhere to go.

The last natural case of smallpox occurred in **Somalia** in October 1977. The patient was a hospital cook named Ali Maow Maalin, and he survived the disease. In 1978 there was still a laboratory accident in England with one death. On 8 May 1980 the WHO officially declared smallpox eradicated.

Smallpox was the first human disease to be completely eradicated. Today smallpox viruses are officially stored in only two **high-security laboratories**, one in the USA and one in Russia. Whether these stocks should be destroyed has been debated for years. In 2011 **rinderpest**, a disease that mainly affected cattle, became the second disease to be eradicated. With polio the world is on a good path today, but has not yet reached the goal.

begriffe.erklaerung: The virus that causes smallpox.
A treatment that prepares the body for a pathogen so that you do not get ill, or get less seriously ill.
Vaccinating on purpose all the people around a case of the disease.
A disease no longer occurs naturally anywhere in the world.
The World Health Organization of the United Nations, based in Geneva.

gewusst: The World Health Organization, which defeated smallpox, has its headquarters in Geneva.
The word “vaccine” is still a reminder of the cowpox that Edward Jenner worked with.
Because smallpox has been eradicated, nobody is routinely vaccinated against it any more.

teile.einleitung: Astrology is the belief that the position of the Sun, Moon and planets says something about people’s fate or character. It is very old, and many people know it from horoscopes in newspapers and apps. But scientific studies have not been able to prove any effect of the stars on our lives.
wichtigste: Astronomy studies heavenly bodies; astrology reads fates from them.
Western astrology has 12 signs of the zodiac.
A horoscope originally shows the position of the heavenly bodies at one point in time.
The Sun also passes through the constellation Ophiuchus, which is not a sign of the zodiac.
Because of precession, star signs and constellations no longer match today.
A blind test by Shawn Carlson in 1985 showed that astrologers did no better than chance.
The famous astronomer Johannes Kepler also drew up horoscopes to earn money.

abschnitte.text: **Astrology** assumes that the position of the heavenly bodies at birth reveals something about a person. It is not the same as **astronomy**, which studies heavenly bodies with scientific methods. A **horoscope** originally shows where the Sun, Moon and planets stood in the sky at a particular moment. Today many people also understand it to mean short predictions in magazines.

Astrology arose more than 2000 years ago in **Mesopotamia**, the area of present-day Iraq. From there it reached the Greeks and Romans, and later Europe and the Arab world. For a long time astrology and astronomy were hardly separate, and star-readers also watched the sky very closely. Even the great astronomer **Johannes Kepler** drew up horoscopes, mainly to earn money.

Western astrology has 12 **signs of the zodiac**, from Aries to Pisces. They are named after constellations through which the Sun seems to travel over the course of a year. In fact, though, the Sun also passes through a 13th constellation, **Ophiuchus**, the serpent bearer. Because the Earth’s axis slowly turns like a spinning top, known as precession, on your birthday the Sun today is usually in a different constellation from your own star sign.

In many tests nobody has been able to prove that the stars influence character or fate. In 1985 the physicist **Shawn Carlson** had astrologers match horoscopes to personality profiles in a blind test. Their hits were no better than random guessing, as the journal Nature reported. That is why astrology is not counted as a science.

abschnitte.titel: Why does it seem so convincing?
abschnitte.text: Many horoscopes are worded so generally that they fit almost everyone. The fact that people still feel such descriptions are very personal is called the **Barnum effect**. In addition, people tend to remember predictions that came true rather than ones that were wrong. For many people astrology is simply entertainment, and it is good to read horoscopes with a critical eye.

begriffe.erklaerung: A chart of the position of the heavenly bodies at one moment, often with an interpretation.
Band of constellations through which the Sun, Moon and planets seem to travel.
Slow spinning-top movement of the Earth’s axis over many thousands of years.
General statements seem as if they were meant quite personally.

gewusst: The Zytglogge in Bern has an astronomical clock from the 16th century that also shows the signs of the zodiac.
One complete turn of the precession of the Earth’s axis takes around 26,000 years.

teile.einleitung: Benjamin Franklin was an American printer, inventor, scientist and politician. With a famous kite experiment he showed that lightning is electrical. He invented the lightning rod and is one of the Founding Fathers of the USA.
wichtigste: Benjamin Franklin lived from 1706 to 1790.
He was born in Boston and later lived mainly in Philadelphia.
In 1752 he proved with a kite in a thunderstorm that lightning is electrical.
From this he developed the lightning rod, which protects buildings from lightning strikes.
He also invented bifocal glasses and an economical stove.
He signed the US Declaration of Independence of 1776.
Today his picture is on the American 100-dollar note.

abschnitte.text: **Benjamin Franklin** was born in Boston on 17 January 1706. He was one of many children of a soap maker and went to school only briefly. At the age of twelve he began an apprenticeship as a **printer** with his brother. Later he founded his own printing business and a successful newspaper in Philadelphia. He taught himself a great deal and read very widely.

Franklin suspected that lightning is made of the same electricity as small sparks. In 1752, during a thunderstorm, he flew a **kite** with a metal key hanging from its string. When the wet string began to conduct, sparks jumped from the key. This showed that thunderclouds are electrically charged. The experiment was very dangerous and must never be copied.

From his experiments Franklin developed the **lightning rod**. It is a metal rod on the roof that is connected by a wire down into the ground. If lightning strikes, the current flows through the wire into the earth instead of setting the building on fire. Lightning rods still protect houses, church towers and high-rise buildings today. Franklin also introduced the terms **positive** and **negative** charge.

Franklin invented **bifocal glasses**, whose lenses are ground for distance at the top and for close-up at the bottom. He built a stove that heated rooms with less wood. He also invented a musical instrument made of glass bowls, the glass harmonica. Franklin did not patent his inventions, because they were meant to benefit everyone. He also founded a public library and a fire brigade in Philadelphia.

Franklin worked for the American colonies to break away from Great Britain. In 1776 he signed the **Declaration of Independence** of the United States. As an envoy in France he won the French over as allies in the War of Independence. In 1787 he helped to draw up the US Constitution. He died in Philadelphia on 17 April 1790.

begriffe.erklaerung: A form of energy produced by charged particles, for example in lightning.
A metal rod with a wire that leads lightning safely into the ground.
Glasses with two areas, for close-up and for distance.
The document of 1776 with which the USA broke away from Great Britain.

gewusst: Franklin was never President of the USA, but he still appears on the largest dollar note printed today.
For many years Franklin wrote a popular almanac full of sayings and advice.

teile.einleitung: A bar chart is a picture that shows numbers with bars. The longer a bar is, the bigger the number it stands for. In this way you can see at a glance what there is most of and what there is least of.
wichtigste: A longer bar means a bigger number.
In a bar chart the bars usually lie horizontally.
The shortest bar shows what there is least of.
If two bars are the same length, both numbers are the same size.
Every bar needs a label so that you know what it stands for.
The numbers on the axis show how much a bar means.
If the bars stand upright, it is often called a column chart.

abschnitte.text: A **chart** is a picture that makes numbers easy to see. In a bar chart each number is drawn as a **bar**. The bars usually lie horizontally, that is, from left to right. If they stand upright like columns, it is often called a **column chart**.

Next to the bars there is a **label**, for example dog, cat or rabbit. Along the **axis** there are numbers that show how much a bar means. You look at how far a bar reaches and read the number there. The longest bar shows what occurs most, and the shortest what occurs least.

Bar charts are often drawn on squared paper, and each **square** stands for a particular amount. If one square stands for one child and the bar for dogs is 6 squares long and the one for cats 4, then 2 more children like dogs. If one square stands for 2 children, then a bar of 5 squares means 10 children. That is why you must always first look at how much one square is worth.

A class counted which colour the children like best: red 5, blue 8 and green 3. In the chart the bar for **blue** is the longest, because 8 is the biggest number. The bar for green is the shortest. You can see straight away that blue is the class’s favourite colour without having to compare the numbers.

In 1786 the Scot **William Playfair** published one of the first bar charts. With it he showed how much trade Scotland did with other countries. Playfair also invented the line graph and the pie chart. Today bar charts are found in newspapers, school books, on websites and in many computer programs.

All the bars should be the same width and start at the same line, otherwise you cannot compare them. The axis should start at **zero** so that small differences do not look bigger than they are. A good title says what the chart is about. Different colours can help to tell the bars apart more easily.

begriffe.erklaerung: A picture that shows numbers clearly.
A line with numbers from which you can read how much a bar means.
A word next to the bar that says what it stands for.
A bar chart with upright bars.

gewusst: If an axis does not start at zero, a chart can make differences look much bigger than they really are.
Among other things, William Playfair worked as a draughtsman for James Watt, the inventor of the steam engine.
A bar chart also works without numbers, because you can compare the lengths directly with your eyes.

teile.einleitung: A bacteriophage, or phage for short, is a virus that infects only bacteria. Phages often look like tiny lunar landers with a head, a tail and little legs. They are the most common life forms on Earth, and researchers would like to use them as a weapon against dangerous bacteria.
wichtigste: A bacteriophage is a virus that infects bacteria but not humans.
The Greek word “phagein” means to eat, so bacteriophage means roughly bacteria eater.
The typical phage T4 consists of a head, a tail and tail fibres.
The phage injects its genetic material into the bacterium.
In the end the bacterium usually bursts and releases many new phages.
Félix d’Hérelle gave bacteriophages their name in 1917.
Phages are found wherever there are bacteria.
In medicine people want to use phages against antibiotic-resistant bacteria.

abschnitte.text: A **bacteriophage** is a virus that can only multiply in bacteria. Like all viruses it has no metabolism of its own and needs a host cell. Each kind of phage is usually specialised in very particular bacteria. That is why phages are harmless to people, animals and plants.

The well-known phage **T4** infects the gut bacterium Escherichia coli. It has an angular **head**, in which the genetic material is packed, a tube-shaped **tail** and thin tail fibres that look like legs. It is only about 0.0002 millimetres long and can only be seen with an electron microscope. But there are also phages with completely different shapes, for example round or thread-like ones.

First the phage attaches itself with its tail fibres to the surface of a suitable bacterium. Then the tail contracts and injects the **genetic material** inside, as if with a syringe. The bacterium is forced to make hundreds of new phages. Finally the cell **bursts** and releases the new phages, which immediately infect more bacteria. Some phages first quietly build their genetic material into the bacterium and only become active later.

In 1915 the English researcher Frederick Twort observed that something invisible was dissolving bacterial colonies. Independently of him, the French-Canadian researcher **Félix d’Hérelle** studied this phenomenon more closely. In 1917 he gave the bacteria eaters their name. Later, together with colleagues, he founded an institute in Tbilisi in Georgia, where phages are still being researched against diseases today.

Today many bacteria have become insensitive to **antibiotics**; they are called resistant. Phages could help here, because they attack only the harmful bacteria in a targeted way. This treatment is called **phage therapy** and has long been used in Georgia and Poland. In Western Europe and Switzerland it is used in individual cases and in studies. Phages also played a big role in the discovery that genetic material is made of DNA.

There are phages wherever bacteria live: in the soil, in the sea, in sewage and in the human gut. According to estimates, there are more phages on Earth than stars in the whole universe. In the sea they kill a large part of the bacteria every day and so influence the cycles of nutrients. The gene scissors **CRISPR** originally come from a defence system with which bacteria protect themselves against phages.

begriffe.erklaerung: A tiny pathogen that can only multiply in other cells.
The building instructions of a living thing or virus, stored in DNA or RNA.
Bacteria become insensitive to medicines that used to kill them.
Treating bacterial infections with bacteriophages.

gewusst: Bacteriophages are probably the most numerous biological entities on Earth.
The genetic engineering method CRISPR was developed from a defence system of bacteria against phages.
A single infected bacterium can release up to several hundred new phages.

teile.einleitung: The innate immune system is our body’s first line of defence against bacteria, viruses and other pathogens. It is there from birth and reacts within minutes to hours. It includes protective layers such as the skin, but also scavenger cells, killer cells and special proteins in the blood.
wichtigste: The innate immune system is present from birth and reacts very quickly.
Neutrophils are the most common white blood cells and are the first to travel to the site of infection.
Ilya Mechnikov described phagocytosis and received the Nobel Prize in 1908.
Toll-like receptors recognise typical molecular patterns of pathogens.
Natural killer cells kill virus-infected cells that carry too little MHC-I.
The complement system of more than 30 plasma proteins marks bacteria and drills holes in their membrane.
Dendritic cells carry antigens to the lymph nodes and so link innate and acquired defence.
Virus-infected cells release interferons to warn their neighbours.

abschnitte.text: Our body has two defence systems that work closely together. The **innate immune system** is present from birth and reacts immediately to anything that looks foreign and dangerous. It recognises pathogens by general features, not by very specific details. The **adaptive immune system**, on the other hand, learns over the course of life and forms antibodies, for example, but it needs a few days to do so. Until then the innate defence keeps the invaders in check.

The first barrier is the **skin**, which keeps out pathogens like a wall. Mucous membranes in the nose, mouth and gut trap germs with sticky mucus. Tears and saliva contain the enzyme **lysozyme**, which breaks down the walls of some bacteria. Stomach acid kills many germs in food. Harmless bacteria on the skin and in the gut also protect us, because they take space away from dangerous pathogens.

If pathogens get in anyway, the **scavenger cells** arrive. **Neutrophils** are the most common white blood cells and are the first to travel to the site of the infection. Large **macrophages** swallow bacteria and cell debris; this process is called **phagocytosis**. The Russian researcher Ilya Mechnikov was the first to describe it and received the Nobel Prize for it in 1908. **Natural killer cells** kill body cells that have been infected by viruses and therefore carry too few identification markers called MHC-I on their surface.

The defence cells have sensors such as **Toll-like receptors**. They recognise typical building blocks of pathogens, for example parts of the bacterial wall. In addition, the **complement system** of more than 30 proteins circulates in the blood; it marks bacteria and drills holes in their outer layer. Cells infected by viruses release **interferons**, which warn neighbouring cells. One of the discoverers of interferons, in 1957, was the Swiss virologist Jean Lindenmann.

An infection often causes **inflammation**. The five classic signs have Latin names: redness, heat, swelling, pain and loss of function. Paleness is not one of them. The blood vessels widen so that more defence cells reach the site of the infection. **Fever** also helps, because many pathogens multiply less well at higher temperatures.

**Dendritic cells** take up parts of pathogens and carry them to the **lymph nodes**. There they show these pieces to the cells of the adaptive immune system. In this way these cells get to know the enemy and can react in a targeted way. The 2011 Nobel Prize in Medicine was awarded for the discovery of dendritic cells and for research on receptors of the innate defence.

begriffe.erklaerung: A germ such as a bacterium or virus that can make you ill.
The eating up of pathogens or cell debris by scavenger cells.
White blood cells with small granules that attack pathogens quickly.
A group of proteins in the blood that marks and attacks bacteria.
Messenger substances with which infected cells warn their neighbours about viruses.

gewusst: The pus in an inflamed wound consists largely of dead scavenger cells.
Plants and insects also have an innate defence; Toll-like receptors were first discovered in fruit flies.
Mechnikov first observed the scavenger cells in see-through starfish larvae into which he had stuck thorns.

teile.einleitung: An action potential is a short electrical pulse with which nerve cells pass on messages. It lasts only about a thousandth of a second and travels along the nerve fibre like a wave. Without action potentials we could not think, feel or move.
wichtigste: At rest, the inside of a nerve cell is negatively charged, at around -70 mV.
From a threshold of around -50 mV an action potential is triggered.
During depolarisation sodium ions flow into the cell.
During repolarisation mainly potassium ions flow out.
The peak of an action potential reaches about +30 mV.
According to the all-or-nothing principle, an action potential happens either fully or not at all.
The strength of a stimulus is coded by the frequency of the action potentials.

abschnitte.text: Nerve cells, also called **neurons**, communicate with electrical signals. Such a signal is called an action potential. It arises at the cell membrane, the thin outer layer of the cell. The voltage is measured in millivolts, mV for short, that is, in thousandths of a volt.

At rest the inside of the cell is negatively charged compared with the outside; this is called the **resting membrane potential**. In a typical nerve cell it is around -70 mV. This voltage arises because there are different numbers of ions, that is, electrically charged particles, inside and outside. The **sodium-potassium pump** keeps this state going by moving 3 sodium ions out and 2 potassium ions in during each cycle.

When a stimulus reaches the **threshold** of around -50 mV, channels for sodium open in the membrane. Sodium ions flow in, and the voltage rises quickly to about +30 mV; this is depolarisation. Then the sodium channels close and potassium ions flow out, so the voltage falls again; this is repolarisation. For a short time the voltage even overshoots below the resting value before everything returns to balance.

An action potential is always equally strong, no matter how strong the stimulus was. If the stimulus stays below the threshold, nothing happens at all; this is the **all-or-nothing principle**. A strong stimulus therefore does not trigger bigger action potentials but more frequent ones. After each pulse comes the **refractory period**, during which that spot briefly cannot be excited, so the signal cannot travel backwards.

Many nerve fibres are surrounded by a fatty sheath, the **myelin sheath**. There the signal jumps from one gap to the next, which is called saltatory conduction. This lets some nerves reach speeds of more than 100 metres per second. Fibres without myelin conduct much more slowly, often only about one metre per second.

The British researchers Alan Hodgkin and Andrew Huxley studied the action potential in the giant nerve fibres of **squid**. These fibres are so thick that fine measuring wires could be pushed inside. In 1952 they described with equations how sodium and potassium produce the signal. For this they received the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 1963.

begriffe.erklaerung: An electrically charged particle, for example sodium or potassium.
The thin layer that surrounds a cell.
The voltage in the cell becomes less negative or even positive.
A short pause during which a spot on a nerve cannot fire again.
An insulating layer around nerve fibres that makes the signal faster.

gewusst: An action potential lasts only about one millisecond, that is, a thousandth of a second.
Heart muscle cells also work with action potentials, but in them they last longer.
Some nerve cells can fire several hundred action potentials per second.

teile.einleitung: Archaeogenetics is a young science that studies ancient genetic material from bones, teeth or hair. In this way it can find out where people came from thousands of years ago, what they looked like and whom they were related to. It combines archaeology, the study of the past, with modern genetics.
wichtigste: Archaeogenetics studies ancient DNA from bones, teeth and other finds.
Real ancient DNA can be recognised by its short pieces and typical damage.
The first farmers in Central Europe came largely from Anatolia.
According to a new analysis from 2023, the Iceman probably had dark skin.
Cheddar Man, who is around 10,000 years old, had dark skin and light eyes.
Ancient DNA is preserved better in cold regions.
Some of the oldest DNA ever read comes from mammoth teeth more than a million years old.

abschnitte.text: Every living thing carries **DNA** in its cells, a kind of blueprint that determines many features. Even after death, small remains of this DNA are preserved in bones and teeth. Archaeogenetics recovers this **ancient DNA** and reads it with modern machines. From this, origin, family relationships and some features such as skin or eye colour can be worked out.

Ancient DNA has usually broken up into many **short pieces** and is chemically damaged. This is exactly how you can tell that it really is old and does not come from people today. Because even a fingerprint can contaminate the sample, the work is done in **clean rooms** in protective suits. With the capture method, human DNA is fished out on purpose from a mixture containing lots of bacterial DNA.

DNA breaks down over time, a bit like a book whose pages slowly crumble. A study of bones of extinct moa birds from New Zealand found a **half-life** of around 521 years. Cold slows down the chemical breakdown, which is why finds from the **permafrost** are especially valuable. In this way genetic material could still be read from mammoth teeth from Siberia that are more than a million years old.

Archaeogenetics shows that Europe was settled several times by new groups. At first **hunter-gatherers** lived here, such as Cheddar Man from England with dark skin and light eyes. Around 8000 years ago farmers arrived who came largely from **Anatolia** in present-day Turkey. About 5000 years ago, herders from the steppes of Eastern Europe also moved in.

The **Iceman**, also called Ötzi, was found in the Ötztal Alps in 1991. A new analysis of his genetic material in 2023 showed that he probably had dark skin and that his ancestors were mostly Anatolian farmers. The Swedish researcher **Svante Pääbo** decoded the genetic material of the Neanderthal and received the Nobel Prize for it in 2022. It turned out that many people today outside Africa carry a little Neanderthal DNA.

begriffe.erklaerung: Molecule in all cells that stores the blueprint of a living thing.
The time after which only half of something is left.
Ground that stays frozen all year round.
A group of living things of one species that live in the same area.

gewusst: From the teeth of people who died in the Middle Ages, researchers were even able to read the genetic material of the plague bacterium.
Archaeogenetics discovered a previously unknown group of humans, the Denisovans, from a tiny finger bone.

teile.einleitung: B cells are white blood cells that belong to our immune system and produce antibodies. Antibodies are like tailor-made catching nets that recognise and mark pathogens. Thanks to B cells, the body can remember a pathogen for many years, which is also why vaccinations work.
wichtigste: B cells are a kind of lymphocyte, that is, a white blood cell.
In humans they mature in the bone marrow.
They owe their name to the bursa of Fabricius, an organ of birds that was studied in chickens.
Activated B cells become plasma cells, which make large amounts of antibodies.
Memory B cells make sure that the body quickly recognises a pathogen again later.
Susumu Tonegawa received the Nobel Prize in 1987 for explaining the variety of antibodies.
According to the clonal selection theory, only B cells with a matching receptor multiply.

abschnitte.text: B cells are **lymphocytes**, a group of white blood cells. They float in the blood and sit mainly in the lymph nodes, the spleen and the tonsils. Each B cell carries its own **B-cell receptor** on its surface, which fits only one particular feature. Such a feature of a pathogen is called an **antigen**.

The letter B comes from the **bursa of Fabricius**, a small organ at the end of the gut in birds. In the 1950s researchers working with chickens discovered that animals without this organ hardly form any antibodies. Humans have no bursa; in us B cells mature in the **bone marrow**. Conveniently, “bone marrow” also begins with B.

When a B cell meets a matching antigen, it is activated and divides many times. According to the **clonal selection theory**, only those B cells whose receptor fits exactly multiply in this way. Many of the offspring become **plasma cells**, which release thousands of antibodies every second. The antibodies attach themselves to viruses or bacteria, make them harmless or mark them for scavenger cells.

The body can form millions of different antibodies, even though it does not have a separate gene for each one. The Japanese researcher **Susumu Tonegawa** showed that gene segments in B cells are recombined, and received the Nobel Prize in Medicine for this in 1987. In the germinal centres of the lymph nodes, B cells change their antibody genes even further; this is called **somatic hypermutation**. Through class switching they also form other classes of antibody such as IgG, IgA or IgE instead of IgM.

Some B cells become **memory B cells**, which often stay in the body for decades. If the same pathogen comes back, they react much faster and more strongly than the first time. This is exactly what **vaccinations** are based on: the body gets to know a harmless part of the pathogen and forms memory cells. That is why you only get many childhood illnesses once.

When B cells work wrongly, they can also cause problems. In **allergies** they form antibodies against harmless substances such as pollen. In some diseases antibodies are wrongly directed against the body itself. Today antibodies are made on purpose in the laboratory and used as medicines against cancer and other diseases.

begriffe.erklaerung: A Y-shaped protein that recognises and marks pathogens.
A feature of a pathogen that an antibody fits.
A kind of white blood cell, for example B cells and T cells.
A mature B cell that produces very many antibodies.
Soft tissue inside the bones in which blood cells are formed.

gewusst: A single plasma cell can produce around 2000 antibodies per second.
Antibodies have the shape of a Y, and they grab the pathogen with their two arms.
The important role of the bursa of Fabricius was discovered more or less by chance, when chickens were being used for a completely different experiment.

teile.einleitung: The Antarctic ice sheet is the largest mass of ice on Earth and covers almost the whole continent of Antarctica. Around 70 per cent of the Earth’s fresh water is stored in it. If all the ice melted, sea level worldwide would rise by around 58 metres.
wichtigste: Around 70 per cent of the Earth’s fresh water is stored in the Antarctic ice.
On average the ice sheet is around 2 kilometres thick.
If all the ice melted, sea level would rise by around 58 metres.
The East Antarctic ice sheet is the larger part.
Under the West Antarctic ice sheet the bedrock lies below sea level in many places.
An ice shelf is a sheet of ice floating on the sea.
The Ross Ice Shelf is the largest ice shelf in Antarctica.
Air bubbles in ice cores reveal what the air was made of in the past.

abschnitte.text: An **ice sheet** is a huge mass of ice that covers a whole country. The **Antarctic ice sheet** is the largest on Earth and covers an area of around 14 million square kilometres. On average it is around **2 kilometres** thick, and at its thickest points more than 4 kilometres. It formed over millions of years from snow that was pressed into ice layer by layer. Its weight pushes the bedrock below deep down into the Earth.

The **Transantarctic Mountains** divide the ice sheet into two parts. The **East Antarctic ice sheet** is much larger and lies mostly on solid land above sea level. The **West Antarctic ice sheet** is smaller but more sensitive. Its bedrock lies below sea level in many places, so warm seawater can get under the ice. A well-known example is the Thwaites Glacier, which is losing ice especially fast.

Where the ice flows off the land out onto the sea, an **ice shelf** forms, that is, a floating sheet of ice. The largest is the **Ross Ice Shelf**, which is about as big as France. Ice shelves hold back the glaciers behind them like a cork in a bottle. If they break off, the glaciers can flow into the sea faster. In 2002, for example, a large part of the Larsen B Ice Shelf broke up within a few weeks.

Researchers drill deep **ice cores** out of the ice sheet. Air from earlier times is trapped in tiny **air bubbles**. From this they can read how much carbon dioxide there used to be in the air and how warm it was. The ice core from the European project EPICA goes back around 800,000 years. The University of Bern is known worldwide for its measurements on such air bubbles.

If the whole Antarctic ice sheet melted, **sea level** would rise by around 58 metres. This will not happen quickly, but even a small part would have big consequences for coastal cities. Satellite measurements show that Antarctica has been losing ice overall for several decades, especially in the west. That is why researchers watch the ice sheet very closely.

begriffe.erklaerung: An enormous mass of ice that covers a whole country or continent.
A thick sheet of ice that reaches out from the land onto the sea and floats.
A long column of ice drilled out of the ice to study earlier times.
The average height of the sea surface.
Water without much salt, as in rivers, lakes and glaciers.

gewusst: Under the Antarctic ice sheet there are hundreds of lakes with liquid water; the largest is Lake Vostok.
Without the weight of the ice, the bedrock of Antarctica would slowly rise by hundreds of metres.
Some icebergs that break off the ice shelf are bigger than a whole Swiss canton.

teile.einleitung: Buoyancy is a force that pushes things upwards in water or in the air. It explains why a wooden boat floats but a stone sinks. Even huge steel ships and hot-air balloons use this force.
wichtigste: Buoyancy is a force that acts upwards in liquids and gases.
A wooden boat floats because wood is lighter than water, that is, it has a lower density.
Buoyancy is exactly as great as the weight of the liquid displaced.
This law is called Archimedes’ principle and goes back to the Greek Archimedes.
Steel ships float because their hollow hull displaces a lot of water.
There is also buoyancy in the air, which is why hot-air balloons rise.

abschnitte.text: When an object dips into water, it pushes water aside. This **displaced water** pushes back on the object from below. This upward force is called **buoyancy**. At the same time gravity pulls the object down. Which of the two forces is stronger decides whether something floats or sinks.

The Greek scholar **Archimedes** lived more than 2200 years ago in Syracuse on Sicily. He found out that buoyancy is as great as the weight of the displaced liquid. According to legend, he got the idea while bathing, when the water in the bath rose. He is then said to have shouted “Eureka”, which means “I have found it”. The law is now called **Archimedes’ principle**.

Whether something floats depends on its **density**, that is, on how heavy a particular volume is. Wood is usually less dense than water and therefore floats. A stone or an iron nail is denser than water and sinks. Ice is only a little lighter than water, which is why only about a tenth of an iceberg sticks out of the sea. The rest stays hidden below the surface.

A lump of steel sinks straight away. But if the steel is shaped into a hollow hull, there is a lot of air inside. The hull then displaces so much water that the buoyancy carries the whole ship. The more heavily a ship is loaded, the deeper it sits in the water. A mark on the hull, the **load line**, shows how deep it may sink at most.

Air also produces buoyancy, only much weaker than water. A **hot-air balloon** rises because warm air is lighter than cold air. Balloons filled with helium rise because helium is much lighter than air. Every January a well-known international balloon festival takes place in Château-d’Oex in Vaud.

Many fish have a **swim bladder** filled with gas. With it they can float without swimming all the time. Submarines fill tanks with water to dive and push it out again with air to rise. In the very salty Dead Sea buoyancy is so strong that people can lie on the surface almost without moving.

begriffe.erklaerung: How heavy a substance is in relation to its size.
The water that an object pushes aside when it dips in.
Buoyancy is as great as the weight of the displaced liquid.
An organ filled with gas with which fish float in the water.

gewusst: Salt water carries better than fresh water, which is why a ship sits a little higher in the sea than on a lake.
A huge cruise ship floats even though it is made of tens of thousands of tonnes of steel.

teile.einleitung: The Avogadro constant tells you how many particles there are in one mole of a substance, namely around 602 sextillion. It links the tiny world of atoms and molecules with amounts that can be weighed on scales. It is named after the Italian researcher Amedeo Avogadro.
wichtigste: The Avogadro constant is exactly 6.02214076 times 10 to the power of 23 particles per mole.
The SI base unit mole is defined by it.
In 1811 Amedeo Avogadro put forward an important hypothesis about gases.
36 g of water are 2 moles and contain around 1.2 times 10 to the power of 24 molecules.
The Avogadro constant times the elementary charge gives the Faraday constant.
The Avogadro constant times the Boltzmann constant gives the universal gas constant R.
For precise measurements, almost perfect spheres of silicon-28 were made.

abschnitte.text: Atoms and molecules are so small that they cannot be counted one by one. That is why chemists group huge numbers of them into one unit, the **mole**, just as twelve eggs are grouped into a dozen. The **Avogadro constant** says how many particles a mole contains: 6.02214076 times 10 to the power of 23. That is a number with 24 digits, around 602 sextillion.

Every substance has a **molar mass**, that is, the mass of one mole in grams. For water it is about 18 grams per mole. So 36 grams of water, about two tablespoons, contain two moles, which is around 1.2 times 10 to the power of 24 water molecules. In this way you can use scales in the laboratory to estimate how many particles react with each other.

Amedeo Avogadro lived from 1776 to 1856 and was a physicist in Turin. In 1811 he put forward **Avogadro’s hypothesis**: equal volumes of different gases at the same pressure and temperature contain the same number of particles. During his lifetime the idea was hardly noticed. Only decades later did chemists realise how important it was and named the constant after him.

In 1865 the Austrian physicist **Josef Loschmidt** was the first to estimate how many gas particles there are in a particular volume, and a related number bears his name. Later the Avogadro constant was measured more and more precisely. In the international **Avogadro Project**, almost perfect spheres of isotopically pure silicon-28 were made and their atoms, so to speak, counted. Since the reform of the International System of Units in 2019, the value has been fixed exactly and defines the mole.

The Avogadro constant links many constants of nature with each other. If you multiply it by the **elementary charge**, the charge of an electron, you get the Faraday constant, which is important in electrolysis. If you multiply it by the **Boltzmann constant**, you get the universal gas constant R. This is needed to calculate how gases behave.

begriffe.erklaerung: The unit for the amount of a substance; one mole contains about 602 sextillion particles.
A particle made of several firmly joined atoms, for example water.
The mass of one mole of a substance in grams.
A number in physics that is the same everywhere in the universe.
The internationally agreed units of measurement such as the metre, kilogram, second and mole.

gewusst: If you laid out a mole of peas side by side, there would be so many that they could cover all the land on Earth many metres deep.
A teaspoon of water already contains more than 100 sextillion water molecules.
The name “Avogadro constant” was only introduced long after Avogadro’s death, partly by the French physicist Jean Perrin.

teile.einleitung: Amoebae are tiny living things made of just one single cell. They have no fixed shape but change their form all the time, which is why in German they are also called “Wechseltierchen”, little changing animals. They are found almost everywhere that is wet or damp.
wichtigste: Amoebae are single-celled organisms, that is, living things made of only one cell.
They change their shape all the time and are therefore also called “changing animals” in German.
They move with false feet.
An amoeba has no mouth and eats by flowing around its food.
Many amoebae live in water and in damp soil.
Under the microscope they usually look almost see-through.
An amoeba has no skeleton; its body is soft.

abschnitte.text: An **amoeba** is a **single-celled organism**: its whole body consists of one single cell. Most amoebae are only a few hundredths of a millimetre in size, but a well-known species called Amoeba proteus grows up to about half a millimetre long. Under the **microscope** they look almost see-through and grainy. Inside you can see the cell nucleus and small bubbles. Because they have no skeleton and no firm outer layer, their body is soft and keeps changing shape.

Amoebae move with **false feet**, also called pseudopodia. The inside of the cell flows in one direction and forms a bulge. The rest of the cell slowly flows after it. In this way the amoeba crawls over the bottom of a pond or over a leaf. This kind of movement is called **amoeboid movement**.

An amoeba has no mouth and can eat at any point of its body. It flows around a food particle, for example a bacterium or an alga, with its false feet. Then it encloses it in a bubble, the **food vacuole**, and digests it there. This process is called **phagocytosis**. It pumps surplus water back out with a pulsing bubble.

Many amoebae live in **fresh water**, for example in ponds, pools and puddles, in Switzerland too. Others live in the sea or in damp **soil**, where they eat bacteria. Some amoebae build themselves a small shell of grains of sand or their own material; they are called **testate amoebae**. If it gets too dry, some species can withdraw into a protective covering and wait.

Amoebae usually multiply by one cell **dividing** into two identical cells. In the soil they help to keep bacteria in check and so are part of a healthy soil. A few species can make people ill, for example **amoebic dysentery**, a bowel illness in warm countries. That is why you should only drink clean water when travelling. Researchers also use amoebae to understand how cells move.

begriffe.erklaerung: A living thing that consists of only one single cell.
Bulges of the cell body with which an amoeba moves and catches food.
Flowing around food and taking it into the cell.
A small bubble inside a cell, for example for food or water.
A device that makes very small things visible by greatly enlarging them.

gewusst: The name amoeba comes from the Greek word for “change”.
White blood cells in the human body also move and eat in a very similar way to amoebae.
Some slime moulds live as single amoebae and join together into one shared structure when food is short.
