teile.einleitung: The Asilomar Conference was a meeting of researchers in California in 1975 about the risks of the new genetic engineering. There the scientists themselves decided which experiments with genetic material had to be carried out with how much care. To this day the conference is a famous example of researchers taking responsibility.
wichtigste: The conference of 1975 focused on the risks of recombinant DNA.
The conference took place in the USA.
The biochemist Paul Berg was a driving force.
As early as 1974 researchers had proposed a voluntary moratorium on certain experiments.
The result was safety measures graded according to risk.
The conference is regarded as a model for self-regulation by science.
In 2017 new Asilomar principles on artificial intelligence were drawn up.

abschnitte.text: At the beginning of the 1970s researchers learnt how to cut up the genetic material of different living things and put it together in new ways. This produces **recombinant DNA**, that is, newly combined genetic material. With it, genes could be inserted into bacteria, for example. But many people wondered whether dangerous pathogens might arise and escape from the laboratory.

In 1974 leading researchers around **Paul Berg** published a letter in a scientific journal. In it they proposed a voluntary **moratorium**, that is, a pause on certain risky experiments. These were not to be carried out until the dangers were better understood. This was unusual, because researchers themselves were giving up experiments that they actually wanted to do.

In February 1975 around 140 experts met at the **Asilomar** conference centre on the Pacific coast in California. Besides biologists, some lawyers and journalists also took part. For several days there were lively discussions about how dangerous the new methods really were. A few years later, in 1980, Paul Berg received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

The conference recommended **graded safety measures**: the riskier an experiment, the stricter the safety rules. These included specially secured laboratories and weakened bacteria that cannot survive outside the laboratory. On this basis the US health authority issued guidelines for research in 1976. Similar rules were later adopted in many countries, including in Europe and Switzerland.

Asilomar is still regarded today as a model for **self-regulation** by science. Critics point out, however, that social and ethical questions were largely left out at the time. In 2017 experts met again at Asilomar and drew up principles for **artificial intelligence**. In Switzerland the people also have a say on genetic engineering; in 2005, for example, an initiative for farming free of genetic engineering was approved.

begriffe.erklaerung: Genetic material that has been put together in the laboratory from parts of different origins.
An agreed pause during which something is not done.
Methods used to change the genetic material of living things on purpose.
A group sets its own rules without the state laying them down.

gewusst: Asilomar is actually a conference centre right on a beach in California.
The disasters people feared from recombinant DNA have not happened so far, and many medicines such as insulin are now made using this technique.

teile.einleitung: Autonomous driving means that a vehicle drives itself completely or partly, without a person steering, braking or accelerating. For this the car needs sensors, fast computers and clever programs. Many companies and researchers are working on it, but completely driverless cars everywhere do not exist yet.
wichtigste: The common classification by the engineering association SAE has six levels of driving automation, from 0 to 5.
At the highest level the car drives everywhere without any person at all.
Lidar scans the surroundings with laser beams; radar uses radio waves and also works in fog.
Cameras recognise traffic signs, traffic lights and road markings.
From 2004 the DARPA Grand Challenge in the desert drove development forward.
In 2005 Stanford University won with the robot car “Stanley”.
From 2016 PostBus tested self-driving minibuses with passengers in Sion.

abschnitte.text: In **autonomous driving** a computer takes over the driver’s tasks. Even today many cars help with **driver assistance systems**, for example lane-keeping assist, which keeps the car in its lane. Other systems brake automatically when an obstacle appears or keep a distance from the car in front. But a truly autonomous car should manage everything on its own, even in difficult situations.

The American engineering association **SAE** divides automation into six levels. At level 0 the person does everything; at levels 1 and 2 assistance systems help, but the person must always pay attention. From level 3 the driver may look away in certain situations but must take over when the car calls. At level 4 the car drives completely on its own in a particular area. At the highest level, 5, it drives everywhere without any person at all, and a steering wheel would no longer be needed.

A self-driving car needs many **sensors**. **Lidar** sends out laser beams and measures how long the light takes to come back, which creates a three-dimensional picture of the surroundings. **Radar** uses radio waves and also works well in fog, rain and darkness. Cameras recognise colours, traffic lights and signs, and ultrasonic sensors help with parking. A computer combines all these data and decides in a split second what to do.

A big boost came from the **DARPA Grand Challenge**, a competition run by a research agency of the US Department of Defense. In 2004 driverless robot cars had to drive through the Mojave Desert, but not a single one reached the finish. By 2005 several vehicles managed it, and the car “Stanley” from **Stanford University** won. Many researchers from these teams later went on to work at large technology companies.

In Switzerland, from 2016, **PostBus** tested self-driving minibuses with real passengers in **Sion**. The small shuttles drove slowly through the old town, and there was always an attendant on board. Later there were further trials, for example in Schaffhausen. Switzerland has changed its Road Traffic Act so that automated vehicles can be allowed under certain conditions.

Autonomous cars could reduce accidents, because most accidents are caused by human mistakes. They could also give older people or people with disabilities more **mobility**. At the same time there are open questions: who is liable in an accident, and how do you protect the cars from hackers? Snow, roadworks and unexpected situations are also still difficult for computers.

begriffe.erklaerung: A sensor that scans the surroundings with laser beams and measures distances.
A sensor that uses radio waves to detect objects and their speed.
Technology in the car that helps the driver with individual tasks.
A system that keeps the car in its lane.
A component that measures something in the surroundings, similar to a sense organ.

gewusst: In the first desert race in 2004, the best robot car only managed about 12 kilometres of the long course.
A lidar can record hundreds of thousands of measuring points per second.
In some cities in the USA robotaxis without anyone at the wheel are already driving around.

teile.einleitung: Species diversity means that there are many different living things on Earth, from tiny beetles to huge whales. Each species has its job in the great web of nature. Sadly, many species are disappearing today, but everyone can do something to help protect them.
wichtigste: Species diversity means that there are many different living things.
A technical word with a similar meaning is biodiversity.
Insects are the group of animals with the most species.
The tropical rainforest is especially rich in species.
Many species are declining because their habitat is disappearing.
Endangered species are listed in the Red List.
The dodo is a well-known example of an extinct bird species.

abschnitte.text: A **species** is a group of living things that are very similar and can have young together, for example red foxes or dandelions. Species diversity means how many different species live in one place or on the whole Earth. The technical word **biodiversity** is a little broader. It also includes the variety within a species and the variety of habitats.

So far researchers have described around two million species, but there are probably many more. The largest group are the **insects**; of beetles alone hundreds of thousands of species are known. Every year thousands of new species are discovered, mainly small animals, fungi and plants. In Switzerland about 56,000 species of animals, plants and fungi are known.

There are especially many species in the **tropical rainforest**, for example on the Amazon or on Borneo. There you can find hundreds of insect species on a single tree. Coral reefs in the sea are also very rich in species. In Switzerland, dry meadows, bogs and natural riverbanks are important habitats with many species.

All living things are linked in a great web called an **ecosystem**. Bees and other insects pollinate fruit trees, for example, and without them there would be far fewer apples and cherries. Fungi and worms break down leaves and make the soil fertile. The more varied an ecosystem is, the better it survives disturbances such as drought or diseases.

Many species are declining because their **habitat** is disappearing, for example because of roads, settlements or intensive farming. Poisons, species brought in from elsewhere and climate change also harm them. Endangered species are recorded in the **Red List**; in Switzerland around a third of the species studied are considered threatened. The dodo, a flightless bird from the island of Mauritius, died out as long ago as the 17th century.

In the garden, native **wild flowers** help, because many insects depend on exactly these. A pile of branches or stones gives hedgehogs, lizards and beetles shelter. A corner of long grass that you do not mow is also valuable. Buying local food and avoiding rubbish also protects nature.

begriffe.erklaerung: A group of living things that are very similar and can have young with each other.
The variety of life: species, habitats and differences within a species.
A habitat with all the living things that live there together and depend on each other.
A list that shows which animal and plant species are endangered.

gewusst: Most of all known animal species are insects.
A handful of garden soil contains more living things than there are people on Earth.
The expression “as dead as a dodo” is an English saying for something that is finished for good.

teile.einleitung: Bracket fungi are fungi that grow on living or dead trees. Many look like little shelves stuck to the side of the trunk. They break down wood and are therefore important helpers in the cycle of the forest.
wichtigste: Bracket fungi grow on tree trunks and branches.
The shape of many bracket fungi is like a little shelf.
Bracket fungi break down the wood and make it crumbly.
Some, like the tinder fungus, feel as hard as wood.
In the past people used the tinder fungus to make fire.
The glacier mummy Ötzi carried pieces of tinder fungus with him.
The chicken of the woods is bright sulphur yellow to orange.
The edible oyster mushroom grows on wood and is also farmed.

abschnitte.text: **Bracket fungi**, or tree fungi, are fungi that grow on wood, for example on trunks, branches or tree stumps. What we see is only the **fruiting body** of the fungus. The actual fungus consists of a web of fine threads, the **mycelium**, which grows deep in the wood. Many bracket fungi form semicircular brackets that sit on the trunk like shelves. Some of them keep growing for many years.

Bracket fungi can do something that hardly any other living thing can: they break down the hard building blocks of **wood**. Depending on the fungus, the wood is left whitish and stringy or brown and broken into cubes. In this way dead wood becomes soil, and the nutrients go back into the ground. Without bracket fungi, huge piles of dead wood would build up in the forest. But some bracket fungi also attack living trees and can weaken them.

The **tinder fungus** grows mainly on beeches and birches and looks like a grey horse’s hoof. It is as hard as wood. In the past people made **tinder** from its inside, a material that starts to glow with just a spark. With it you could make a fire by striking sparks with a flint. The glacier mummy **Ötzi**, around 5300 years old, also carried pieces of tinder fungus in his equipment.

The **chicken of the woods** is bright sulphur yellow to orange and stands out at once in the forest. The **oyster mushroom** grows in clusters on deciduous wood and is now farmed on straw or wood waste and sold. The birch polypore grows only on birches; Ötzi also had pieces of it with him. The honey fungus forms whole clusters on tree stumps and can make trees ill.

Not all bracket fungi are edible; many are tough, bitter or even poisonous. Anyone who collects mushrooms should therefore always have them checked at a **mushroom inspection**. In Switzerland many municipalities have official mushroom inspectors who offer this check free of charge. In some cantons there are also days when picking is not allowed, or limits on how much may be collected.

begriffe.erklaerung: The visible part of a fungus, which forms spores.
A web of fine fungal threads that grows in wood or soil.
A material that catches fire easily, used for making fire.
Tiny germs with which fungi spread.

gewusst: Some bracket fungi grow a new layer every year and can live for several decades.
In the past a leather-like material for hats and bags was even made from the tinder fungus.
A single large bracket fungus can release billions of spores.

teile.einleitung: Alzheimer’s disease is a disease of the brain in which nerve cells gradually die. People who have it forget more and more and over time need help in everyday life. It is the most common form of dementia and mainly affects older people.
wichtigste: Alois Alzheimer described the disease for the first time in 1906.
His first described patient was called Auguste Deter.
Plaques of beta-amyloid build up between the nerve cells.
Inside the nerve cells the tau protein forms tangles of fibres.
The biggest risk factor is older age.
Usually the first thing affected is remembering new information.
There is no treatment that cures the disease (as of 2026).

abschnitte.text: In Alzheimer’s disease more and more nerve cells in the **brain** slowly die, and their connections are lost. As a result memory, thinking and sense of direction get worse. The disease is the most common form of **dementia**, a general term for the loss of mental abilities. It usually develops over many years and slowly gets worse.

From 1901 the German doctor **Alois Alzheimer** cared for the patient **Auguste Deter** in Frankfurt. She was only around 50 years old but was becoming more and more forgetful and confused. After her death Alzheimer examined her brain under the microscope and found striking deposits. In 1906 he presented the case, and later the disease was named after him.

Between the nerve cells, clumps of the protein **beta-amyloid** form, which are called plaques. Inside the cells the **tau protein** clumps together into tangles of fibres. In addition, there is too little of the messenger substance acetylcholine, which nerve cells need to communicate. Over time the brain shrinks, especially in the area responsible for memory.

At the beginning, people find it hard to remember **new information**, for example a conversation from the day before. Old memories from childhood often remain for a long time. Later people sometimes cannot find the right words or get lost in familiar places. In the late stage they need help with almost everything in everyday life.

The most important risk factor is **age**, because the disease becomes much more common from about 65. The gene variant **ApoE4** also increases the risk of the common late-onset form. Exercise, a healthy diet, an active life with lots of contact with other people and good hearing can lower the risk. In Switzerland about 150,000 people live with dementia (as of about 2024).

Many medicines slow down the breakdown of **acetylcholine** and can ease the symptoms of mild to moderate dementia for a while. Newer drugs attack the amyloid deposits and can slow down the course of the disease a little. So far, however, the disease cannot be cured. Patience, understanding and support from relatives and professionals are important, for example from Alzheimer Switzerland.

begriffe.erklaerung: A general term for illnesses in which memory and thinking get much worse.
A deposit of clumped protein between the nerve cells.
A messenger substance with which nerve cells pass on signals.
Something that increases the likelihood of getting an illness.

gewusst: People with Alzheimer’s often still recognise music from their youth when they have forgotten many other things.
Auguste Deter was captured in a photograph that can now be seen in many books about Alzheimer’s.
The changes in the brain often begin many years before anyone notices anything.

teile.einleitung: An outlier is a value in a set of data that differs greatly from all the other values. It can be a mistake, for example a typing error, or a real and interesting special case. Anyone who works with data has to recognise outliers and think carefully about what to do with them.
wichtigste: An outlier is a value that lies far away from the other values in a set of data.
In the list 12, 14, 13, 95 and 15, the number 95 is an outlier.
The arithmetic mean is changed a lot by outliers, the median hardly at all.
Outliers can come from measuring or typing errors, but they can also be real values.
You should check an outlier first and not simply delete it.
In a scatter plot an outlier shows up as a point far away from the others.
In German an outlier is called an “Ausreisser”.

abschnitte.text: An **outlier** is a measurement that does not fit the pattern of the rest of the data. If a class measures their height, for example, and everyone is between 140 and 160 centimetres, a value of 16 centimetres would immediately look suspicious. The English word **outlier** means something that lies outside. Whether a value is an outlier always depends on how the other values are spread out.

The **arithmetic mean** adds up all the values and divides by how many there are. For the numbers 10, 12, 11, 13 and 54 this gives 100 divided by 5, that is, 20. Yet four of the five values are only between 10 and 13. The **median**, that is, the middle value of the ordered list, is 12 here and describes the data much better. That is why the median is often preferred for data with outliers.

In a **scatter plot** an outlier stands out as a single point far away from the cloud of points. In a **box plot**, a diagram made of a box with two lines, outliers are also often drawn as single points. A well-known rule of thumb comes from the American statistician John Tukey. According to it, a value counts as unusual if it lies very far outside the range in which the middle half of the data lie.

Often there is a **measuring error** behind it, such as a wrongly read thermometer or broken scales. It is also often a typing error, for example 95 instead of 15 or a forgotten decimal point. But sometimes an outlier is completely real, for example a record jump in sport or a particularly hot summer’s day. Such real outliers can even lead to new discoveries.

First you check whether the value is a mistake or a real value. If it is a mistake, you correct it or leave it out, giving a reason. If it is real, it stays in the data and you mention it in the report. Simply deleting values that do not fit so that the result looks nicer is considered dishonest in science. That is why good researchers always write down what they have done with outliers.

begriffe.erklaerung: A value that differs greatly from the other values in a set of data.
The average: add up all the values and divide by how many there are.
The value in the middle when all the values are put in order of size.
A diagram in which each measurement is drawn as a point.
A wrong value that came about while measuring or writing down.

gewusst: A single outlier can shift the average of a whole class a lot, but the median hardly at all.
Some important discoveries began with researchers taking a strange measurement seriously instead of throwing it away.
The term “outlier” literally means something like “one that lies outside”.

teile.einleitung: Ammonites were sea creatures with a spirally coiled shell that lived millions of years ago. They are among the best-known fossils of all and are related to today’s squid and octopuses. They are often found in the limestones of the Jura in Switzerland too.
wichtigste: Ammonites lived in the sea and are now extinct.
Their shell usually looks like a coiled snail.
They were related to squid and belonged to the cephalopods.
The animal lived in the front chamber of its shell.
The gas-filled chambers were used for floating in the water.
They are named after the Egyptian god Ammon with ram’s horns.
Because their species changed quickly, they are important index fossils.

abschnitte.text: An ammonite had a **shell** made of lime, usually coiled up like a flat spiral. Inside, walls divided it into many **chambers**. The animal itself lived only in the front, largest chamber, the living chamber. Tentacles probably stuck out of the opening, as in today’s squid.

The rear chambers were filled with gas and some liquid. Through a thin tube, the **siphuncle**, the animal could change the amount of liquid. In this way it could float, rise or sink in the water, similar to a submarine. The **nautilus**, which still lives today in the Indian and Pacific Oceans, works on the same principle.

The first ammonites appeared about 400 million years ago in the **Devonian**. They developed thousands of different species and lived in all the seas of the world. They died out 66 million years ago together with the dinosaurs. Most were the size of the palm of a hand, but the largest known ammonite was about 1.75 metres across.

Because ammonite species changed quickly, each species lived for only a relatively short time. If a particular species is found in a layer of rock, you therefore know roughly how old the layer is. Such fossils are called **index fossils**. The species can be recognised, among other things, by the **suture line**, the often branched line where the chamber walls meet the outer shell.

At the time of the ammonites, a large part of today’s Switzerland lay under a warm, shallow sea. Lime mud and dead animals settled on the seabed and turned into limestone. That is why ammonites are often found in the **Jura**, for example in quarries and by the side of paths. They also occur in the limestone Alps, some high up in the mountains.

The name goes back to the Egyptian god **Ammon**, who was shown with ram’s horns. The coiled shells reminded people of such horns, which is why they used to be called horns of Ammon. In some regions people thought they were snakes turned to stone. Today ammonites are popular collector’s items and decorative stones.

begriffe.erklaerung: Petrified remains or imprint of a living thing from prehistoric times.
Group of animals with tentacles on the head, such as squid.
Fossil used to work out the age of a layer of rock.
Wavy line where the chamber walls meet the shell.
Tube that connects the chambers and controls floating.

gewusst: The largest known ammonite was found in Seppenrade in Germany in 1895.
Some ammonites shimmer in rainbow colours because their shell was made of mother-of-pearl.
There were also ammonites with straight or hook-shaped shells.

teile.einleitung: An upwelling zone is a region of the sea where cold, nutrient-rich water rises from the depths to the surface. Especially many algae grow there, and they are food for huge shoals of fish. Although upwelling zones cover only a small part of the oceans, they are among the richest fishing waters in the world.
wichtigste: In an upwelling zone, cold, nutrient-rich deep water rises to the surface.
Because of the Earth’s rotation, Ekman transport deflects surface water at an angle to the wind.
In the northern hemisphere the water is moved on average about 90 degrees to the right.
Off Peru and Chile the Humboldt Current forms a large upwelling zone.
Off Namibia the Benguela Current causes an upwelling zone.
The Peruvian anchoveta provides one of the largest single catches in the world.
At the equator in the Pacific, upwelling happens because the trade winds drive the water apart.

abschnitte.text: In the depths of the sea, **nutrients** from sunken, decomposed living things collect. At the surface these nutrients are often lacking, because algae use them up quickly. In an **upwelling zone**, cold deep water flows upwards and brings the nutrients into the light. Then especially many algae grow there, similar to plants in a freshly fertilised garden.

Wind pushes the surface water along, but because of the **Earth’s rotation** it is deflected. This effect is called **Ekman transport**, named after a Swedish oceanographer. In the northern hemisphere the water is moved on average about 90 degrees to the right, in the southern hemisphere to the left. If the wind blows along a coast so that the water is pushed away from the land, deep water rises to fill the gap.

Off the coast of Peru and Chile flows the cold **Humboldt Current**, with one of the largest upwelling zones on Earth. Off Namibia in south-west Africa the **Benguela Current** causes upwelling. Other important areas lie off California and off north-west Africa. Water also rises at the equator in the Pacific, because the trade winds drive the surface water apart on both sides of the equator.

Upwelling zones cover only a tiny part of the sea’s surface, but they provide a large part of the world’s fish catch. Off Peru lives the **Peruvian anchoveta**, which makes up one of the largest single catches in the world. Many seabirds, seals and whales find plenty of food here. During an **El Niño** the upwelling off Peru weakens, and fish stocks can collapse sharply.

The cold water cools the air above it, so it hardly ever rains on these coasts. That is why deserts often lie next to upwelling zones, such as the **Atacama** in Chile or the **Namib** in Namibia, where fog often drifts in from the sea. Beneath very productive upwelling zones, a lot of dead plankton sinks into the depths. Bacteria break it down and use up oxygen in the process, so low-oxygen layers of water form there.

begriffe.erklaerung: Substances that plants and algae need to grow.
Deflection of wind-driven water by the Earth’s rotation.
Tiny living things that float in the water.
Steady wind near the equator.

gewusst: On islands off Peru, the many fish-eating seabirds have left layers of droppings metres thick, which used to be dug up as fertiliser.
In the Namib there are beetles that collect water drops on their backs from the fog, which forms because of the cold sea.

teile.einleitung: Antimatter is a kind of mirror image of normal matter: its particles have the same mass but the opposite electric charge. When matter and antimatter meet, they destroy each other and pure energy is produced. At CERN in Geneva researchers make tiny amounts of it and study it.
wichtigste: Antimatter is made of antiparticles, the counterparts of normal particles.
Antiparticles have the same mass as normal particles but the opposite charge.
The antiparticle of the electron is called the positron and is positively charged.
When a particle and its antiparticle meet, they turn into energy.
Paul Dirac predicted antimatter in 1928, and the positron was discovered in 1932.
At CERN in Geneva antihydrogen atoms are made and studied.
Why there is almost only matter in the universe is a great mystery.

abschnitte.text: Everything around us is made of **matter**, that is, of atoms with protons, neutrons and electrons. For almost every one of these particles there is an **antiparticle** with the same mass but the opposite charge. The electron is negatively charged; its antiparticle, the positron, is positive. The antiproton, on the other hand, is negatively charged, even though the proton is positive.

When a particle meets its antiparticle, both disappear and energy is produced, usually in the form of flashes of light. This process is called **annihilation**. The whole mass is turned into energy according to Einstein’s formula E = mc². That is why antimatter cannot be kept in normal containers, but only in strong magnetic fields in a vacuum.

In 1928 the British physicist **Paul Dirac** used an equation to predict that antiparticles must exist. As early as 1932 the American Carl Anderson discovered the positron in cosmic rays from space. In 1955 the antiproton was also detected in the USA. In 1995 CERN managed for the first time to make individual atoms of **antihydrogen**.

**CERN** near Geneva is one of the most important centres of antimatter research. There a special facility slows down antiprotons so that researchers can trap them. In this way antihydrogen atoms have been held in magnetic traps for several minutes. In 2023 an experiment at CERN showed that antimatter is also pulled downwards by gravity.

Antimatter sounds like science fiction, but it is used in hospitals. In **positron emission tomography**, PET for short, patients receive a weakly radioactive substance that sends out positrons. The radiation produced makes tumours in the body visible, for example. Some natural substances too, such as some of the potassium in bananas, send out positrons now and then.

At the **Big Bang**, equal amounts of matter and antimatter were probably created. Actually, the two should have destroyed each other completely. Even so, our universe today consists almost only of matter. Why this is so is one of the great unsolved questions in physics.

begriffe.erklaerung: The counterpart of a particle, with the same mass but the opposite charge.
The positively charged antiparticle of the electron.
A particle and an antiparticle destroy each other and become energy.
A large European research centre for particle physics near Geneva.

gewusst: All the antimatter made at CERN so far would only be enough to light a light bulb for a few minutes.
Thunderstorms can produce antimatter for a short time, as satellites have measured.

teile.einleitung: Alexander Fleming was a Scottish doctor and researcher who discovered penicillin in 1928. Penicillin was one of the first antibiotics and has since saved countless lives. Fleming received the Nobel Prize for his discovery in 1945.
wichtigste: Alexander Fleming lived from 1881 to 1955 and came from Scotland.
In 1928 he discovered that a mould can kill bacteria.
He found the mouldy dish when he came back from holiday.
The substance from the mould is called penicillin and works against bacteria.
Antibiotics such as penicillin do not help against viruses, for example with flu.
During the Second World War penicillin was produced in large quantities for the first time.
In 1945 Fleming received the Nobel Prize in Medicine.

abschnitte.text: Alexander Fleming was born on a farm in **Scotland** in 1881. He moved to London, studied medicine and worked at **St Mary’s Hospital**. In the First World War he treated wounded soldiers and saw how many died of infected wounds. After that he looked for substances that fight dangerous bacteria.

A few years before penicillin, Fleming discovered **lysozyme**, a substance in tears and saliva that holds back bacteria. In the summer of 1928, before going on holiday, he left dishes of staphylococcus bacteria standing in the laboratory. When he came back, a **mould** had grown on one dish. Around the mould the bacteria had disappeared, and Fleming called the unknown substance penicillin.

Penicillin is one of the **antibiotics**, that is, medicines against bacteria. It attacks the **cell wall** of the bacteria so that they can no longer grow and burst. Human cells have no such cell wall and are therefore hardly harmed. Antibiotics do not help against viruses, however, for example with flu or a cold.

Fleming did not manage to obtain the active substance in pure form and in larger amounts. Only around 1940 did the researchers **Howard Florey** and **Ernst Boris Chain** in Oxford achieve this. During the Second World War, penicillin was then produced in large quantities, mainly in the USA. It saved the lives of many wounded soldiers and later of millions of other people.

In 1945 Fleming, Florey and Chain jointly received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. Fleming became world-famous and was knighted, which is why he is often called Sir Alexander Fleming. He died in London in 1955. In his Nobel Prize speech he already warned that antibiotics used wrongly can lead to **resistant bacteria**, which is a big problem today.

begriffe.erklaerung: Medicine that kills bacteria or slows down their growth.
Tiny living things made of one cell; some cause illness.
Fungus that grows as a furry layer on food.
When bacteria are no longer affected by a medicine.
Substance in tears and saliva that weakens bacteria.

gewusst: Fleming’s discovery was an accident, because he had not tidied his laboratory before going on holiday.
Fleming was buried in St Paul’s Cathedral in London, a great honour in Great Britain.
Fleming sometimes painted small pictures by letting bacteria of different colours grow on culture plates.

teile.einleitung: Bacteria are tiny living things that can only be seen with a microscope. They consist of a single cell and live almost everywhere on Earth, including in and on our bodies. Some make us ill, but most are harmless or even very useful.
wichtigste: Bacteria are single-celled living things without a true cell nucleus.
Most are only about a thousandth of a millimetre in size.
They are found in the soil, in water, in the air and in living things.
They multiply by dividing into two cells.
Some bacteria cause diseases such as tonsillitis or tuberculosis.
Many bacteria are useful, for example in making yoghurt and cheese.
Medicines called antibiotics help against bacteria that cause illness.

abschnitte.text: A bacterium is usually only about one **micrometre** in size, that is, a thousandth of a millimetre. A thousand bacteria side by side would only be one millimetre long. Bacteria are **single-celled organisms**; their whole body consists of one cell. Unlike animal and plant cells, they have no true cell nucleus. Their genetic information floats freely in the cell.

By their shape, people distinguish round **cocci**, rod-shaped bacteria and spiral-shaped spirilla. Some have flagella, small threads with which they move along. Bacteria multiply by **cell division**: one cell becomes two. Under good conditions some species divide about every 20 minutes. In this way millions arise from one bacterium in a few hours.

Around 1676 the Dutchman **Antonie van Leeuwenhoek** was one of the first people to see bacteria through a microscope he had built himself. He called them “little animals”. In the 19th century Louis Pasteur and Robert Koch showed that bacteria can cause diseases. In 1882 Robert Koch discovered the pathogen that causes tuberculosis. In 1928 Alexander Fleming found penicillin, the first antibiotic.

**Lactic acid bacteria** turn milk into yoghurt, quark and cheese. The holes in Emmental come from bacteria that produce gas as the cheese ripens. Sauerkraut is also made with the help of bacteria. In the soil, bacteria break down leaves and dead animals into humus. In sewage works they clean our waste water.

Trillions of bacteria live in our gut; they are called the **gut flora**. They help with digestion and protect against pathogens. Many bacteria also live on the skin and in the mouth. But some bacteria are dangerous, for example salmonella in food that has gone off. That is why washing your hands with soap is a simple and effective protection.

**Antibiotics** are medicines that kill bacteria or stop them from growing. They do not work against viruses, for example with flu. If antibiotics are taken too often or wrongly, bacteria can become insensitive to them. Such bacteria are called **resistant**. That is why you should only take antibiotics as instructed by the doctor.

begriffe.erklaerung: A living thing that consists of only one single cell.
A device that greatly magnifies very small things.
A medicine against bacteria that cause illness.
The many useful bacteria that live in our gut.

gewusst: About as many bacterial cells live in your body as your body’s own cells.
Some bacteria live in boiling hot springs or in permanent ice.

teile.einleitung: Bertrand Piccard is a Swiss adventurer, doctor and pioneer who was the first to travel round the Earth in a balloon without stopping. Later he also flew round the world in an aeroplane powered only by solar energy. He comes from a famous family of researchers and explorers.
wichtigste: Bertrand Piccard was born in Lausanne in 1958.
His father Jacques Piccard dived into the Mariana Trench in 1960, and his grandfather Auguste Piccard flew into the stratosphere in a balloon.
As a young man he went hang-gliding.
In 1999, with Brian Jones, he circled the Earth non-stop in the balloon Breitling Orbiter 3.
The journey took about 20 days and ended in Egypt.
In 2015 and 2016 he flew round the world in the solar aeroplane Solar Impulse 2.
He campaigns for clean technologies and climate protection.

abschnitte.text: Bertrand Piccard was born in **Lausanne** on 1 March 1958. He studied medicine and worked as a **psychiatrist**, that is, a doctor who helps people with mental health problems. Alongside this he became known as an adventurer and aviation pioneer. Today he gives talks all over the world and runs a foundation for environmentally friendly solutions.

In 1931 his grandfather **Auguste Piccard** was one of the first to rise into the stratosphere in a balloon, to a height of around 16 kilometres. In 1960 his father **Jacques Piccard**, together with Don Walsh, dived in the submersible Trieste to the deepest point of the Mariana Trench. Bertrand grew up with these stories and met famous astronauts at an early age. So the family explored the sky, the deep sea and the whole Earth.

As a young man Piccard was passionate about **hang-gliding**, in which you glide through the air hanging from a triangular wing. He was one of the pioneers of this sport and also performed aerobatic figures. He also flew over valleys and peaks in the Swiss Alps. In doing so he learnt a lot about wind, courage and concentration.

abschnitte.titel: Round the Earth in a balloon
abschnitte.text: On 1 March 1999 Piccard set off with the Briton **Brian Jones** in the balloon **Breitling Orbiter 3** from Château-d’Oex in the canton of Vaud. The two travelled in a small cabin eastwards round the Earth on the high-altitude winds. After about 20 days and more than 40,000 kilometres they landed in the desert in **Egypt** on 21 March. It was the first non-stop balloon flight round the world.

Together with the engineer **André Borschberg**, Piccard developed the aeroplane **Solar Impulse**, which flies only on solar energy. Thousands of solar cells on the huge wings charge batteries during the day so that it can also fly at night. With Solar Impulse 2 the two took turns flying round the Earth; the start and finish was Abu Dhabi, and the flight lasted from March 2015 to July 2016. In this way they showed what is possible with renewable energy.

After the round-the-world flight Piccard founded the **Solar Impulse Foundation**. It looked for 1000 solutions that protect the environment and are still economical, for example energy-saving machines or new building materials. Piccard wants to show that protecting the environment can also bring jobs and profit. He has received many awards in Switzerland and abroad for his achievements.

begriffe.erklaerung: A doctor who treats people with mental illnesses.
A layer of the atmosphere about 10 to 50 kilometres above the ground.
An air sport in which you glide through the air hanging from a triangular wing.
A component that turns sunlight into electricity.
A strong wind high up in the air that can carry balloons a long way.

gewusst: The cartoonist Hergé was inspired by Auguste Piccard to create the character Professor Calculus in the Tintin comics.
Solar Impulse 2 had a larger wingspan than a jumbo jet but weighed only about as much as a car.
The cabin of the balloon Breitling Orbiter 3 now hangs in a museum in Washington.

teile.einleitung: An atomic clock is the most accurate kind of clock there is. It measures time using the vibrations of atoms, which always happen at exactly the same speed. Without atomic clocks there would be no GPS, and the internet would not be so well synchronised either.
wichtigste: The second is defined using the element caesium-133.
Exactly 9,192,631,770 oscillations of the caesium radiation make one second.
Since 1967 the second has been defined by atoms instead of by the Earth’s movement.
Louis Essen built the first working caesium atomic clock in 1955.
Optical atomic clocks are even more accurate and could redefine the second in future.
Leap seconds adjust atomic time to the Earth’s rotation and are to be abolished by 2035 at the latest.
Radio-controlled clocks in Switzerland usually receive their time signal from the DCF77 transmitter near Frankfurt.

abschnitte.titel: How does an atomic clock work?
abschnitte.text: Every clock needs something that swings regularly; in a pendulum clock it is the pendulum. In an atomic clock it is the **atoms** of the element caesium, which absorb and give off radiation of a very particular frequency. This oscillation is exactly the same in all caesium-133 atoms. The clock counts the oscillations, and exactly **9,192,631,770** of them make one second.

In the past the second was based on the rotation of the Earth, that is, on the length of a day. But the Earth does not turn completely evenly; among other things, it is slightly slowed down by the tides. That is why since 1967 the **second** has been defined using caesium atoms. This made time independent of the Earth’s movement.

In 1955 the British physicist **Louis Essen** built the first working caesium atomic clock at the National Physical Laboratory in England. Today’s caesium fountain clocks lose or gain less than a second in millions of years. Even more accurate are **optical atomic clocks**, which work with atoms such as strontium and visible light. Because their frequency is much higher, they can divide time more finely, which is why they are candidates for a new definition of the second.

Every **GPS** satellite carries atomic clocks on board. A radio signal travels around 300 metres in one microsecond, that is, a millionth of a second. So even a tiny error in the clocks would throw the positioning out by many metres. Mobile phone networks, power grids and banks also need very precise time.

Many alarm clocks and wall clocks are **radio-controlled clocks**, which regularly correct their time by radio. In Switzerland they usually receive the signal from the long-wave transmitter **DCF77** in Mainflingen near Frankfurt. The Federal Institute of Metrology METAS in Bern-Wabern is responsible for Switzerland’s official time. It runs its own atomic clocks there, which are compared with clocks all over the world.

Because the Earth does not turn completely evenly, atomic time and solar time slowly drift apart. To make up for this, a **leap second** has been added to world time UTC now and then since 1972. For computers and networks, however, such extra seconds are a nuisance and can cause errors. That is why the General Conference on Weights and Measures decided in 2022 to abolish leap seconds by 2035 at the latest.

begriffe.erklaerung: A tiny particle from which all substances are built.
How often something repeats per second.
A soft, silvery-gold metal whose atoms are used for atomic clocks.
The time used worldwide, on which all time zones are based.
An extra second that is added so that the clock time matches the Earth’s rotation.

gewusst: Optical atomic clocks are so accurate that they can measure that time passes very slightly faster on a higher floor.
The clocks in GPS satellites have to be corrected because of Einstein’s theory of relativity, otherwise the positioning would soon be wrong.
The name DCF77 contains the number 77 because the transmitter broadcasts on a frequency of 77.5 kilohertz.

teile.einleitung: Euglena is a tiny green living thing made of just one single cell that lives in fresh water. Like a plant it can make food with sunlight, and at the same time it swims about like an animal with a flagellum. That makes it an exciting example of the fact that not all living things can simply be sorted into plants or animals.
wichtigste: Euglena is green and consists of only one cell.
It has a small red eyespot.
It swims with a long flagellum.
It likes to swim towards the light.
It has something of a plant and something of an animal.
It has an elongated shape.
When very many euglenas live in a pond, the water turns green.

abschnitte.text: Its scientific name is **Euglena**, and in German it is called the “little eye animal”. It is only about a twentieth of a millimetre long. That is why you can only see it under the **microscope**. Its cell is elongated and can change its shape; it stretches out and contracts again. Inside there are many green grains, the **chloroplasts**, which give euglena its colour.

At the front, euglena has a small red **eyespot**. Together with a light-sensitive area on the flagellum, it helps to tell where the light is coming from. With its long **flagellum**, a whip-like extension, it then swims straight towards the light. But it cannot really see; it only tells light from dark.

In the light, euglena makes its own food like a plant through **photosynthesis**. In the dark it can also take up dissolved nutrients from the water, similar to an animal. Because it swims and moves, people used to think it was an animal, hence its German name. Today it is classified neither as a plant nor as an animal, but in a separate group of single-celled organisms.

Euglenas live in **fresh water**, for example in pools, ponds, ditches and puddles. They feel especially at home in water with lots of nutrients, for example near farms. When there are very many of them, the whole water turns green; this is called an **algal bloom**. You can find them in almost every small body of water in Switzerland too.

Euglenas multiply by one cell dividing lengthwise into two cells. In this way huge numbers can arise in a short time. They are food for tiny water animals such as water fleas. In schools and research euglenas are popular because they make it easy to watch how a **single-celled organism** lives and moves.

begriffe.erklaerung: Living thing that consists of only one single cell.
Long, whip-like extension with which a cell moves along.
Making food from light, water and carbon dioxide.
Green body in cells in which photosynthesis takes place.

gewusst: If a euglena lives in the dark for a long time, it can lose its green colour and become colourless.
A euglena is so small that about twenty of them in a row fit into one millimetre.

teile.einleitung: The anomaly of water is a special property: water is densest at about 4 degrees Celsius and expands when it freezes. That is why ice is less dense than liquid water and floats on top. Almost all other substances behave exactly the other way round, which is why it is called an anomaly, that is, an exception.
wichtigste: Anomaly means a departure from the rule.
Most substances contract when they cool, but water only does so down to about 4 degrees Celsius.
At about 4 degrees Celsius water has its greatest density.
When it freezes, water expands by about nine per cent.
Ice floats because it is less dense than liquid water.
That is why lakes freeze from the top down, and fish survive at the bottom.
Freezing water can split rocks and make pipes burst.

abschnitte.text: Normally substances contract when they get colder and so become denser. Water only does this down to about **4 degrees Celsius**. If it cools further, it expands again. When it freezes, its volume even increases by about nine per cent. This exception is called the **anomaly of water**.

A water molecule consists of one oxygen atom and two hydrogen atoms. The molecules attract each other through so-called **hydrogen bonds**. In ice they arrange themselves in a fixed lattice with many six-sided gaps. As a result ice takes up more space than liquid water, in which the molecules can move closer together.

Because ice has a lower **density** than water, it floats on the surface. An ice cube in a glass sticks out of the water a little. With an **iceberg** in the sea, about nine tenths lies below the surface of the water. That is why you only see the tip of the iceberg, which can be dangerous for ships.

In winter a lake cools from the top. The heaviest water, at 4 degrees, sinks to the bottom, while colder water stays on top and freezes into a **layer of ice**. This layer protects the lake below like a lid against even more cold. So the water at the bottom of deep lakes stays at about 4 degrees, and fish and other animals can survive the winter.

When water freezes in cracks in rocks, it expands and can split stones; this is called **frost weathering**. In the Alps this causes rockfall and scree slopes. Roads also get cracks and potholes in winter. Water pipes and glass bottles in the freezer can burst when the water in them freezes.

In Switzerland large lakes only freeze over completely in very cold winters. Such a frozen lake is called a **“Seegfrörni”** in Swiss German. The last one on Lake Zurich was in the winter of 1963. At that time thousands of people walked across the lake. Because winters are getting warmer, this has become very rare today.

begriffe.erklaerung: A departure from the normal rule.
It says how much mass there is in a particular space.
A tiny particle made of several atoms joined together.
Freezing water expands in cracks and breaks rock apart.

gewusst: If ice were heavier than water, many lakes would freeze solid from the bottom up in winter.
When it freezes, one litre of water becomes about 1.09 litres of ice.

teile.einleitung: In biology, adaptation means that living things have features that make it easier for them to survive in their environment. A polar bear is perfectly built for the cold, a cactus for dryness. Such adaptations have arisen over many generations through evolution.
wichtigste: An adaptation is a feature that makes survival in a particular environment easier.
Thanks to its broad, hairy hind feet, the mountain hare hardly sinks into the snow.
Cacti have spines instead of large leaves so that less water evaporates.
The rock ptarmigan turns white in winter and is so camouflaged in the snow.
When a harmless hoverfly looks like a wasp, this is called mimicry.
According to Bergmann’s rule, related animals in cold regions are often larger.
According to Allen’s rule, mammals in cold regions have shorter ears and tails.

abschnitte.text: The individuals of a species are never quite the same; each has small differences. Those that fit their environment better are more likely to survive and have more offspring that inherit the feature. This process is called **natural selection**. Charles Darwin described it in 1859 in his famous book on the origin of species, and in this way **evolution** happens over many generations.

The **mountain hare** and the **rock ptarmigan** in the Swiss Alps turn white in winter and can hardly be seen in the snow. The mountain hare’s broad, thickly furred hind feet work like snowshoes. According to Bergmann’s rule, related animals in cold regions are often larger, because a large body loses less heat. Allen’s rule says that ears and tails are shorter there, as with the Arctic fox compared with the desert fox.

Instead of large leaves, cacti have **spines**, through which hardly any water evaporates. In their thick stems they store water for long dry periods. The dromedary carries a store of fat in its **hump**, which it can live on when there is little food. The fennec, a desert fox, has huge ears through which it gives off heat.

Many animals are camouflaged by their colour, for example bush crickets that look like leaves. Penguins have a black back and a white belly, so that from above they are hard to see against the dark water and from below against the bright sky. In **mimicry** a harmless animal imitates a dangerous one. So the hoverfly looks like a wasp, and birds prefer to leave it alone.

Plants are also adapted to their habitat. Alpine plants such as edelweiss have fine hairs that protect them from cold, wind and strong sunshine. Many mountain plants grow as flat **cushions** on the ground, where it is warmer and less windy. Water lilies have large floating leaves so that they get enough light in the water.

Adaptation still goes on today, often faster than you might think. Some insects, for example, become resistant to the poisons used to fight them. But if the environment changes too quickly, for example through **climate change**, many species cannot adapt in time. That is why protecting habitats is so important.

begriffe.erklaerung: The slow change of living things over many generations.
Living things that are better adapted are more likely to survive and pass on their features.
A harmless animal looks like a dangerous one to fool enemies.
An animal looks so like its surroundings that it can hardly be spotted.

gewusst: The Arctic fox has such small ears that they almost disappear in its thick winter coat.
In winter the rock ptarmigan even has feathered feet that work like snowshoes.
After rain some cacti can greatly increase their weight by storing water.

teile.einleitung: Astronomy is the science that studies stars, planets and space. Researchers in this field are called astronomers. They study how stars form, how far away galaxies are and whether there are planets around other stars.
wichtigste: Astronomy is one of humanity’s oldest sciences.
Astronomers study stars, planets, galaxies and the whole universe.
In 1609 Galileo Galilei was one of the first to point a telescope at the sky.
Nicolaus Copernicus realised that the Earth goes round the Sun.
Today space is observed with huge telescopes on mountains and in space.
In 1995 two Geneva astronomers discovered the first planet around a Sun-like star.
Astronomy is not the same as astrology, which draws up horoscopes.

abschnitte.text: The word **astronomy** comes from Greek and means roughly “law of the stars”. Astronomers observe heavenly bodies and try to understand how they work. These include planets, moons, stars, galaxies, comets and black holes. They combine observations with physics, mathematics and chemistry.

Thousands of years ago the Babylonians, Egyptians and Maya were already watching the sky and making calendars. For a long time people believed that the Earth stood at the centre of the world. In 1543 **Nicolaus Copernicus** described how the Earth and the other planets go round the Sun. In 1610 Galileo Galilei discovered four moons of Jupiter with his telescope, and later Isaac Newton explained the movement of the planets with gravity.

The most important tool is the **telescope**, which collects faint light and magnifies distant objects. Large observatories stand on high mountains or in deserts, for example the Very Large Telescope in Chile. Switzerland is a member of the European Southern Observatory ESO, which runs such telescopes. Space telescopes such as the **James Webb Space Telescope**, launched in 2021, see space without the disturbing atmosphere.

The distances in space are so great that they are measured in **light years**. A light year is the distance light travels in one year, about 9.5 trillion kilometres. The nearest star after the Sun, Proxima Centauri, is about 4.2 light years away. Our Milky Way is just one of many billions of galaxies in the universe.

In 1995 **Michel Mayor** and Didier Queloz of the Geneva Observatory discovered the first planet orbiting a Sun-like star. For this they received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2019. As early as 1933 the Swiss Fritz Zwicky suspected that there is invisible dark matter in space. In many Swiss towns there are public observatories where you can look through a telescope yourself.

The two words sound similar but mean something completely different. Astronomy is a **natural science** that checks its statements with observations and measurements. Astrology, on the other hand, claims that the position of the stars influences people’s lives, and draws up horoscopes. There is no scientific evidence for this.

begriffe.erklaerung: A device that collects light and shows distant things bigger and brighter.
The distance light travels in one year.
A huge collection of billions of stars, like our Milky Way.
A planet that orbits not our Sun but another star.

gewusst: When you look at the starry sky, you see the light of some stars as it was sent out hundreds of years ago.
So far researchers have discovered several thousand exoplanets.
Light pollution from street lamps makes it hard to see many stars in towns.

teile.einleitung: Albrecht von Haller was a doctor, naturalist and poet from Bern in the 18th century. He is regarded as the founder of experimental physiology and studied the plants of Switzerland. With his poem “Die Alpen” (The Alps) he made the mountain world famous all over Europe.
wichtigste: Albrecht von Haller was born in Bern in 1708 and lived in the 18th century.
He studied medicine in the Netherlands with the famous doctor Herman Boerhaave.
His poem “Die Alpen” praises the mountain world and the simple life of the mountain people.
From 1736 he taught medicine and natural history at the University of Göttingen.
He is regarded as the founder of experimental physiology.
He recognised that muscles are irritable and contract when stimulated.
He wrote a large work about the plants of Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: Albrecht von Haller was born in **Bern** in 1708. Even as a child he was considered a child prodigy who learnt many languages and wrote poems. He studied medicine in Tübingen and in Leiden in the Netherlands with **Herman Boerhaave**, one of the most famous doctors of his time. From 1736 he taught at the newly founded University of **Göttingen** in Germany. In 1753 he returned to Bern, where he died in 1777.

In 1729, after a journey through the Swiss mountains, Haller wrote the poem **“Die Alpen”** (The Alps). In it he describes the magnificent landscape and praises the simple, honest life of the mountain people. At that time many people still thought of the mountains as eerie and dangerous. Haller’s poem was translated into many languages and awakened **enthusiasm for the Alps** in Europe. It helped to bring many travellers to Switzerland later on.

Haller wanted to know exactly how the body works and did many **experiments** to find out. He showed that muscles contract when stimulated and called this property **irritability**. Nerves, on the other hand, pass on sensations. He summed up his findings in an eight-volume textbook on **physiology**. That is why he is regarded as the founder of experimental physiology.

Haller walked a great deal through Switzerland and collected plants. This led to a large work on the **flora** of Switzerland describing more than two thousand species. In Göttingen he founded a **botanical garden**. He also had a long-running argument with the Swede Carl Linnaeus about the best way to classify plants.

Haller wrote and read an incredible amount, including thousands of book reviews. He was a polymath, that is, a person who was at home in many subjects. In Bern he also served as an official and looked after, for example, the **salt works** at Roche in Vaud. Today a monument in front of the University of Bern and a street remind people of him. His picture was also on an earlier Swiss **500-franc note**.

begriffe.erklaerung: The science of how the body and its organs work.
A planned test used to check a question.
The ability of a muscle to react to a stimulus by contracting.
All the plant species that grow in a particular area.
A person who does research in and knows about very many fields of knowledge.

gewusst: As a child Haller is said to have written his own dictionaries and biographies of famous people.
Haller’s poem “Die Alpen” helped Switzerland become a popular place to travel to.
Linnaeus named the plant genus Halleria after him, even though the two argued fiercely.

teile.einleitung: Ada Lovelace was an English mathematician who lived in the 19th century. She is regarded as the first computer programmer in history, because she developed an algorithm for a calculating machine long before real computers existed. Even then she realised that such machines could do much more than just calculate.
wichtigste: Ada Lovelace lived in England from 1815 to 1852.
She was the daughter of the famous poet Lord Byron.
Her mother encouraged her interest in mathematics from an early age.
She worked with the inventor Charles Babbage.
In 1843 she published an algorithm for Babbage’s planned Analytical Engine.
This makes her regarded as the first programmer in history.
The programming language Ada was named after her.

abschnitte.text: Ada Lovelace was born in London on 10 December 1815 as Augusta Ada Byron. Her father was the poet **Lord Byron**, who left the family shortly after her birth. Her mother, Anne Isabella Milbanke, had her taught mathematics and science. Through her marriage she later became Countess of Lovelace, hence her well-known name.

In 1833, at the age of 17, Ada met the mathematician and inventor **Charles Babbage**. He showed her a calculating machine he had built. Later Babbage planned a much larger machine, the **Analytical Engine**, which was to be controlled with punched cards. Ada was thrilled by the idea and kept in touch with him for many years.

An Italian engineer had written an article about the Analytical Engine, which Ada translated into English. In 1843 she added her own notes, which were much longer than the article itself. In the last note she described step by step how the machine could calculate special numbers, the **Bernoulli numbers**. These exact instructions are regarded as the first computer program in history.

Ada realised that such a machine could work not only with numbers. She wrote that it could also handle other symbols and, for example, produce music, if these were translated into numbers. That is exactly what today’s computers do with pictures, texts and songs. However, the Analytical Engine was never completed.

Ada Lovelace died of cancer on 27 November 1852, aged only 36. For a long time her work was almost forgotten; it was only rediscovered in the 20th century. Around 1980 a programming language was named **Ada** after her. On Ada Lovelace Day in October, women in science and technology are celebrated around the world.

begriffe.erklaerung: Exact step-by-step instructions for solving a task.
An algorithm written down so that a machine can carry it out.
A card with holes that was used in the past to give machines instructions.
A mechanical calculating machine that Charles Babbage planned but never finished building.

gewusst: Ada Lovelace herself called her way of thinking “poetical science”.
Her notes from 1843 were about three times as long as the article she translated.

teile.einleitung: AlphaFold is a computer program using artificial intelligence that predicts the three-dimensional shape of proteins. It was developed by the company DeepMind, which belongs to Google. It solved one of the hardest problems in biology in a short time.
wichtigste: AlphaFold predicts the 3D structure of proteins from their amino acid sequence.
At the CASP competition in 2020, AlphaFold 2 reached an accuracy close to experimental methods.
In 2021 a freely available AlphaFold database went online.
Today this database contains more than 200 million predicted protein structures.
The pLDDT value shows how reliable the prediction is for each amino acid.
AlphaFold 3 can also predict complexes of proteins with DNA, RNA and small molecules.
In 2024 Demis Hassabis and John Jumper received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for it, together with David Baker.

abschnitte.text: **Proteins** are tiny machines in all living things, for example enzymes, hormones or antibodies. They consist of a long chain of building blocks, the **amino acids**. This chain folds into a very particular three-dimensional shape. Only this shape decides what a protein can do, similar to the way the shape of a key decides which lock it opens.

For a long time, protein shapes had to be worked out with elaborate experiments, for example with **X-ray crystallography**. This often takes months or years for a single protein. Since 1994 there has been the **CASP** competition, in which research groups compare their prediction programs. For decades, however, the computer results were often inaccurate.

AlphaFold is a **neural network** that was trained with tens of thousands of known protein structures. It compares the sequence of a protein with related sequences from other living things. Positions that have changed together usually lie close to each other in the folded protein. From such clues the program calculates the most likely shape.

A first version of AlphaFold took part in CASP in 2018 and was already the best. In 2020 AlphaFold 2 reached an accuracy for many proteins that came close to experiments. Many experts spoke of a breakthrough that largely solved a problem more than 50 years old. In 2024 **Demis Hassabis** and **John Jumper** received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for it, together with David Baker, who designs new proteins on the computer.

Together with the European Bioinformatics Institute, DeepMind put a freely available **database** online in 2021. Soon more than 200 million structures were published in it, almost all known proteins. Each prediction has a pLDDT value, which shows in colour how sure the program is. Researchers all over the world, including in Switzerland, use these data every day.

With AlphaFold researchers can understand more quickly how diseases arise and where medicines might act. The predictions also help with enzymes that are meant, for example, to break down plastic. AlphaFold 3 from 2024 also predicts how proteins interact with **DNA**, RNA and small molecules. Even so, experiments are still needed to check the predictions.

begriffe.erklaerung: A substance made of a folded chain of amino acids.
A small building block from which proteins are made.
The chain of a protein folds into a fixed three-dimensional shape.
Computer programs that learn from many examples and recognise patterns.
A number from 0 to 100 that shows how sure an AlphaFold prediction is.

gewusst: In the past researchers sometimes needed several years for a single protein structure; AlphaFold often manages it in minutes.
The database contains proteins from bacteria, plants, animals and humans.
CASP is a competition in which the correct answers are not known to the participants beforehand.

teile.einleitung: Alfred de Quervain was a Swiss geophysicist and meteorologist who researched the weather, earthquakes and the ice of Greenland. Because of his daring journeys to Greenland he is regarded as a pioneer of Swiss polar research. He was also very important for earthquake measurement and for research on the Jungfraujoch.
wichtigste: Alfred de Quervain was a geophysicist and meteorologist.
His most important place of work was in Zurich.
In 1909 he made his first research journey to Greenland.
There he used pilot balloons to study the winds at high altitude.
He is regarded as a pioneer of Swiss polar research.
Together with Auguste Piccard he developed a seismograph.
He played an important role for the Swiss Seismological Service.
He campaigned for an observatory on the Jungfraujoch.

abschnitte.text: Alfred de Quervain was born in Uebeschi in the canton of Bern in 1879 and died in Zurich in 1927. He studied natural sciences and became a **geophysicist** and **meteorologist**, that is, an expert on the Earth and the weather. His most important place of work was the then Central Meteorological Institute in **Zurich**, which later became MeteoSwiss. He also taught at the University of Zurich. He was a keen mountaineer and adventurer.

In 1909 de Quervain travelled to **Greenland** for the first time, to the west coast of the huge island. There he sent up **pilot balloons** and followed them with a measuring telescope. From their flight he calculated how strongly and in which direction the wind was blowing at high altitude. Such measurements above the ice were completely new at that time. He also climbed a little way up onto the ice sheet.

In 1912 de Quervain led a larger **Swiss Greenland Expedition**. A group of four men crossed the **ice sheet** from the west coast to the east coast. They pulled their sledges with dogs over hundreds of kilometres of ice and reached heights of more than 2000 metres. A second group stayed in the west and took measurements on the glaciers. The expedition made de Quervain famous and is regarded as the beginning of **Swiss polar research**.

Besides the weather, de Quervain also worked on **earthquakes**. In Zurich he helped to build up the Swiss **Seismological Service**, which records and analyses earthquakes. Together with the physicist **Auguste Piccard** he developed an especially sensitive **seismograph**. This device had a very heavy mass that made even the finest ground movements visible. Today the Swiss Seismological Service is based at ETH Zurich.

De Quervain realised how valuable measurements are high in the mountains, where the air is thin and clean. He urged the Swiss government to build an **observatory** on the **Jungfraujoch**. He did not live to see the research station open in 1931. Today the Sphinx Observatory stands there at around 3570 metres, where researchers from many countries study air, climate and radiation.

begriffe.erklaerung: A scientist who researches the weather and the air.
The science of the physical processes in and on the Earth, for example earthquakes.
A small balloon whose flight is followed to measure the wind high up.
A device that records shaking of the ground, for example during earthquakes.
A huge, thick layer of ice that covers almost a whole country, as in Greenland.

gewusst: De Quervain wrote a book about his crossing of Greenland that inspired many young people in Switzerland to go on polar journeys.
The research station on the Jungfraujoch is one of the highest in the world and can be reached by train.
His fellow researcher Auguste Piccard later became world-famous for flights into the stratosphere.

teile.einleitung: Alchemy was an old teaching that combined the study of nature, craft skills and mysterious ideas. Many alchemists dreamed of turning base metals into gold or finding a remedy for a long life. Even though they never managed it, they developed equipment and methods from which chemistry later arose.
wichtigste: Alchemy is a forerunner of today’s chemistry.
Many alchemists wanted to make gold from base metals.
They called the miracle substance they were looking for the “philosopher’s stone”.
An “elixir of life” was supposed to give a very long life.
The Arab scholar Jabir ibn Hayyan, called “Geber” in Europe, was a famous alchemist.
Alchemists used distillation, for example to get alcohol from wine.
Words such as “alcohol” and “alkali” come from Arabic.
Paracelsus from Einsiedeln said, in essence: “The dose makes the poison”.

abschnitte.text: **Alchemy** arose around 2000 years ago, probably in Alexandria in Egypt, and was practised until modern times. It combined experiments with metals and substances with philosophy, astronomy and religious ideas. Many alchemists believed that all things are made of the **four elements** earth, water, air and fire. That is why they thought it possible to turn one substance into another. Their writings were often full of symbols and riddles so that outsiders would not understand them.

abschnitte.titel: Gold and the elixir of life
abschnitte.text: The most famous goal was to turn base metals such as lead into **gold**. For this, people searched for the **philosopher’s stone**, a mysterious substance that was supposed to bring about this change. Another goal was the **elixir of life**, which was supposed to cure illnesses and give a very long life. Some princes paid alchemists because they hoped to become rich. Those who failed were sometimes punished as frauds.

In the Middle Ages alchemy flourished in the **Arab world**. The scholar **Jabir ibn Hayyan**, called “Geber” in Europe, described many substances and methods. Arab researchers improved equipment such as the still. This knowledge reached Europe via Spain and Italy. That is why many technical words such as “alcohol”, “alkali” and also the word “alchemy” itself come from Arabic.

Alchemists worked in **laboratories** with furnaces, glass flasks, crucibles and scales. In **distillation**, a liquid is heated, the vapour is collected and cooled down again. In this way, for example, alcohol was obtained from wine. Dissolving, melting, filtering and crystallising were also among their methods. In the process they discovered substances such as various acids and, in Hamburg in 1669, even the element **phosphorus**.

**Paracelsus** was born around 1493 near Einsiedeln in today’s canton of Schwyz and was a doctor and alchemist. He wanted to use alchemy not for gold but for **remedies**. The saying “The dose makes the poison” comes from him, in essence. By this he meant that almost any substance can be useful in small amounts and harmful in large amounts. Paracelsus taught in Basel for a while and is regarded as a pioneer of modern pharmacology.

In the 17th and 18th centuries researchers began to measure and weigh substances precisely instead of trusting in secret powers. The Englishman **Robert Boyle** criticised the teaching of the four elements. Isaac Newton also still spent a lot of time on alchemy. Little by little, modern **chemistry**, which works with elements and atoms, came into being. Today we know that gold cannot be made by chemical means.

begriffe.erklaerung: A person who practised alchemy in the past and wanted to transform substances.
A hoped-for miracle substance that was supposed to turn metals into gold.
A separation method in which a liquid is turned into vapour and the vapour is cooled down again.
A basic substance that cannot be broken down any further chemically.
A dreamed-of potion that was supposed to give a very long life.

gewusst: The alchemist Johann Friedrich Böttger was actually looking for gold and instead helped to invent European porcelain in Saxony.
Phosphorus was discovered in 1669 by an alchemist who was actually looking for the philosopher’s stone.
Today physicists can make tiny amounts of gold from other elements in particle accelerators, but it is much more expensive than real gold.

teile.einleitung: The 3Rs principle is a rule for research with animals. The three Rs stand for the English words replace, reduce and refine. The aim is for as few animals as possible to suffer as little as possible.
wichtigste: The 3Rs principle was set out in 1959 by William Russell and Rex Burch.
Replace means replacing animal experiments with other methods, for example tests on cell cultures.
Reduce means using fewer animals thanks to careful planning of experiments.
Refine means reducing the strain on the animals, for example with painkillers and better housing.
In Switzerland the cantonal veterinary office must approve every animal experiment.
The strain on the animals is divided into severity grades from 0 to 3.
The national competence centre for the 3Rs is called the Swiss 3R Competence Centre.

abschnitte.text: The zoologist **William Russell** and the microbiologist **Rex Burch** from Great Britain published a book on more humane experimental techniques in 1959. In it they described the three Rs for the first time. For a long time the idea received little attention. Today it is part of the laws and guidelines for animal experiments in many countries.

For the first R, researchers look for methods with no animals at all. Examples are **cell cultures**, that is, cells that grow in dishes in the laboratory. Computer models and small copies of organs made of cells, called organoids, can also help. Some skin tests for cosmetics are now carried out only on artificially grown skin.

The second R is about getting useful results with as few animals as possible. For this, researchers plan their experiments carefully and use **statistics** to work out how many animals are really needed. When data are shared with other research groups, experiments do not have to be done twice. Modern imaging also helps, because the same animal can be examined several times.

The third R requires that the animals suffer as little as possible. This includes **painkillers** and anaesthesia during procedures. Better housing with nesting material, hiding places and companions of the same species is also part of it. Researchers also decide in advance at what point an experiment will be stopped so that an animal does not suffer unnecessarily.

In Switzerland the **Animal Welfare Act** regulates animal experiments, and the cantonal veterinary office must approve every experiment. For stressful experiments it must weigh the knowledge to be gained against the strain on the animals; this is called **weighing of interests**. The strain is rated with a severity grade from 0 to 3, where 0 means no strain and 3 means severe strain. Mice are used most often.

The **Swiss 3R Competence Centre** was founded in 2018 and promotes new methods that replace, reduce or refine animal experiments. Universities, authorities, industry and animal welfare organisations take part in it. It supports research projects and offers courses for researchers. In this way the 3Rs principle should be put into practice even better in everyday laboratory work.

begriffe.erklaerung: A scientific experiment in which living animals are used.
Cells that grow outside a body in a dish in the laboratory.
A number from 0 to 3 that says how much an experiment strains an animal.
Comparing the benefit of something with its harm and then deciding.
The authority that looks after animal health and animal welfare.

gewusst: The abbreviation 3Rs sounds simple, but the idea behind it is more than 65 years old.
In Swiss experiments the mouse is by far the most common laboratory animal.
In Switzerland fish and birds also count as laboratory animals and are protected by law.

teile.einleitung: Andreas Vesalius was a 16th-century doctor who renewed the study of the structure of the human body. Instead of relying only on old books, he examined the body himself. His famous work “De humani corporis fabrica” was printed in Basel in 1543.
wichtigste: Andreas Vesalius was born in Brussels in 1514.
His great work on anatomy is called “De humani corporis fabrica”.
He corrected the teachings of the ancient doctor Galen on many points.
The old books contained mistakes because they were based on dissections of animals.
