In his lessons Vesalius did the dissecting himself instead of just reading aloud.
His work became famous for its large, accurate woodcuts.
A skeleton he prepared has been preserved in the Anatomical Museum in Basel.
He worked as personal physician to Emperor Charles V.

abschnitte.text: Andreas Vesalius was born in 1514 in **Brussels**, which then belonged to the Habsburg Netherlands. His family had long served the emperors as doctors and apothecaries. He studied in Leuven and Paris and became a professor in **Padua** in Italy at the age of only 23. Later he became **personal physician** to Emperor **Charles V** and then to his son Philip II of Spain. He died in 1564 on the Greek island of Zakynthos on his way back from a pilgrimage.

For more than a thousand years the writings of the Greek doctor **Galen** were regarded in Europe as beyond question. But Galen had mainly examined **animals** such as monkeys and pigs, because at that time it was not allowed to open up humans. That is why many of his descriptions did not fit humans. Vesalius found out, for example, that the human lower jaw consists of a single bone and not two. Altogether he corrected Galen on a great many points.

In the past, in **anatomy lessons**, the professor read aloud from a book while an assistant opened the body. Vesalius did the **dissection** himself and showed the students everything exactly. He only wanted to believe what he had seen with his own eyes. This attitude was an important step towards modern **medicine** based on observation.

In 1543 his main work **“De humani corporis fabrica”** appeared, which means “On the Fabric of the Human Body”. It has seven books on bones, muscles, blood vessels, nerves, organs and the brain. It became famous for its large, very accurate **woodcuts**, in which skeletons and muscle figures pose in front of landscapes. The work was printed in **Basel** by the printer Johannes Oporinus, because Basel was one of the best printing cities at that time.

While Vesalius was supervising the printing in Basel in 1543, he carried out a public dissection there. Afterwards he put the bones of the dead man together into a **skeleton** and gave it to the university. This skeleton can still be seen today in the **Anatomical Museum in Basel**. It is regarded as the oldest surviving anatomical specimen in the world. In this way Switzerland remembers one of the most important doctors in history.

begriffe.erklaerung: The study of the structure of the bodies of humans and animals.
Opening up and examining a dead body in order to study it.
A doctor who personally looks after the health of a ruler.
A picture carved into a block of wood and then printed onto paper.
A body part or living thing that has been preserved for teaching and research.

gewusst: Vesalius was only 28 years old when his “Fabrica” appeared.
The wooden blocks for the pictures in the “Fabrica” were carried over the Alps from Venice to Basel.
The woodblocks of the “Fabrica” survived for almost 400 years and were only destroyed in the Second World War.

teile.einleitung: AlphaGo is a computer program that plays the ancient board game Go. In 2016 in Seoul it beat the top South Korean player Lee Sedol 4 to 1 and surprised the whole world. It was developed by the company DeepMind using methods of artificial intelligence.
wichtigste: AlphaGo is a Go program by the company DeepMind.
The board game Go originally comes from China.
A normal Go board has 19 lines in each direction.
Go was considered much harder than chess for computers, because there are many more possible games.
In 2016 AlphaGo beat the South Korean Lee Sedol 4 to 1 in Seoul.
Move 37 in the second game amazed the experts.
In 2017 AlphaGo Zero learnt the game only by playing against itself.

abschnitte.text: **Go** is a board game from **China** that has been played for several thousand years. Two people take turns placing black and white stones on the crossing points of a board with 19 by 19 lines. The aim is to surround more territory than the opponent. Opposing stones that are completely surrounded are captured. Go is especially popular in China, Japan and South Korea.

A Go board has 361 points, and with each move there are a great many options. That is why there are unimaginably more possible **games** than in chess. A computer cannot possibly calculate them all. In addition, it is hard to judge who is ahead in a position. For a long time experts therefore believed that computers would only beat professionals in many decades’ time.

AlphaGo was developed by the London company **DeepMind**, which belongs to Google. It uses **neural networks**, which are roughly modelled on the brain. First it learnt from games played by humans. Then it played millions of games against itself and kept getting better. It combines a clever search for good moves with an assessment of the position.

In March 2016 AlphaGo played in **Seoul** against **Lee Sedol**, one of the best players in the world. Millions of people followed the five games. In the second game AlphaGo played the famous **move 37**, which professionals at first thought was a mistake but which turned out to be brilliant. AlphaGo won 4 to 1. Lee Sedol won the fourth game with a surprising move of his own.

In 2017 DeepMind presented **AlphaGo Zero**, which learnt only by playing against itself, without any human examples at all. It became even stronger than all earlier versions. Later the program AlphaZero learnt chess and shogi in a similar way. The methods behind AlphaGo later helped with **AlphaFold**, which predicts the shape of proteins. For this, DeepMind’s boss Demis Hassabis received a share of the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2024.

begriffe.erklaerung: Computer programs that solve tasks that would otherwise need human thinking.
A computer model made of many linked computing nodes that learns from examples.
An old Chinese board game with black and white stones in which you conquer territory.
A learning method in which a program plays countless games against itself.

gewusst: Before the match against Lee Sedol, AlphaGo had already beaten the European champion Fan Hui 5 to 0 in 2015.
Lee Sedol retired from professional Go in 2019 and named the strength of AI as one reason.
A documentary film called “AlphaGo” was made about the match in Seoul.

teile.einleitung: The ampere is the unit used to measure electric current. It says how much electric charge flows through a wire per second. It is named after the French physicist André-Marie Ampère.
wichtigste: The ampere is the unit of electric current, abbreviated A.
It is named after the physicist André-Marie Ampère.
In formulas, current is written with the letter I.
Current is measured with an ammeter.
One ampere times one second gives one coulomb, the unit of charge.
Since 2019 the ampere has been defined using the elementary charge.
A device on 230 volts with 2 amperes has a power of 460 watts.

abschnitte.text: The **ampere** is one of the seven **base units** in the International System of Units, like the metre or the second. It measures **electric current**, that is, how much electric charge flows through a conductor per second. You can imagine it like water in a pipe: the current corresponds to the amount of water flowing through per second. In formulas the letter **I** stands for current. With a current of 1 ampere, around 6 billion billion electrons flow past a point every second.

Voltage, current and resistance are connected by **Ohm’s law**: current equals voltage divided by resistance. So if 12 volts are applied to a resistance of 4 ohms, 3 amperes flow. You get the **power** in watts by multiplying voltage by current. A device on 230 volts that draws 2 amperes therefore has 460 watts. Amperes times seconds gives the charge in **coulombs**.

Depending on the model, a mobile phone charger supplies about 1 to 3 amperes. A kettle draws around 8 to 10 amperes from the socket. In Swiss homes the circuits are usually protected with **fuses** of 10 or 13 amperes. If more current flows, the fuse switches off so that the wires do not get too hot. A lightning bolt, on the other hand, reaches tens of thousands of amperes.

Current is measured with an **ammeter**. It is built into the circuit so that all the current has to flow through it. This is called a **series circuit**. Often a multimeter is used, which can measure voltage, current and resistance. For large currents there are also clamp meters, which you simply put around a cable.

**André-Marie Ampère** lived in France from 1775 to 1836. He discovered that two wires carrying current attract or repel each other and is regarded as one of the founders of electrodynamics. The ampere used to be defined by this force between two wires. Since 2019 it has been defined using the **elementary charge**, the smallest charge that occurs freely. This means it is based on an unchanging constant of nature.

begriffe.erklaerung: How much electric charge flows through a conductor per second.
The push that makes the current flow, measured in volts.
How strongly a material holds back the current, measured in ohms.
The unit of electric charge, one ampere times one second.
The smallest electric charge, carried by an electron or proton.

gewusst: Even a few hundredths of an ampere can be dangerous for people, which is why you never play with sockets.
Ampère never went to school and taught himself much from the great encyclopaedia in his father’s library.
The ampere is the only electrical unit among the seven base units.

teile.einleitung: The aeolipile is a hollow metal ball that turns by itself because of escaping steam. It was described almost 2000 years ago by the Greek engineer Hero of Alexandria. This makes it an early form of the steam turbine, long before there were steam engines.
wichtigste: The aeolipile is a ball that is turned by steam.
Hero of Alexandria described it in the 1st century AD.
It is regarded as an early form of the steam turbine.
It turns according to the principle of recoil.
Its name recalls Aeolus, the Greek god of the winds.
In ancient times it was probably used as an astonishing demonstration.
It shows how heat is turned into movement.

abschnitte.text: At the bottom there is a closed boiler with water, under which a fire burns. Two pipes lead up from the boiler and hold a **hollow ball** that can turn, as if on an axle. On the ball there are two small **outlet tubes**, bent so that they point in opposite directions. When the water boils, the steam flows through the pipes into the ball and hisses out of the tubes.

The steam shoots backwards out of the tubes and so pushes the ball forwards. You also know this **principle of recoil** from a balloon that whizzes off when you let go of it. Because the two tubes point in opposite directions, a **turning movement** results. In this way the ball can spin very fast.

**Hero** lived in the 1st century AD in Alexandria, a famous city of scholars in Egypt. He wrote books about mechanics, surveying and devices that work with air, water and steam. In them he also described automatic machines, for example temple doors that opened as if by magic. Even before him, the Roman architect Vitruvius mentioned similar steam balls.

The name comes from **Aeolus**, the Greek god of the winds, and the Latin word for ball. So the aeolipile was in a sense a wind ball. As far as we know today, in ancient times it was not used as a machine but as a **demonstration** that amazed the spectators. Why nobody built a useful machine from it is still an exciting question for historians.

The aeolipile shows on a small scale how **heat energy** is turned into movement. Only around 1600 years later were steam engines built that powered factories, locomotives and ships. In the 19th century the modern **steam turbine** was developed, which today produces electricity in many power stations. Rockets and the jet engines of aeroplanes also use the same principle of recoil.

begriffe.erklaerung: Machine in which steam turns a wheel, for example to produce electricity.
When something is pushed out backwards, the body moves forwards.
The time of the ancient Greeks and Romans around 2000 years ago and earlier.
One form of energy is turned into another, for example heat into movement.

gewusst: A lawn sprinkler that is turned by the water spraying out works on the same principle as the aeolipile.
In physics lessons the aeolipile is often rebuilt with simple materials to show the principle of recoil.

teile.einleitung: Algorithmic bias means that a computer program systematically treats certain groups of people unfairly. This often happens with artificial intelligence that learns from data containing old injustices. Because such programs now help decide on job applications, loans or face recognition, the subject is very important.
wichtigste: Algorithmic bias means systematically unfair results of an algorithm for certain groups.
A common cause is distorted or unbalanced training data.
The study “Gender Shades” showed that face analysis was most often wrong for women with dark skin.
A large online retailer stopped an AI tool because it put applications from women at a disadvantage.
The US system COMPAS was criticised in 2016 for unequal error rates.
Features such as the postcode can act as a stand-in for a person’s origin.
Bias is uncovered by checking the results separately for each group.

abschnitte.text: An **algorithm** is an exact sequence of steps by which a computer solves a task. Many modern programs learn their rules themselves from large numbers of examples; this is called **machine learning**. If such a program keeps giving worse results for certain groups, for example by gender, skin colour or age, this is called **algorithmic bias**. The program does not mean to be unfair; it simply takes over patterns from its data.

The most common cause is unbalanced **training data**. If a program sees almost only photos of light-skinned men, for example, it recognises other faces less well. Data from the past can also contain injustices that the program then carries on. Even if a feature such as origin is not in the data at all, other details such as the **postcode** can act as a stand-in. Sometimes the mistake lies in what the developers set as the goal.

In 2018 **Joy Buolamwini** and Timnit Gebru studied face analysis programs from large companies in the study **“Gender Shades”**. For light-skinned men they were almost always right, but for women with dark skin they were wrong much more often. A large online retailer dropped a tool for pre-selecting job applications because it rated applications from women lower. It had learnt from earlier hiring in which mainly men had been taken on.

In the USA the system **COMPAS** estimates whether offenders might commit crimes again. In 2016 journalists showed that its errors were unequally spread between black and white defendants. In forward-looking police work, called **predictive policing**, a dangerous loop can arise. If more checks are carried out in one neighbourhood, more offences are found there, and the program sends even more checks there. In this way the pattern reinforces itself.

abschnitte.titel: What can be done about it
abschnitte.text: It is important to check a program’s results **separately for each group**, for example by gender or age. More balanced data and diverse development teams also help. Independent experts can check programs in what are called **audits**. In 2024 the European Union passed a law on artificial intelligence with strict rules for risky uses. In Switzerland too there is discussion about how to protect people from discrimination by algorithms.

The results of computer programs are not automatically neutral or correct. When an app or an AI makes a decision, you may ask how it was reached. In Switzerland the **Data Protection Act** gives people the right, for certain automated decisions, to be informed and to ask for a review by a human. Thinking critically helps you spot mistakes made by machines.

begriffe.erklaerung: An exact sequence of steps by which a computer solves a task.
The examples from which a learning program works out its rules.
When people are treated unfairly because of a feature such as gender or origin.
Computer programs that solve tasks that would otherwise need human thinking.
An independent check of whether a system works fairly and correctly.

gewusst: Joy Buolamwini noticed the problem when a program only recognised her face after she had put on a white mask.
Translation programs also used to show bias, for example when they automatically chose male forms for jobs like “doctor” and female forms for “nurse”.
A program can even be unfair when everyone involved had only good intentions.

teile.einleitung: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek was a cloth merchant from the Netherlands who built tiny microscopes in his spare time. With them he was one of the first people to see bacteria and other microorganisms. He opened people’s eyes to a world that had been invisible until then.
wichtigste: Leeuwenhoek lived in the Netherlands about 350 years ago.
He was actually a cloth merchant and not a trained researcher.
He built his microscopes himself, each with only a single lens.
He was one of the first people to see bacteria.
He even found tiny living things in the plaque on the teeth in his own mouth.
He called the living things little animals.
He sent his reports to researchers in London.

abschnitte.text: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek was born in 1632 in the town of **Delft** in the Netherlands and died there in 1723. He was a **cloth merchant** and sold fabrics; later he also held a post with the town. He never went to university and spoke only Dutch. Even so, he became one of the most famous naturalists of his time.

Cloth merchants used magnifying glasses to check the quality of fabrics, and that is probably how Leeuwenhoek got his idea. He ground tiny **lenses** and used them to build more than 500 simple microscopes. Each had only a single lens, which sat between two small metal plates. His best instruments magnified more than 200 times and were therefore much stronger than other microscopes of his time.

Leeuwenhoek examined all sorts of things, for example rainwater, pond water, blood and plants. In doing so he discovered tiny living things that moved and called them **little animals**. He was one of the first to see single-celled organisms and **bacteria**, for example in the plaque from his own teeth. He also described red blood cells and fine muscle fibres.

Leeuwenhoek wrote down his observations in many letters and sent them to the **Royal Society** in London, a famous association of researchers. Altogether there were several hundred letters over about 50 years. At first some researchers did not believe him and had his claims checked. When others also saw the little animals, he was made a member in 1680.

Leeuwenhoek is regarded as one of the founders of **microbiology**, the science of microorganisms. Only around 200 years later did people understand that some bacteria cause diseases. Today we know that microbes live everywhere, in the soil, in water and in our bodies. Only a few of his own microscopes have survived, and they are considered valuable museum pieces.

begriffe.erklaerung: A device with which you can see very small things greatly enlarged.
A curved, see-through piece of glass that makes things look bigger.
Tiny living things made of only one cell, which can only be seen with a microscope.
The science that studies tiny living things such as bacteria.

gewusst: Leeuwenhoek’s microscopes were so small that you had to hold them right up to your eye.
He was born in the same year and in the same town as the famous painter Johannes Vermeer.
Leeuwenhoek kept secret how he made his especially good lenses.

teile.einleitung: Alexander Graham Bell was a Scottish-American inventor who is regarded as the inventor of the telephone. In 1876 he received a patent in the USA for a device that could transmit the human voice over a wire. Throughout his life he also worked for deaf people.
wichtigste: Alexander Graham Bell lived from 1847 to 1922.
He was born in Edinburgh in Scotland and later lived in Canada and the USA.
He is regarded as the inventor of the telephone.
In 1876 he received the patent for the telephone.
Other inventors such as Philipp Reis and Antonio Meucci also worked on similar devices.
Bell taught deaf children and adults.
The decibel, the unit for loudness, is named after him.

abschnitte.text: Alexander Graham Bell was born in **Edinburgh** on 3 March 1847. His father and grandfather worked on speech and pronunciation. His mother was hard of hearing, and his later wife Mabel was deaf too. In 1870 the family moved to Canada, and soon afterwards Bell went to Boston in the USA.

In Boston Bell worked as a teacher of **deaf** people. He taught them to speak with the help of a special phonetic alphabet developed by his father. In doing so he studied very closely how sound and speech are produced. Later he also supported Helen Keller, a deafblind young woman who became a famous writer.

Bell wanted to turn sound into electrical signals and send them over a wire. On 7 March 1876 he received the American **patent** for the telephone. A few days later the first understandable conversation took place with his assistant Thomas Watson in the next room. In 1877 he founded the Bell Telephone Company with partners.

At that time several inventors were working on the telephone at the same time. The German **Philipp Reis** had already shown a device that transmitted sounds in 1861 and called it a Telephon. The Italian Antonio Meucci had also developed a speaking device but could not afford the patent. On the same day as Bell, Elisha Gray also handed in an idea for a telephone at the patent office.

Bell also invented the **photophone**, which transmitted sounds using beams of light. He experimented with flying machines, kites and fast boats that skim over the water. Bell was one of the first presidents of the National Geographic Society. He died in Canada on 2 August 1922, and in his honour the telephones in North America fell silent for one minute.

The telephone changed the world, because people could talk to each other instantly over great distances. In Switzerland the first telephone network opened in Zurich in 1880. The landline telephone later became the mobile phone and the **smartphone**. The unit bel and the better-known decibel, used to measure loudness, are reminders of Bell.

begriffe.erklaerung: A legal right that decides who may use and sell an invention.
A person cannot hear anything or almost anything.
A unit used to measure how loud a sound is.
Vibrations in the air that we hear as tones and noises.

gewusst: Bell was only 29 years old when he received the patent for the telephone.
Bell suggested “Ahoy” as a greeting on the telephone, but “Hello” caught on instead.

teile.einleitung: The Argo programme is a worldwide network of measuring robots that drift through the oceans on their own, diving up and down as they go. Around 4000 of these floats measure the temperature and saltiness of the sea at the same time. Their data help us to understand the climate and the oceans better.
wichtigste: Argo floats are autonomous drifting buoys that dive up and down in the ocean.
Around 4000 floats are at work in the world’s oceans at the same time.
A typical float makes a measurement profile about every 10 days.
Standard floats measure down to around 2000 metres deep.
A float changes its depth by pumping oil into an outer bladder.
The CTD sensor measures conductivity, temperature and pressure.
The name recalls the ship of the Argonauts in the Greek legend.

abschnitte.text: Argo is an international programme for **ocean observation** in which many countries take part. The first measuring buoys were put out around the year 2000. Today around 4000 instruments drift, evenly spread out, in all the oceans. They are called **floats**.

A float is a tube about one to two metres long with measuring instruments and batteries. To dive, it pumps oil from an outer **bladder** into the inside, which makes its volume smaller and it sinks. When it pumps the oil back into the bladder, it becomes bigger, gets more buoyancy and rises. In this way it uses **Archimedes’ principle**, without any propeller at all.

Usually a float drifts with the current for about nine days at a depth of around 1000 metres. Then it sinks to about 2000 metres and afterwards slowly rises to the surface. On the way up it measures a **profile**, that is, values at many different depths. When it reaches the top, it sends the data by **satellite** to data centres and dives again.

The **CTD sensor** measures conductivity, temperature and pressure. The salt content is calculated from the conductivity, and the depth from the pressure. Newer **BGC-Argo floats** also measure oxygen, acidity and chlorophyll, a sign of algae. There are also deep-sea floats that can dive much deeper than 2000 metres.

The oceans store a large part of the extra heat that stays on Earth because of **climate change**. With Argo you can follow exactly how the sea is warming and how currents are changing. The data are freely available to everyone and are used in weather forecasts and climate models. The name Argo fits with the Jason satellites, which measure the height of the sea surface, because in the legend the hero Jason sailed on the ship **Argo**.

begriffe.erklaerung: Measuring buoy that drifts and dives in the sea on its own.
Measurements from the depths to the surface at one place.
How much salt is dissolved in seawater.
Device that detects, for example, temperature or pressure.

gewusst: An Argo float can work for several years and make more than a hundred dives.
Before Argo there were almost no measurements from many remote ocean areas, because hardly any ships go there.

teile.einleitung: A command is a clear instruction to a robot or computer telling it what to do. Machines do not think for themselves but carry out every command exactly as it is given. Anyone who puts several commands together in the right order is writing a program.
wichtigste: A command is an instruction telling a robot or computer what to do.
A robot also carries out a wrong command without thinking.
Commands are carried out one after the other, so the order is important.
On many learning robots the up arrow means drive forwards.
Two quarter turns to the right make a half turn.
Several commands that solve a task together are called a program.

abschnitte.text: A **command** is the smallest instruction that a robot or computer understands, for example “drive forwards” or “turn left”. Machines have no will of their own and do not understand vague wishes. They do exactly what the command says, even if it is wrong. So if a robot drives into the wall, the mistake was usually in the command and not with the robot.

Many learning robots know the commands forwards, backwards, turn left and turn right. A **quarter turn** is a turn of 90 degrees. If a robot is facing north and turns right a quarter turn twice, it then faces south. If it turns left once from north, it faces west. You have to put yourself in the robot’s place, because its left is not always our left.

A robot always carries out commands **one after the other**, one at a time. If it is on square 2, goes 3 squares forwards and then 1 square back, it ends up on square 4. If you swap commands such as “turn” and “drive”, it ends up in a completely different place. It is like baking a cake: baking first and then adding the eggs does not work.

In many Swiss schools children learn to program with small robots in the subject **Media and Computer Science**. With the Bee-Bot, a robot bee, you press arrow buttons on its back; the up arrow means drive forwards. The **Thymio** was developed partly at EPFL in Lausanne and can be programmed on a computer. With block languages such as Scratch, commands are also put together like puzzle pieces.

Several commands that solve a task together are called a **program**. Good programs use tricks, for example a **loop**, which repeats commands several times instead of writing them out many times. With conditions such as “if an obstacle comes, then stop”, the robot reacts to its surroundings. A mistake in a program is called a **bug**, and finding and fixing it is called debugging. The same principle is found in every app, every game and every washing machine.

begriffe.erklaerung: A single instruction that a robot or computer carries out.
A sequence of commands that together solve a task.
A part of a program that repeats commands several times.
A mistake in a program.
Exact step-by-step instructions for solving a task.

gewusst: A bug is an insect, and in 1947 a moth really was found in a computer, where it had caused a fault.
A computer can carry out billions of simple commands per second.
A recipe is also a kind of program made of commands in a fixed order.

teile.einleitung: Antibiotic resistance means that bacteria have become unaffected by antibiotics. Then these important medicines no longer work, and infections are hard to treat. Experts count this among the greatest health problems of our time.
wichtigste: Antibiotics work against bacteria, but not against viruses.
Unnecessary use encourages resistance, because sensitive bacteria die and resistant ones survive.
Bacteria can exchange resistance genes with each other via plasmids.
The enzyme beta-lactamase makes many bacteria resistant to penicillin.
MRSA stands for methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus.
Reserve antibiotics are only used when others fail because of resistance.
Switzerland is tackling the problem with the StAR strategy and monitoring it with ANRESIS.

abschnitte.text: Antibiotics are medicines that kill **bacteria** or stop them from growing. The first known antibiotic, **penicillin**, was discovered by chance by Alexander Fleming in 1928. Since the 1940s antibiotics have saved millions of lives, for example in pneumonia or blood poisoning. But they do not work against viruses, for example with flu or an ordinary cold.

Bacteria multiply very quickly, and in the process small changes in their genetic material happen by chance. Some of these changes protect a bacterium against an antibiotic. When the antibiotic is used, the sensitive bacteria die, but the resistant ones survive and multiply. In this way **resistance** spreads, similar to natural selection.

Many bacteria produce the enzyme **beta-lactamase**, which breaks down penicillin and similar drugs. Others simply pump the antibiotic back out of the cell. It is especially dangerous that bacteria can pass on resistance genes, often on small rings of genetic material called **plasmids**. This horizontal gene transfer even works between different kinds of bacteria.

A well-known example is **MRSA**, a methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus, which causes problems mainly in hospitals. When no normal drug works any more, **reserve antibiotics** are needed, which are used only sparingly. But against some germs hardly any medicine works now. According to a large study in the medical journal “The Lancet”, around 1.27 million people worldwide died directly from infections with resistant bacteria in 2019.

Since 2015 the Confederation has followed the **StAR** strategy, which looks at people, animals, farming and the environment together. This approach is called One Health, that is, a single health for all. The **ANRESIS** centre monitors across the country how common resistant bacteria are in hospitals and laboratories. Far fewer antibiotics are now used in animal farming than in the past.

You should only take antibiotics if a doctor prescribes them. You should take them exactly as agreed and not simply use leftovers yourself later. Leftover medicines belong back at the chemist’s, not down the drain. Regular **handwashing** and vaccinations help to prevent infections, so that fewer antibiotics are needed.

begriffe.erklaerung: A medicine that kills bacteria or stops them from growing.
The ability of bacteria to withstand a medicine.
A small ring of genetic material that bacteria can pass on to each other.
An emergency drug that is only used when other antibiotics fail.

gewusst: Alexander Fleming already warned in his Nobel Prize speech in 1945 that bacteria could become resistant to penicillin.
Resistant bacteria have even been found in soil samples that were frozen long before antibiotics were invented.
For decades only a few completely new groups of antibiotics have been discovered.

teile.einleitung: An algorithm is an exact set of instructions that describes step by step how to solve a task. You can compare it with a recipe or instructions for making something. Computers need algorithms for everything they do, from the calculator to the search engine.
wichtigste: An algorithm consists of steps in the right order.
A recipe or a set of craft instructions is also a kind of algorithm.
For a computer an algorithm has to be very exact, because a computer guesses nothing.
An algorithm is finished when the task is solved.
The word goes back to the scholar Al-Khwarizmi.
A computer program is an algorithm in a programming language.
Algorithms sort, search, calculate and find routes.

abschnitte.text: An algorithm is a set of **instructions** made of clear steps that are carried out in a fixed **order**. When brushing your teeth, for example, the toothpaste goes onto the brush first, and only then do you brush. A good algorithm is unambiguous, so that each step can only be understood in one way. It must also be finished after a limited number of steps, when the task is solved.

A **recipe** is a typical algorithm: weigh the ingredients, mix, bake. Craft instructions, directions for a route or the rules for solving a Rubik’s Cube are algorithms too. Many algorithms contain **conditions**, for example: if it is raining, take an umbrella. Others contain repetitions such as: stir until the mixture is smooth.

A person thinks along when instructions are vague, but a computer guesses nothing. That is why an algorithm for a computer has to be completely exact. It is written in a **programming language** such as Python or Scratch, and then it becomes a program. A small mistake in one step can make the whole program calculate wrongly.

More than 2000 years ago the Greek mathematician **Euclid** described an algorithm for finding the greatest common divisor of two numbers. Sorting algorithms put lists into the right order, for example names in alphabetical order. Sat navs use algorithms to calculate the shortest route from Zurich to Bern. Search engines and video platforms use algorithms to decide which results appear at the top.

The word algorithm comes from the name of the scholar **Al-Khwarizmi**, who lived in Baghdad around 820. His book about calculating with Indian numerals was translated into Latin, and his name became “algorismus”. In the 19th century the Englishwoman **Ada Lovelace** wrote an algorithm for a planned calculating machine. That is why she is regarded as one of the first programmers in the world.

Algorithms help to do tasks quickly, reliably and always in the same way. They control traffic lights, SBB timetables and washing machines. But some algorithms also decide which adverts or videos you see. That is why it is good to know that behind many screens there are rules that people have set.

begriffe.erklaerung: Exact step-by-step instructions for solving a task.
An algorithm written in a programming language for the computer.
A step that is only carried out if something is true, for example “if, then”.
A part of an algorithm that is repeated several times.
Putting things into a particular order, for example by size or alphabetically.

gewusst: Euclid’s algorithm is more than 2000 years old and is still used in computers today.
With the right algorithm you can always solve a scrambled Rubik’s Cube, no matter what it looks like.
Even the game “I packed my suitcase” follows a fixed rule that you could write down as an algorithm.

teile.einleitung: An adjuvant is an additive in a vaccine that strengthens the reaction of the immune system. The name comes from the Latin word adiuvare, which means “to help”. Thanks to adjuvants, many vaccines work better and need less active ingredient.
wichtigste: An adjuvant strengthens the immune response to the antigen of a vaccine.
The name comes from the Latin adiuvare, to help.
Aluminium salts have been used most often for around a hundred years.
Inactivated vaccines in particular often need an adjuvant.
The oily adjuvant MF59 contains the natural substance squalene.
Modern adjuvants such as AS01 specifically activate receptors of the innate immune system.
Local reactions such as redness at the injection site can be somewhat stronger.

abschnitte.text: A vaccine contains an **antigen**, that is, a feature of the pathogen that the body is meant to recognise. An **adjuvant** is a helper substance that makes sure the immune system reacts more strongly to it. It works like an alarm signal that makes the defences pay attention. It is not itself an active ingredient against a disease.

**Inactivated vaccines** contain only killed pathogens or individual parts of them. Because these do not multiply, they give the body fewer danger signals than live vaccines. An adjuvant makes up for this. As a result, less antigen per dose or fewer doses overall are often needed, which is important when vaccines are scarce.

The oldest and most common adjuvants are **aluminium salts**, which have been used since the 1920s. They hold the antigen at the injection site and attract immune cells. They are found, for example, in vaccines against tetanus, diphtheria and hepatitis B. The amounts are very small and are checked by expert authorities such as Swissmedic.

The adjuvant **MF59** is an oil-in-water emulsion with **squalene**, a natural substance that also occurs in the human body and used to be obtained mainly from shark liver. It is used in some flu vaccines for older people. Newer adjuvants such as AS01 specifically activate receptors of the innate immune system. AS01 is found, for example, in a vaccine against shingles.

With vaccines containing an adjuvant, local reactions such as **redness**, swelling and pain at the injection site are often somewhat stronger. Tiredness or a slight fever for one or two days can also occur. These reactions show that the immune system is working, and they usually pass quickly. Every vaccine is tested for effectiveness and safety in large studies before it is approved.

begriffe.erklaerung: Helper substance that strengthens the effect of a vaccine.
Feature of a pathogen against which the body builds up protection.
Vaccine containing killed pathogens or parts of pathogens.
Oily natural substance found in some adjuvants.

gewusst: The strengthening effect of aluminium salts was discovered more or less by chance in the 1920s.
One ingredient of modern adjuvants comes from the bark of the South American soapbark tree.
In German the plural of Adjuvans is Adjuvanzien; in English it is simply adjuvants.

teile.einleitung: Auguste Piccard was a Swiss physicist and inventor from Basel. In 1931 he was the first person to rise into the stratosphere in a balloon, that is, to more than 15 kilometres high. Later he built submersibles for the deep sea.
wichtigste: Auguste Piccard was born in Basel in 1884 and died in Lausanne in 1962.
In 1931 he was the first person to rise into the stratosphere in a balloon.
For this he invented an airtight aluminium capsule with pressure equalisation.
In 1932 he set off from Dübendorf near Zurich on a second, even higher flight.
After that he developed the bathyscaphe, a submersible for great ocean depths.
His son Jacques and his grandson Bertrand also became famous adventurers.
Piccard is regarded as the model for the comic character Professor Calculus in “The Adventures of Tintin”.

abschnitte.text: **Auguste Piccard** was born in Basel on 28 January 1884. He had a twin brother, Jean Piccard, who also became a scientist. Auguste studied mechanical engineering and physics at **ETH Zurich**. From 1922 he was professor of physics at the university in Brussels. He was very tall, had wild hair and round glasses.

Piccard wanted to study **cosmic rays** at high altitude. For this he developed a ball-shaped, airtight **pressurised cabin** made of aluminium. On 27 May 1931 he set off from Augsburg with his assistant Paul Kipfer in the balloon FNRS. The two reached almost 16 kilometres and landed in the evening on a glacier in Tyrol. In 1932, starting from Dübendorf with Max Cosyns, he even reached more than 16 kilometres.

The **stratosphere** is a layer of the Earth’s atmosphere. Depending on the place, it begins at a height of about 8 to 17 kilometres. There the air is very thin and freezing cold, and a person cannot breathe without protection. That is why Piccard’s closed cabin was so important. Today’s airliners with pressurised cabins use the same idea.

After his high-altitude flights Piccard turned to the sea. He invented the **bathyscaphe**, a submersible that works like a balloon under water. A large float full of petrol provides buoyancy, and a steel sphere protects the people inside. In 1953 he and his son Jacques dived more than 3000 metres deep in the submersible Trieste. Later, in 1960, Jacques Piccard reached the deepest point of the oceans in the Mariana Trench with the Trieste.

The Piccards are a famous Swiss family of researchers. His son **Jacques Piccard** dived almost 11 kilometres deep together with Don Walsh in 1960. His grandson **Bertrand Piccard** and Brian Jones were the first to fly round the Earth in a balloon without stopping, in 1999. From 2015 to 2016 Bertrand flew round the world with André Borschberg in the solar aeroplane Solar Impulse 2. So the family reaches from the sky to the bottom of the sea.

begriffe.erklaerung: A layer of the atmosphere from about 10 kilometres high, with very thin, cold air.
An airtight room in which the air pressure stays comfortable for people.
A submersible invented by Piccard for very great ocean depths.
High-energy particles that hit the Earth from space.

gewusst: The cartoonist Hergé used Auguste Piccard as the model for the absent-minded Professor Calculus.
On his first stratosphere flight Piccard did not land as planned but on a glacier in the Ötztal Alps.

teile.einleitung: Alfred Wegener was a German meteorologist and polar explorer. He became famous for the idea that the continents slowly move across the Earth. Many people laughed at it at the time, but today we know that he was basically right.
wichtigste: Alfred Wegener was born in Berlin in 1880.
He was mainly a meteorologist, that is, a weather and climate researcher.
His best-known idea is the theory of continental drift.
He first travelled to Greenland with the Danish Danmark Expedition.
In 1912 and 1913 he crossed the Greenland ice sheet with Johan Peter Koch.
In 1930 he died on an expedition on the ice sheet, together with Rasmus Villumsen.
The Alfred Wegener Institute in Bremerhaven bears his name.

abschnitte.text: Alfred Wegener was born in **Berlin** on 1 November 1880. He studied natural sciences and was especially interested in weather and air. In 1906 he and his brother Kurt set a record in a balloon when they stayed in the air for more than 52 hours. His father-in-law was the famous climate researcher **Wladimir Köppen**, with whom he also wrote books.

Wegener noticed that the coasts of South America and Africa fit together like pieces of a jigsaw puzzle. He also found the same rocks and fossils on continents that are now far apart. In 1912 he presented his theory of **continental drift**, and his book about it came out in 1915. He thought that all the continents once formed one original supercontinent, which is now called **Pangaea**.

Most geologists rejected Wegener’s idea. Their main objection was that he could not explain what force moves the huge continents. Only in the 1960s did researchers find evidence of the movement on the seabed. From this came the theory of **plate tectonics**, which is now part of basic knowledge.

From 1906 to 1908 Wegener took part in the Danish **Danmark Expedition** and studied weather and ice in north-east Greenland. On another expedition in 1912 and 1913 he crossed the ice sheet with the Danish officer Johan Peter Koch. They spent the winter on the ice, which hardly anyone had dared to do before. From 1924 Wegener was a professor in Graz in Austria.

In 1930 Wegener led a large German expedition to Greenland. In the middle of the ice sheet the research station **Eismitte** (Mid-Ice) was set up to measure the weather there through a whole winter. In autumn Wegener brought supplies there by dog sledge and then set off back in severe cold. He and his Greenlandic companion **Rasmus Villumsen** died on the way; Wegener’s body was only found in the spring of 1931.

Today Wegener is regarded as one of the most important pioneers of the earth sciences. The **Alfred Wegener Institute** in Bremerhaven researches the polar regions and the oceans. A crater on the Moon and one on Mars are also named after him. His story shows that correct ideas sometimes take a long time to be accepted.

begriffe.erklaerung: The science of the weather and of the Earth’s atmosphere.
The idea that the continents move very slowly across the Earth.
A huge original supercontinent in which almost all the land masses were once joined.
A thick layer of ice that covers a whole country almost completely.
The modern theory that the Earth’s crust consists of moving plates.

gewusst: Wegener’s balloon flight with his brother lasted more than 52 hours and was a world record at the time.
Today the continents move about as fast as fingernails grow, that is, a few centimetres a year.
Wegener’s grave still lies in the Greenland ice sheet and disappeared deep under the snow long ago.

teile.einleitung: The Antarctic Treaty is an international agreement that sets out how countries may deal with Antarctica. It was signed in Washington in 1959 and makes the icy continent a place for peace and research. Military activity, nuclear tests and mining for mineral resources are banned there.
wichtigste: The Antarctic Treaty was signed in Washington in 1959 by 12 countries.
It came into force in 1961 and applies to the area south of 60 degrees south latitude.
Antarctica may only be used peacefully, above all for science.
Nuclear explosions and storing nuclear waste are expressly banned.
The territorial claims of individual countries were frozen.
The Environmental Protocol of 1991 bans mining for mineral resources.
Today more than 50 countries take part in the treaty, including Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: **Antarctica** is the continent around the South Pole and is almost completely covered by ice. No people live there permanently, only researchers at stations. In the 20th century seven countries claimed parts of it: Argentina, Australia, Chile, France, Great Britain, New Zealand and Norway. Some of these claims overlapped, which led to disputes. At the same time there was growing fear that Antarctica could become the scene of military conflicts during the **Cold War**.

After the International Geophysical Year of 1957 to 1958, in which many countries did research together in Antarctica, people wanted to secure this cooperation. So on 1 December 1959, 12 countries signed the Antarctic Treaty in **Washington**. They included the USA and the Soviet Union, which otherwise faced each other as enemies. The treaty came into force in 1961. It applies to all land and ice south of 60 degrees south latitude.

Antarctica may only be used for **peaceful purposes**; military bases and weapons tests are banned. Nuclear explosions and storing radioactive waste are expressly forbidden. All countries may do research freely and should share their results. The existing **territorial claims** were frozen, which means they count neither as recognised nor as given up. No new claims may be made, and observers may inspect all stations at any time.

In 1991 an additional agreement to protect the environment, the **Environmental Protocol**, was adopted in Madrid. It declares Antarctica a nature reserve devoted to peace and science. Since then, mining for mineral resources such as oil, coal or metals has been banned. Waste has to be taken away again, and animals such as penguins and seals must not be disturbed. Since then dogs may no longer be brought to Antarctica either.

Today many countries run research stations in Antarctica, for example the USA with the Amundsen-Scott Station right at the South Pole. Researchers there study the **climate**, the ice, the animals and the night sky. Cores drilled from the ice contain trapped air that is hundreds of thousands of years old. From this they can read how the Earth’s climate changed in the past. Switzerland has no station of its own, but Swiss researchers take part in international projects.

begriffe.erklaerung: The icy continent around the South Pole.
A country’s demand that a particular area belongs to it.
Here, an additional agreement that adds to an existing treaty.
Valuable raw materials in the ground such as oil, coal or metals.

gewusst: The Antarctic Treaty was one of the first arms control agreements during the Cold War.
Antarctica is the coldest, driest and windiest continent on Earth.
The Environmental Protocol can be reviewed in 2048 at the earliest, and even then changes need broad agreement.

teile.einleitung: Ardipithecus is a genus of early hominins that lived in East Africa about 5.8 to 4.4 million years ago. The partial skeleton “Ardi”, found in Ethiopia, is famous and reveals a lot about our early ancestors. Ardipithecus could probably both walk upright and climb trees well.
wichtigste: The partial skeleton Ardi of the species Ardipithecus ramidus is around 4.4 million years old.
The fossils were found in Ethiopia.
The research team was led by the US palaeoanthropologist Tim White.
The detailed description of Ardi appeared in 2009.
A big toe that could be spread out points to climbing in trees.
The older species Ardipithecus kadabba is around 5.8 to 5.2 million years old.
The name Ardipithecus means roughly ground ape.

abschnitte.text: Ardipithecus is one of the **early hominins**, that is, early relatives of modern humans. Two species are known, the older **Ardipithecus kadabba** and the younger **Ardipithecus ramidus**. They lived long before the famous Lucy, who is around 3.2 million years old. The name is made up of a word from the Afar language for ground and the Greek word for ape.

The fossils were discovered from the 1990s onwards in the **Afar region** in north-east Ethiopia, in the area of the River Awash. An international team led by **Tim White** dug there for years and found more than a hundred pieces of bone. The most important find is the partial skeleton Ardi, a female. Because the bones were very fragile and crushed, the analysis took around 15 years until publication in 2009.

Ardi was about 1.2 metres tall, and her brain was about as big as a chimpanzee’s. Her pelvis suggests that she could walk **upright on two legs** on the ground. At the same time she had a **big toe that could be spread out**, with which she could hold on to branches like with a hand. Her long arms and hands were also well suited to climbing.

Remains of plants and animals such as monkeys, antelopes and birds were found together with Ardi. They show that Ardipithecus ramidus probably lived in a **wooded area** and not in open savannah. The teeth suggest that it ate fruit, leaves and other plant parts, perhaps also small animals. The canine teeth were small, smaller than in today’s chimpanzees.

Ardi showed that our ancestors did not simply look like chimpanzees. People used to think that **walking upright** only developed in the open savannah. But Ardipithecus lived in the forest and still partly walked on two legs. Experts are still discussing how closely Ardipithecus is related to humans.

begriffe.erklaerung: Petrified remains or traces of living things from earlier times.
Early relatives of humans who lived millions of years ago.
Researcher who studies the development of humans using fossils.
Walking on two legs with an upright body.

gewusst: Ardi is more than a million years older than the famous skeleton Lucy.
The word ramid in Ardipithecus ramidus comes from the Afar language and means root.

teile.einleitung: Alfred Russel Wallace was a British naturalist who discovered evolution by natural selection at almost the same time as Charles Darwin. He travelled for years through South America and South-East Asia and collected tens of thousands of animals there. The Wallace Line, an invisible boundary between the Asian and Australian animal worlds, is named after him.
wichtigste: Alfred Russel Wallace came from Great Britain and lived from 1823 to 1913.
He discovered natural selection independently of Darwin.
In 1858 the ideas of Darwin and Wallace were presented together in London.
His collection from South America burned with the ship on the way home in 1852.
For years he collected animals in the Malay Archipelago.
The Wallace Line separates the Asian and Australian animal worlds.
Among other places, it runs between the islands of Bali and Lombok.
Wallace is often regarded as the founder of biogeography.

abschnitte.text: Alfred Russel Wallace was born in Wales in 1823 and grew up in modest circumstances. He first worked as a **land surveyor** and teacher and taught himself natural history. He was especially interested in beetles and butterflies. Later he earned his money by collecting animals and selling them to museums and collectors. He died in England in 1913 at the great age of 90.

In 1848 Wallace travelled with his friend Henry Walter Bates to the **Amazon** in South America. For four years he collected animals and plants there. On the journey home in 1852 the ship caught **fire** in the middle of the Atlantic and sank. Almost his whole collection burned, and Wallace drifted for days in a lifeboat until another ship rescued him. Even so, he did not give up.

From 1854 to 1862 Wallace explored the **Malay Archipelago**, that is, the world of islands between Malaysia, Indonesia and New Guinea. He collected well over a hundred thousand animals there, mainly insects, but also birds such as **birds of paradise**. Many of them were still unknown to science. He described his travels in the book “The Malay Archipelago”, which became very popular.

During a bout of fever in the Malay Archipelago in 1858, Wallace had a big idea. He realised that the animals that are best adapted to their environment are more likely to survive and have offspring. This principle is called **natural selection**. He sent his essay to **Charles Darwin**, who had long been researching the same idea. On 1 July 1858 the work of both researchers was presented together at the Linnean Society in **London**.

Wallace noticed that the animal life on neighbouring islands can be very different. On **Bali** mainly Asian animals live, but on nearby **Lombok** there are already many animals with Australian relatives, such as cockatoos. The boundary between them is now called the **Wallace Line**. It runs through deep sea channels that never dried out even during the Ice Ages. Because Wallace researched why animals live where they do, he is regarded as the founder of **biogeography**.

begriffe.erklaerung: Living things that are better adapted to their environment are more likely to survive and pass on their features.
The slow change of living things over many generations.
The science of which animals and plants live where on Earth and why.
A group of many islands lying close together.
An imaginary boundary in South-East Asia between the Asian and Australian animal worlds.

gewusst: Darwin was so alarmed by Wallace’s letter that he quickly finished writing his famous book on the origin of species.
A frog that can glide through the air on large webbed feet is named after him: Wallace’s flying frog.
The sea channel between Bali and Lombok is only about 35 kilometres wide, but it separates two animal worlds.

teile.einleitung: Attention is the ability to concentrate on something particular and block out other things. Every second our brain receives far more impressions than it can process, so it chooses. How well we can pay attention depends on sleep, breaks, our surroundings and even on drinking.
wichtigste: Paying attention means concentrating on something.
A mobile phone that keeps beeping is especially disturbing during homework.
A short break with some movement helps you concentrate again.
Anyone who does two tasks at once usually makes more mistakes.
Anyone who looks at their phone while crossing the road does not notice cars.
You often hear your own name straight away even in a noisy room.
Drinking enough water helps the brain to stay attentive.

abschnitte.text: **Attention** is like a spotlight in your head that shines on what is important. Eyes, ears and skin constantly deliver a great many impressions, but only a small part is consciously noticed. The brain filters what is important at the moment and blocks out the rest. This selection is called **selective attention**.

In a well-known experiment people were asked to count how often players in a film passed a ball to each other. Many of them missed a person in a **gorilla costume** walking right through the picture. This shows that we can overlook things even though they are right in front of us. On the other hand, at a noisy party you often hear your own name straight away; this is called the **cocktail party effect**.

The brain cannot really concentrate on two difficult tasks at the same time. With so-called **multitasking** it jumps quickly back and forth, so you make more mistakes and take longer. A phone that keeps beeping pulls you out of your work again and again. In **traffic** distraction is dangerous, because anyone looking at their phone does not notice approaching cars or bikes.

A quiet place helps with homework, and the phone is best left in another room. After working for a while, a **short break** with some movement does you good, for example a few star jumps or a walk to the window. Enough **sleep**, regular meals and drinking water also help the brain. It is best to split big tasks into small steps.

Attention has been studied in psychology and brain research for more than a hundred years. Experts distinguish, for example, between concentrating on one thing for a long time and switching quickly between tasks. Some people find it harder to stay attentive, for example people with **ADHD**. With understanding, good support and suitable strategies, they too can learn well.

abschnitte.text: A fully grown ostrich can be more than 2.5 metres tall and weigh well over 100 kilograms. The males have black plumage with white wing and tail feathers; the females are greyish brown. The neck and legs are long and almost bare. The ostrich is the only bird with just **two toes** on each foot, one of them with a strong claw. Its **eyes**, about 5 centimetres across, are the largest of all land animals and bigger than its brain.

In the wild the common ostrich lives only in **Africa**. It is found in **savannahs**, semi-deserts and open grasslands, for example in Kenya, Tanzania, Namibia and South Africa. It used to live in North Africa and the Middle East as well, but it was wiped out in many places there. It can go a long time without drinking, because it takes in a lot of water from plants. Ostriches often roam together with zebras and antelopes.

Ostriches mainly eat plants such as grasses, seeds, leaves and flowers. Sometimes they also snap up insects or small animals such as lizards. Because they have no teeth, they swallow **small stones**. These help to grind up the tough food in the stomach. An ostrich can have up to about one kilogram of such stones in its stomach.

With its long, muscular legs the ostrich reaches about **70 km/h**, making it the fastest bird on foot. A single stride at full speed can be several metres long. If it cannot flee, it defends itself with **kicks** that can even injure a lion. It does not bury its head in the sand when in danger. The myth probably arose because ostriches lie flat on the ground when in danger and because they turn the eggs in the nest with their beaks.

The nest is a shallow hollow in the sand. An ostrich egg is about 15 centimetres long and weighs around 1.5 kilograms, about as much as two dozen hens’ eggs. The shell is so thick and hard that a person can stand on it. During the day it is usually the females that sit on the eggs, at night the males. The parents regularly **turn** the eggs with their beaks.

Thousands of years ago people in Africa already used empty ostrich eggshells as water containers. In the 19th and early 20th centuries **ostrich feathers** were so popular as hat decorations that huge ostrich farms were set up in South Africa. Today ostriches are kept in many countries for meat, leather and feathers, including on a few farms in Switzerland. In the wild the common ostrich is not considered endangered, but some subspecies have become rare.
